mcqs.q: How many neutrons are present in 59/27 Co?
mcqs.why: Formula: Number of neutrons = mass number A - atomic number Z. Substitution: Neutrons = 59 - 27 = 32. Cobalt-59 also has 27 protons and, as a neutral atom, 27 electrons.

mcqs.q: How many electrons can the s, p, d and f sub-shells hold at maximum?
mcqs.why: A shell is divided into sub-shells s, p, d and f, spectroscopic terms for sharp, principal, diffused and fundamental. Their maximum capacities are s 2, p 6, d 10 and f 14 electrons respectively.

mcqs.q: What is the electronic distribution of beryllium (Z = 4) in energy levels and sub-shells?
mcqs.why: Beryllium has 4 electrons. Two fill the K level in sub-shell 1s, and the next two go into the L level in sub-shell 2s, because electrons fill the lowest energy sub-shell first. So its configuration is 1s2 2s2, arrangement K = 2, L = 2.

lessons.title: Project Work
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • A radioactive tracer is a radioactive isotope given to a patient whose movement through the body is followed with a detector.
  • Iodine-131 concentrates in the thyroid gland and is used as a cure for goitre; Iodine-123 is used for brain imaging.
  • Cobalt-60 and radium irradiation are used in the treatment of cancer and the diagnosis of tumors.
  • Sodium-24 is used to identify blood circulation problems, and Carbon-14 traces the path of carbon in photosynthesis.
  • Rutherford model: a small heavy positive nucleus with electrons revolving around it; Bohr model: electrons only in fixed shells of fixed energy.

Solved Exercises

Exercise — Project Work

Q: Project Work: The study of atomic structure and the nucleus produced a new field of medicine called nuclear medicine. Describe the use of radioactive tracers to detect and treat diseases.

Ans: A radioactive tracer is a radioactive isotope given to a patient (by injection or by mouth) whose movement through the body can be followed with a detector, because it emits radiations; the isotope concentrates in the organ being studied, so doctors can detect a defect and also treat disease. Uses given in this unit: Iodine-131 becomes concentrated in the thyroid gland and is used as a cure for goitre; Iodine-123 (123/53 I) is used for brain imaging; Deuterium (D), heavy Carbon (C-13), heavy Nitrogen (N-15), heavy Oxygen (O-18) and heavy Iodine-131 are used as tracer elements in biochemical and physio-chemical research to trace the path of an element; Radium irradiation and Cobalt-60 (60/27 Co) are used in the treatment of cancer and for the diagnosis of tumors; Sodium (Na-24) is used for the identification of blood circulation problems in patients; and Carbon-14 is used to trace the path of carbon in photosynthesis. A project report should name the isotope, the organ or process it traces, and whether it is used for detection (diagnosis) or for treatment.

Q: Project Work: In groups of 5 to 8 students, make and present different models based on Rutherford and Bohr's atomic theories.

Ans: For the group presentation, make two models and present the difference between them. Rutherford's model: a small, heavy, positively charged nucleus in the centre containing the protons (and neutrons), with electrons revolving around it at high speed like planets around the sun, and most of the space of the atom shown empty — this model came from the gold-foil experiment, but it could not explain the stability of the atom or its line spectrum. Bohr's model: the same central nucleus, but with the electrons placed only in fixed circular shells (K, L, M...) of fixed energy drawn as definite rings around the nucleus; an electron in a shell does not lose energy, it absorbs energy to jump to a higher shell and radiates energy when it falls to a lower shell. Presenting both models side by side shows that Bohr kept Rutherford's nucleus and removed its defects by fixing the orbits and their energies.

chapters.title: Unit 3: Periodic Table and Periodicity of Properties

lessons.title: Multiple Choice Questions
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • Iodine is in the same family (group VII, halogens) as fluorine.
  • Potassium (K) has the smallest ionization energy among K, P, S and Ca.
  • Configuration 2,8,1 means group I and the third period: group from valence electrons, period from number of shells.
  • Silicon is most similar to carbon because both are in group IV.
  • s-block elements are metals; helium (He) has the largest ionization energy among Na, Al, H and He.
  • Elements in a group have similar chemical properties; 8 valence electrons means the noble family.
  • The modern periodic table is based on atomic number, and the shielding effect is due to electrons.

Solved Exercises

Exercise — Choose the Correct Option

Q: i. Which of the following elements is in the same family as fluorine?

Options: (a) silicon (b) antimony (c) iodine (d) arsenic

Correct answer: iodine

Q: ii. Which of the following would have the smallest ionization energy?

Options: (a) K (b) P (c) S (d) Ca

Correct answer: K

Q: iii. An element has configuration 2, 8, 1. It belongs to __________.

Options: (a) group I and III period (b) group III and I period (c) group I and VII period (d) group VII and III period

Correct answer: group I and III period

Q: iv. Which of the following elements would be most similar to carbon?

Options: (a) nitrogen (b) boron (c) oxygen (d) silicon

Correct answer: silicon

Q: v. s-block elements are:

Options: (a) metals (b) non-metals (c) metalloids (d) transition

Correct answer: metals

Q: vi. Which of the following would have the largest ionization energy?

Options: (a) Na (b) Al (c) H (d) He

Correct answer: He

Q: vii. Elements in a __________ have similar chemical properties.

Options: (a) period (b) group (c) both a and b (d) neither a nor b

Correct answer: group

Q: viii. An element has 8 electrons in its valence shell. It is a member of:

Options: (a) alkali family (b) halogen family (c) noble family (d) carbon family

Correct answer: noble family

Q: ix. The modern periodic table is based on:

Options: (a) atomic number (b) mass number (c) neutron number (d) isotope number

Correct answer: atomic number

Q: x. Shielding effect is due to:

Options: (a) neutron (b) proton (c) proton and neutron (d) electron

Correct answer: electron

mcqs.q: i. Which of the following elements is in the same family as fluorine?
mcqs.why: Fluorine is a halogen in group VII. Iodine is also a halogen in group VII, so it is in the same family as fluorine. Silicon, antimony and arsenic belong to other groups.

mcqs.q: ii. Which of the following would have the smallest ionization energy?
mcqs.why: Potassium (K) is a large group I atom in period 4 with strong shielding, so its single valence electron is held weakly and removed most easily, giving it the smallest ionization energy of the four.

mcqs.q: iii. An element has configuration 2, 8, 1. It belongs to __________.
mcqs.why: The element has one electron in its outermost shell, so it is in group I, and it has three shells (2, 8, 1), so it is in the third period. Group number comes from valence electrons and period number from the number of shells.

mcqs.q: iv. Which of the following elements would be most similar to carbon?
mcqs.why: Carbon is in group IV with four valence electrons. Silicon is directly below carbon in group IV and also has four valence electrons, so elements in the same group show the most similar chemical properties.

mcqs.q: v. s-block elements are:
mcqs.why: The s-block consists of group I and group II elements, which are metals such as the alkali metals and alkaline earth metals. Transition elements form the separate d-block in the middle of the table.

mcqs.q: vi. Which of the following would have the largest ionization energy?
mcqs.why: Helium has a very small atom with its two electrons in the first shell, held very strongly by the nucleus and with no shielding from inner shells, so it has the largest ionization energy of these elements.

mcqs.q: vii. Elements in a __________ have similar chemical properties.
mcqs.why: Elements in the same group have the same number of electrons in their outermost shell, and chemical properties depend mainly on these valence electrons, so group members show similar chemical properties.

mcqs.q: viii. An element has 8 electrons in its valence shell. It is a member of:
mcqs.why: Eight electrons in the valence shell is a complete octet, the stable arrangement of the noble gases in group VIII. Such an element therefore belongs to the noble family.

mcqs.q: ix. The modern periodic table is based on:
mcqs.why: Moseley showed that properties depend on atomic number, the number of protons and electrons, not on atomic mass. The modern periodic law states that properties of elements are a periodic function of their atomic number.

mcqs.q: x. Shielding effect is due to:
mcqs.why: The inner-shell electrons lie between the nucleus and the valence electrons and shield them from the full pull of the nucleus. This reduction of the nuclear hold by inner electrons is the shielding effect.

lessons.title: Short Answers
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • Hydrogen is in group I but is not an alkali metal: it is a non-metal gas that forms a diatomic molecule.
  • Ionization energy increases across period 3: Na < Mg < S < Ar (496, 738, 1000, 1521 kJ/mol).
  • Group number equals the number of electrons in the outermost shell: K group I, Ne group VIII, Be group II, Cl group VII, C group IV.
  • Oxygen is the most electronegative of C, N, O, Br and S (3.5) and belongs to group VI.
  • First ionization energy increases across a period and decreases down a group.
  • Period 2 group VII is fluorine; period 4 group III is gallium; period 5 group VI is tellurium; period 1 group VIII is helium.
  • Representative elements are the s-block and p-block elements; transition elements are the d-block elements.
  • The s-block has only two groups because one s orbital holds a maximum of two electrons; sulphur is a representative element.

Solved Exercises

Exercise — Short Questions

Q: (i) Which element of group IA is not an alkali metal and why?

Ans: Hydrogen. Although hydrogen is placed in group I because it has one electron in its outermost shell (configuration 1), it is not an alkali metal: it is a non-metal and a gas, it forms a diatomic molecule and gains or shares an electron like a non-metal, instead of showing the metallic, electropositive character of the alkali metals Li, Na and K.

Q: (ii) Place the following elements in order of increasing ionization energy: Na, S, Mg and Ar.

Ans: Na < Mg < S < Ar. All four are in period 3, and ionization energy increases from left to right in a period because the nuclear charge increases and the atomic radius decreases in the same shell, so the valence electron is held more strongly. The book's values are Na 496, Mg 738, S 1000 and Ar 1521 kJ/mol.

Q: (iii) Name the group and state the group number of each of the following elements: (a) K (b) Ne (c) Be (d) Cl (e) C

Ans: (a) K — alkali family (alkali metals), group I. (b) Ne — noble family (noble gases), group VIII. (c) Be — alkaline earth family (alkaline earth metals), group II. (d) Cl — halogen family, group VII. (e) C — carbon family, group IV. The group number equals the number of electrons in the outermost shell of each element.

Q: (iv) Which element is the most electronegative among C, N, O, Br and S? Which group does it belongs to?

Ans: Oxygen (O) is the most electronegative of these elements, with an electronegativity of 3.5 on the Pauling scale given in this unit. It belongs to group VI, the oxygen family.

Q: (v) How do the first ionization energies of representative elements vary across a period and down a group?

Ans: Across a period, from left to right, the first ionization energy increases, because electrons are added to the same shell, the nuclear charge increases and the atomic radius decreases, so the outermost electron is pulled more strongly. Down a group, the first ionization energy decreases, because a new shell is added, the atomic radius increases and the shielding effect increases, so the outermost electron is held less strongly and is removed easily.

Q: (vi) Which element is found in, (a) Period 2, group VII (b) Period 4, group III (c) Period 5, group VI (d) Period 1, group VIII

Ans: (a) Fluorine (F) — period 2, group VII, the first halogen. (b) Gallium (Ga) — period 4, group III, in the boron family. (c) Tellurium (Te) — period 5, group VI, in the oxygen family. (d) Helium (He) — period 1, group VIII, the first noble gas.

Q: (vii) How will you differentiate between representative and transition elements?

Ans: Representative elements are all the s-block and p-block elements (groups I to VIII); their outermost s or p sub-shell is in the process of completion and they show regular, predictable properties. Transition elements are the d-block elements placed between the s-block and the p-block in the middle of the table; they are elements which show variable valency, and the lanthanide and actinide series placed below the table are the f-block (inner transition) elements.

Q: (viii) Make a general sketch of the periodic table showing s, p, d and f-block elements (without showing the symbols of elements)

Ans: In words, the sketch is drawn as follows. On the extreme left draw a block of 2 vertical columns — this is the s-block (groups I and II). In the middle draw a wider block of 10 vertical columns — this is the d-block, the transition metals. On the extreme right draw a block of 6 vertical columns — this is the p-block (groups III to VIII). The s-block and p-block together are the representative elements. Below the main table, separated from it, draw two horizontal rows of 14 boxes each — this is the f-block, the lanthanide series on top and the actinide series below it. Seven horizontal rows (periods) run across the main table.

Q: (ix) Why the s-block elements have two groups only?

Ans: The s sub-shell consists of only one s orbital, which can hold a maximum of two electrons. An s-block element can therefore have only one or two electrons in the outermost s sub-shell, giving only two possible valence-electron arrangements. Hence the s-block has only two groups: group I (one valence electron) and group II (two valence electrons).

Q: (x) What type of element is Sulphur (S), a representative element, a transition element or lanthanide element?

Ans: Sulphur is a representative element. It is a p-block element in group VI and period 3 (configuration 2,8,6), and all s-block and p-block elements are called representative elements. It is neither a transition element nor a lanthanide element.

mcqs.q: Which element of group IA is not an alkali metal?
mcqs.why: Hydrogen is placed in group I because it has one electron in its only shell, but it is a non-metal and a gas that forms a diatomic molecule and gains or shares an electron, unlike the metallic alkali metals lithium, sodium and potassium.

mcqs.q: What is the order of increasing ionization energy for Na, S, Mg and Ar?
mcqs.why: All four elements are in period 3, and ionization energy increases from left to right in a period because nuclear charge increases and atomic radius decreases. The book values are Na 496, Mg 738, S 1000 and Ar 1521 kJ/mol.

mcqs.q: Neon (Ne) belongs to which family and group?
mcqs.why: Neon has a complete outermost shell (2,8), the stable arrangement of the noble gases. It therefore belongs to the noble family, group VIII, while potassium is group I, chlorine group VII and carbon group IV.

mcqs.q: Which element is the most electronegative among C, N, O, Br and S, and to which group does it belong?
mcqs.why: Oxygen has an electronegativity of 3.5 on the Pauling scale given in this unit, higher than carbon, nitrogen, bromine and sulphur in the list. Oxygen belongs to group VI, the oxygen family.

mcqs.q: How does the first ionization energy change across a period from left to right?
mcqs.why: Across a period, electrons are added to the same shell while the nuclear charge increases and the atomic radius decreases, so the outermost electron is pulled more strongly and more energy is needed to remove it.

mcqs.q: Which element is found in period 2, group VII?
mcqs.why: Period 2, group VII is the first halogen position in the table, occupied by fluorine. Chlorine is the period 3 halogen, oxygen is in group VI and neon is in group VIII of period 2.

mcqs.q: Representative elements are:
options: Only the d-block elements in the middle of the table
Only the lanthanide and actinide series
Only the group VIII noble gases
All the s-block and p-block elements (groups I to VIII)
mcqs.why: Representative elements are all the s-block and p-block elements, whose outermost s or p sub-shell is in the process of completion. The d-block elements are the transition elements, and the lanthanides and actinides are the f-block inner transition elements.

mcqs.q: In a general sketch of the periodic table, the s-block is drawn as:
options: A block of 10 vertical columns in the middle
A block of 2 vertical columns on the extreme left
A block of 6 vertical columns on the extreme right
Two horizontal rows of 14 boxes below the table
mcqs.why: The s-block has only groups I and II, so it is drawn as two vertical columns on the extreme left. The 10-column middle block is the d-block, the 6-column right block is the p-block, and the two rows of 14 below are the f-block.

mcqs.q: Why do the s-block elements have two groups only?
options: The s sub-shell has only one orbital, which can hold a maximum of two electrons
The s sub-shell can hold a maximum of eight electrons
All s-block elements have exactly two shells
The s-block contains only two periods
mcqs.why: An s-block element can have only one or two electrons in its outermost s sub-shell, giving only two valence-electron arrangements. Hence the s-block has only group I (one valence electron) and group II (two valence electrons).

mcqs.q: What type of element is sulphur (S)?
mcqs.why: Sulphur is a p-block element in group VI and period 3 with configuration 2,8,6. All s-block and p-block elements are called representative elements, so sulphur is neither a transition element nor a lanthanide.

lessons.title: Detailed Answers
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • Mendeleev's table (1869) was based on atomic mass; the modern table by Moseley is based on atomic number.
  • Modern periodic law: properties of elements are a periodic function of their atomic number; the modern table has 118 elements, 8 groups and 7 periods.
  • Atomic radius is the distance from the nucleus to the valence shell of an isolated atom; covalent radius = d/2 for two bonded similar atoms.
  • Atomic radius increases down a group (new shell, shielding) and decreases across a period (increased nuclear charge).
  • Electronegativity is the attraction of an atom in a covalent bond for the shared pair; group VII is most electronegative, fluorine highest at 4.0, cesium lowest at 0.7.
  • Shielding effect: inner electrons reduce the nuclear hold on valence electrons; down a group it makes ionization energy, electron affinity and electronegativity decrease.
  • Electron affinity is the energy released when an electron is added to a gaseous atom, e.g. Cl(g) + e- -> Cl-(g), E.A. = -348.8 kJ/mol.
  • Periodicity of properties is the repetition of properties at intervals when elements are arranged by increasing atomic number.

Solved Exercises

Exercise — Long Questions

Q: (i) How modern periodic table is different from the Mendeleev's periodic table?

Ans: Mendeleev's table (1869) was based on atomic mass: he arranged 65 elements in order of their increasing atomic masses in periods and groups, and stated the old periodic law that the properties of elements are a periodic function of their atomic weights. He left vacant spaces for undiscovered elements and predicted their properties. The modern periodic table was put forward by Henry Gwyn Jeffreys Moseley and is based on atomic number: the modern periodic law states that the physical and chemical properties of the elements are a periodic function of their atomic number. In its simplified form it has eight vertical columns called groups or families and seven horizontal rows called periods, it contains 118 elements, and the position of each element is fixed by its electronic configuration — the group by its valence electrons and the period by its number of shells. Arranging by atomic number also removes the misfits of the mass order, because properties depend on the number and arrangement of electrons in the atom, not on atomic mass.

Q: (ii) Differentiate between atomic radii and covalent radii. Explain the trends of atomic radius in the periodic table.

Ans: Atomic radius is the distance between the nucleus and the valence shell (outer shell) of an isolated atom; it is represented by 'r' and is expressed in nanometre (1.0 x 10^-9 m) or picometre (pm = 1.0 x 10^-12 m). Covalent radius is one half of the distance between the nuclei of two similar atoms of the same molecule containing a single covalent bond, i.e. covalent radius (r) = d/2, where d is the bond distance; for example, the covalent radius of H2 is d/2. An atom in isolation has a different size from the same atom in combination, so the two radii are not the same. Trends of atomic radius: (a) In a group, the atomic radius increases from top to bottom, due to the addition of a new shell in each successive period and the shielding effect of the inner electrons. (b) In a period, the atomic radius decreases from left to right, because electrons are added to the same shell while the number of protons increases; the increased nuclear charge pulls the electrons nearer to the nucleus.

Q: (iii) What is electronegativity? Identify the most and least electronegative groups of elements in the periodic table. Why is fluorine special in terms of electronegativity?

Ans: Electronegativity is the ability of an atom in a covalent bond to attract the shared pair of electrons towards itself; in other words, it is the power of attraction for the shared pair of electrons, and it is represented by E.N. The most electronegative group is group VII, the halogens, at the upper right of the table, while the least electronegative group is group I, the alkali metals, at the lower left — cesium has the lowest value, 0.7. Fluorine is special because it has the highest electronegativity of all elements, 4.0 on the Pauling scale developed from bond energies of diatomic molecules. It has a very small atomic radius and a strong nuclear pull on the shared pair, so, as this unit notes, fluorine is the most reactive and most electronegative element, which makes elemental fluorine a dangerously powerful oxidant.

Q: (iv) Define shielding effect and draw its affects upon the ionization energy, electron affinity and electronegativity.

Ans: Shielding effect: the electrons in an atom are distributed in different shells. The valence electrons spend most of their time away from the nucleus, and the inner orbital electrons between them and the nucleus shield them, so they do not feel the full pulling effect of the positive charge of the nucleus. This reduction of the hold of the nucleus on the valence electrons by the inner electrons is called the shielding effect or screening effect. As the number of shells increases, the shielding effect increases. Its effects (shown in Table 3.9 of this unit, where I.P., E.A. and E.N. values all increase together from left to right in a period and decrease down a group): down a group a new shell is added at each step, shielding increases and wins over the increased nuclear charge, so ionization energy, electron affinity and electronegativity all decrease and atomic radius increases. Across a period no new shell is added, shielding stays almost constant while the nuclear charge increases, so the increasing nuclear charge dominates over the shielding effect and ionization energy, electron affinity and electronegativity all increase, while atomic radius decreases.

Q: (v) Explain the following terms. (a) Periodicity of properties (b) Electron affinity (c) Modern periodic law

Ans: (a) Periodicity of properties: in the same group, all the elements have similar general physical and chemical properties, and after a certain interval the properties of given elements are repeated. This repetition of the properties in different groups and periods of the periodic table, when the elements are arranged in increasing order of their atomic numbers, is called the periodicity of properties. (b) Electron affinity: the minimum amount of energy released when an electron is added to a gaseous atom of an element in its outermost shell to form an anion is called electron affinity. It is represented by E.A., is assigned negative values and is expressed in kJ/mol, e.g. Cl(g) + e- -> Cl-(g), E.A. = -348.8 kJ/mol. (c) Modern periodic law: the physical and chemical properties of the elements are the periodic function of their atomic number. The modern periodic table is formed on the basis of this law.

mcqs.q: Mendeleev's periodic table was based on:
mcqs.why: Mendeleev (1869) arranged 65 elements in order of increasing atomic masses and stated that properties are a periodic function of atomic weights. The modern table, by contrast, is based on atomic number, as put forward by Moseley.

mcqs.q: According to the modern periodic law, the physical and chemical properties of elements are a periodic function of their:
mcqs.why: The modern periodic law, given by Henry Gwyn Jeffreys Moseley, states that the physical and chemical properties of the elements are a periodic function of their atomic number, because properties depend on the number and arrangement of electrons.

mcqs.q: Atomic radius is defined as:
options: The distance between the nucleus and the valence shell of an isolated atom
Half the distance between the nuclei of two bonded atoms
The distance between two nuclei in a molecule
The diameter of the nucleus of an atom
mcqs.why: Atomic radius is the distance between the nucleus and the valence (outer) shell of an isolated atom, represented by r and expressed in nanometre or picometre. Half the distance between two bonded nuclei is instead the covalent radius.

mcqs.q: Covalent radius is calculated as:
options: r = d x 2, where d is the bond distance
r = d, where d is the full bond distance
r = d/2, where d is the distance between the nuclei of two similar bonded atoms
r = d/8, where d is the bond distance
mcqs.why: Covalent radius is one half of the distance between the nuclei of two similar atoms in a molecule containing a single covalent bond, so covalent radius r = d/2. For example, the covalent radius in H2 is d/2.

mcqs.q: How does atomic radius change down a group and across a period?
options: It decreases down a group and increases across a period
It increases both down a group and across a period
It increases down a group and decreases across a period
It decreases both down a group and across a period
mcqs.why: Down a group a new shell is added at each step and shielding increases, so atomic radius increases. Across a period electrons enter the same shell while nuclear charge increases, pulling electrons nearer, so atomic radius decreases.

mcqs.q: Electronegativity is the ability of an atom in a covalent bond to:
options: Attract the shared pair of electrons towards itself
Lose its valence electrons to another atom
Donate a lone pair to another atom
Attract protons from the nucleus of another atom
mcqs.why: Electronegativity, represented by E.N., is the power of an atom in a covalent bond to attract the shared pair of electrons towards itself. It is measured on the Pauling scale developed from bond energies of diatomic molecules.

mcqs.q: Which group is the most electronegative, and which element has the highest electronegativity of all?
options: Group I (alkali metals); cesium, with a value of 0.7
Group VI (oxygen family); oxygen, with a value of 3.5
Group VIII (noble gases); neon, with a value of 4.0
Group VII (halogens); fluorine, with a value of 4.0
mcqs.why: The halogens of group VII, at the upper right of the table, are the most electronegative group, and fluorine has the highest value of all elements, 4.0, because of its very small atomic radius and strong nuclear pull. Cesium, at the bottom of group I, has the lowest value, 0.7.

mcqs.q: The shielding effect is the reduction of the hold of the nucleus on the valence electrons caused by:
options: The neutrons present inside the nucleus
The inner electrons between the nucleus and the valence electrons
The electrons of neighbouring atoms in the compound
The protons added across a period
mcqs.why: Valence electrons spend most of their time away from the nucleus, and the inner orbital electrons between them and the nucleus shield them, so they do not feel the full positive charge of the nucleus. This is the shielding or screening effect, which increases as the number of shells increases.

mcqs.q: Down a group, increased shielding causes ionization energy, electron affinity and electronegativity to:
options: All decrease, while atomic radius increases
All increase, while atomic radius decreases
Stay constant, while atomic radius increases
Increase for ionization energy but decrease for electronegativity
mcqs.why: Down a group a new shell is added at each step, so shielding increases and wins over the increased nuclear charge. Ionization energy, electron affinity and electronegativity therefore all decrease, and atomic radius increases.

mcqs.q: Electron affinity is:
options: The energy needed to remove an electron from a gaseous atom
The energy released when two atoms share a pair of electrons
The minimum amount of energy released when an electron is added to a gaseous atom to form an anion
The energy needed to break a covalent bond in a molecule
mcqs.why: Electron affinity (E.A.) is the minimum energy released when an electron is added to a gaseous atom in its outermost shell to form an anion, for example Cl(g) + e- -> Cl-(g), E.A. = -348.8 kJ/mol. The energy needed to remove an electron is ionization energy, not electron affinity.

lessons.title: Test Yourself and Practice Problems
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • The second period starts with lithium (2,1), ends with neon (2,8) and contains 8 elements.
  • The second noble gas is neon (Ne), in period 2 and group VIII.
  • Potassium is in group I (2,8,8,1); arsenic is in period 4 (2,8,18,5); titanium is in group IV.
  • Calcium (2,8,8,2) has 4 shells and 2 valence electrons; an element in period III, group II has configuration 2,8,2.
  • Ionization energy increases across a period (N > C > Be) and decreases down a group (Mg > Ca > Sr).
  • All group I elements (H, Li, Na, K) have exactly one valence electron and are more reactive than group II elements.
  • Cesium (0.7) at the bottom of group I is the least electronegative element; group VII halogens have the highest electronegativity values.
  • Sulphur resembles selenium because both are in group VI with six valence electrons.

Solved Exercises

Practice Problem 3.1

Q: Which is the first element of the second period of the periodic table?

Ans: Lithium (Li). The second period begins with lithium, whose electronic configuration is 2,1, so a new (second) shell is started.

Q: Which one is the last element of the second period of the periodic table?

Ans: Neon (Ne). It has the configuration 2,8, so its second shell is complete and the period ends.

Q: How many elements are in that period?

Ans: 8 elements: Li, Be, B, C, N, O, F and Ne. The 2nd and 3rd periods are short periods, each containing eight elements.

Practice Problem 3.2

Q: Identify the second noble gas.

Ans: Neon (Ne). The noble gases in order are helium (He), neon (Ne), argon (Ar) and so on, so the second noble gas is neon, in period 2 and group VIII.

Test Yourself (Page 72)

Q: To which group does the element Potassium belong?

Ans: Group I. Potassium (K) has one electron in its outermost shell (2,8,8,1), so it belongs to group I, the alkali family.

Q: To which period does the element Arsenic belong?

Ans: Period 4. Arsenic (As) has electrons in four shells (2,8,18,5), and the number of shells gives the period number.

Q: To which group does the element Titanium belong?

Ans: Group IV. Titanium (Ti) is a transition element placed in group IV of the periodic table, between group III and group V in the d-block.

Q: State whether the following elements are metals or non-metals: Cesium, Boron, Selenium, Phosphorous, Astatine, and Osmium.

Ans: Cesium (Cs) — metal (alkali metal, group I). Boron (B) — metalloid, as shown in the periodic table in this unit. Selenium (Se) — non-metal. Phosphorus (P) — non-metal. Astatine (At) — non-metal (halogen, group VII). Osmium (Os) — metal (transition element).

Q: How many shells and valence electrons, the element Calcium have?

Ans: Calcium (Ca) has the electronic configuration 2,8,8,2. It therefore has 4 shells and 2 valence electrons in its outermost shell, which is why it is in group II.

Q: Element X is located in period III, group II of the periodic table, deduce its electronic configuration.

Options: (a) 2,2 (b) 2,3 (c) 2,8,2 (d) 2,8,3

Correct answer: 2,8,2

Practice Problem 3.3

Q: Which atom in each of the following sets has the largest ionization energy? (a) Be, C, N (b) Mg, Ca, Sr (c) Sn, Se, F

Ans: (a) N — ionization energy increases from left to right in a period, and N is the rightmost of the three in period 2. (b) Mg — ionization energy decreases down a group, and Mg is at the top of group II among the three. (c) F — F is at the top and to the right, with the smallest atomic radius, so its valence electron is held most strongly and it has the largest ionization energy.

Test Yourself (Page 79)

Q: Use a periodic table, to complete the last two diagram for sodium (Na) and potassium (K). [Electron diagrams for some of the Group-I elements: Hydrogen, Lithium, Sodium, Potassium]

Ans: Sodium (Na, atomic number 11) has the configuration 2,8,1, so its diagram has three shells holding 2, 8 and 1 electrons. Potassium (K, atomic number 19) has the configuration 2,8,8,1, so its diagram has four shells holding 2, 8, 8 and 1 electrons. In each diagram only one electron is placed in the outermost shell.

Q: What do you notice about the number of electrons in the valence energy level in each case?

Ans: In every case there is exactly one electron in the valence (outermost) energy level: H = 1, Li = 2,1, Na = 2,8,1 and K = 2,8,8,1. This common single valence electron is why all these elements are placed in group I and show similar chemical properties.

Q: Explain why elements from group-I are more reactive than elements from group-II of the periodic table (Hint: Think back to 'ionization energy').

Ans: A group-I element has only one valence electron, and it needs to lose only that one electron to get a stable complete outer shell. Its first ionization energy is low, so this electron is removed easily and the element reacts readily. A group-II element must lose two electrons, which needs the first plus the much larger second ionization energy, so it is less reactive than the group-I element in the same period.

Test Yourself (Page 84)

Q: The least electronegative element is Cs (0.7), can you guess where is it located in the table?

Ans: Cesium (Cs) is located at the bottom of group I, on the extreme left and lower side of the periodic table (period 6, group I). Electronegativity decreases down a group and is lowest for the large atoms at the bottom left.

Q: Can you tell, elements of which group have the highest electronegativity values?

Ans: Group VII, the halogens. Electronegativity increases across a period towards the right, so the halogens, near the upper right corner of the table, have the highest values, with fluorine (4.0) the highest of all elements.

Practice Problem 3.4

Q: Is sulphur more likely to be similar to selenium (Se) or to chlorine (Cl) in its chemical properties?

Ans: Sulphur is more likely to be similar to selenium (Se). Sulphur and selenium are both in group VI and have six electrons in their outermost shell, and elements in the same group show similar chemical properties. Chlorine is only a neighbour of sulphur in period 3, but it is in group VII with seven valence electrons, so its properties differ.

mcqs.q: Which is the first element of the second period of the periodic table?
mcqs.why: The second period begins with lithium, whose electronic configuration is 2,1, so a new second shell is started. The period then runs through Be, B, C, N, O and F to Ne.

mcqs.q: Which one is the last element of the second period of the periodic table?
mcqs.why: Neon has the configuration 2,8, so its second shell is complete and the second period ends with it. Fluorine (2,7) comes just before neon, and argon ends the third period.

mcqs.q: How many elements are in the second period?
mcqs.why: The second period contains 8 elements: Li, Be, B, C, N, O, F and Ne. The 2nd and 3rd periods are short periods, each containing eight elements.

mcqs.q: Which is the second noble gas?
mcqs.why: The noble gases in order are helium (He), neon (Ne), argon (Ar) and so on. The second noble gas is therefore neon, which is in period 2 and group VIII.

mcqs.q: To which group does the element potassium belong?
mcqs.why: Potassium (K) has one electron in its outermost shell, with configuration 2,8,8,1. The number of valence electrons gives the group, so potassium belongs to group I, the alkali family.

mcqs.q: To which period does the element arsenic belong?
mcqs.why: Arsenic (As) has electrons in four shells, with configuration 2,8,18,5. The number of shells gives the period number, so arsenic belongs to period 4.

mcqs.q: How many shells and valence electrons does the element calcium have?
mcqs.why: Calcium has the electronic configuration 2,8,8,2. It therefore has electrons in 4 shells and 2 electrons in its outermost shell, which is why it is placed in group II.

mcqs.q: Element X is located in period III, group II of the periodic table. What is its electronic configuration?
mcqs.why: Period III means three shells and group II means two valence electrons, giving the configuration 2,8,2, which is magnesium. The configuration 2,8,3 would be a group III element of period III.

mcqs.q: Which atom in the set Be, C, N has the largest ionization energy?
mcqs.why: Ionization energy increases from left to right in a period, and nitrogen is the rightmost of Be, C and N in period 2. Its valence electrons are therefore held most strongly of the three.

mcqs.q: What do you notice about the number of electrons in the valence energy level of H, Li, Na and K?
options: There are two electrons in the valence level in each case
The number increases by one from H to K
There is exactly one electron in the valence level in each case
Only sodium and potassium have one valence electron
mcqs.why: Hydrogen has 1, lithium 2,1, sodium 2,8,1 and potassium 2,8,8,1, so each has exactly one electron in the outermost level. This common single valence electron is why all of them are placed in group I and show similar properties.

mcqs.q: Why are group I elements more reactive than group II elements of the same period?
options: A group I element gains one electron very easily
A group I element loses only one electron and has a low first ionization energy
A group II element has a smaller atomic radius
A group I element has a complete outer shell
mcqs.why: A group I element needs to lose only one electron to get a stable complete outer shell, and its first ionization energy is low, so the electron is removed easily. A group II element must lose two electrons, needing the first plus the much larger second ionization energy.

mcqs.q: Cesium (Cs), the least electronegative element (0.7), is located:
options: At the top of group VII, in period 2
At the bottom of group VIII, in period 6
At the top of group I, in period 2
At the bottom of group I, in period 6
mcqs.why: Electronegativity decreases down a group and is lowest for the large atoms at the bottom left of the table. Cesium sits at the bottom of group I in period 6, on the extreme left and lower side of the periodic table.

mcqs.q: Elements of which group have the highest electronegativity values?
options: Group II, the alkaline earth metals
mcqs.why: Electronegativity increases across a period towards the right, so the halogens of group VII, near the upper right corner of the table, have the highest values, with fluorine (4.0) the highest of all elements.

mcqs.q: Sulphur is more likely to be similar in chemical properties to which element?
mcqs.why: Sulphur and selenium are both in group VI and have six electrons in their outermost shell, and elements in the same group show similar chemical properties. Chlorine is only a period neighbour of sulphur but is in group VII with seven valence electrons.

mcqs.q: In the set Cesium, Boron, Selenium, Phosphorus, Astatine and Osmium, which element is a metalloid?
mcqs.why: In the periodic table given in this unit, boron is shown as a metalloid. Cesium and osmium are metals, while selenium, phosphorus and astatine are non-metals.

lessons.title: Project Work
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • Dobereiner (1817) grouped similar elements in triads; the middle element atomic weight was the mean of the other two.
  • Newland (1864) gave the law of octaves: every eighth element resembled the first when arranged by atomic mass.
  • Mendeleev (1869) arranged 65 elements by atomic mass, left gaps for undiscovered elements and predicted their properties.
  • Moseley based the modern periodic table on atomic number: properties of elements are a periodic function of their atomic number.
  • The modern table has 118 elements, 92 found naturally on Earth and the rest prepared artificially.

Solved Exercises

Exercise — Project Work

Q: Prepare a report tracing the evolution of the current periodic table since 1900. Cite the chemists involved and their major contributions.

Ans: Report outline from the chemists named in this unit, whose work the modern table rests on: (1) J. W. Dobereiner (1817) classified chemically similar elements in groups of three, called triads, on the basis of their atomic masses; in a triad the atomic weight of the middle element was the arithmetic mean of the other two, e.g. (7 + 39)/2 = 23 for Na in the Li, Na, K triad. (2) J. Newland (1864) arranged the elements in order of increasing atomic masses in groups of seven, the law of octaves, in which every eighth element had properties similar to the first, e.g. Li resembles Na and F resembles Cl; it failed to classify all the elements. (3) Lothar Meyer in Germany and Dmitri Mendeleev in Russia (1869) independently developed very similar arrangements: arranging the elements in order of increasing atomic mass, certain physical and chemical properties were repeated at regular intervals. Meyer plotted atomic volumes (densities) against atomic masses and found similar elements at similar positions. Mendeleev arranged 65 elements in periods and groups in the form of a table, left vacant spaces for elements not yet discovered, and predicted the properties of certain elements very accurately. (4) Henry Gwyn Jeffreys Moseley, an English physicist, put forward the modern periodic table based on atomic number, giving the modern periodic law — the properties of the elements are a periodic function of their atomic number. A student's report should present these stages in order, with the table of 118 elements (92 found naturally on Earth and the rest artificially prepared) as the present end point.

lessons.title: Multiple Choice Questions
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • An atom with a charge is called an ion; a group VI element gains two electrons and forms an X2- ion.
  • Potassium and fluorine form a 1:1 compound (KF) because K+ and F- have equal and opposite charges.
  • A calcium atom loses two electrons to become Ca2+; carbon and oxygen (two non-metals) form a covalent compound.
  • Ionic bonding involves loss and gain of electrons; fluorine oxide is F2O because two F- ions balance one O2- ion.
  • H2O contains two (not three) pairs of shared electrons; O2- has the neon configuration, not argon's.
  • Calcium oxide, magnesium oxide and sodium chloride are all ionic compounds.

Solved Exercises

Exercise — Choose the Correct Option

Q: i. An atom with a charge is called:

Options: (a) an electron (b) a molecule (c) a metal (d) an ion

Correct answer: an ion

Q: ii. An element X is in group VI of the periodic table. The ion will be represented by:

Options: (a) X+ (b) X- (c) X2- (d) X2+

Correct answer: X2-

Q: iii. Which pair of elements will join to form a compound with one to one ratio?

Options: (a) Magnesium and Chlorine (b) Sodium and Oxygen (c) Potassium and Fluorine (d) Lithium and Sulphur

Correct answer: Potassium and Fluorine

Q: iv. When calcium atom become a Calcium ion (Ca2+):

Options: (a) it loses an electron (b) it loses two electrons (c) it gains electron (d) gains two electrons

Correct answer: it loses two electrons

Q: v. Which two elements will form a covalent compound?

Options: (a) Sodium and Oxygen (b) Copper and Oxygen (c) Carbon and Oxygen (d) Magnesium and Oxygen

Correct answer: Carbon and Oxygen

Q: vi. In the formation of an ionic bond, the atoms taking part:

Options: (a) only gain electrons (b) share electrons (c) lose and gain of electrons (d) only lose electrons

Correct answer: lose and gain of electrons

Q: vii. Fluorine has an electronic configuration 2, 7 and Oxygen 2, 6. The formula of fluorine oxide will be:

Options: (a) FO (b) F2O (c) FO2 (d) F2O2

Correct answer: F2O

Q: viii. Which of these statements about covalent bonds is incorrect?

Options: (a) HCl contains one pair of shared electron (b) CCl4 contains four pairs of shared electrons (c) H2O contains three pairs of shared electrons (d) NH3 contains three pairs of shared electrons

Correct answer: H2O contains three pairs of shared electrons

Q: ix. Which of the following ions do not have the electronic configuration of an argon atom?

Options: (a) Ca2+ (b) S2- (c) K+ (d) O2-

Correct answer: O2-

Q: x. Which one of the groups below contains only ionic compounds?

Options: (a) Calcium Oxide, Hydrogen Chloride, Magnesium Oxide (b) Calcium Oxide, Magnesium Oxide, Sodium Chloride (c) Carbon Dioxide, Copper Sulphate, Hydrogen Chloride (d) Copper Sulphate, Methane, Sodium Chloride

Correct answer: Calcium Oxide, Magnesium Oxide, Sodium Chloride

mcqs.q: i. An atom with a charge is called:
mcqs.why: When an atom loses or gains electrons it carries a charge, and a charged atom is called an ion. A positive ion is a cation and a negative ion is an anion.

mcqs.q: ii. An element X is in group VI of the periodic table. The ion will be represented by:
mcqs.why: A group VI element has six valence electrons and needs two more electrons to complete its octet. Gaining two electrons gives it a charge of 2-, so its ion is written X2-, like O2-.

mcqs.q: iii. Which pair of elements will join to form a compound with one to one ratio?
mcqs.why: Potassium forms K+ and fluorine forms F-, so one ion of each balances the charges and the compound KF has a 1:1 ratio. Magnesium and chlorine give MgCl2 (1:2), and sodium or lithium with oxygen or sulphur give 2:1 compounds.

mcqs.q: iv. When calcium atom become a Calcium ion (Ca2+):
mcqs.why: Calcium (2,8,8,2) loses its two outermost electrons to attain the stable argon configuration. Losing two electrons, each of negative charge, leaves the ion with a 2+ charge, Ca2+.

mcqs.q: v. Which two elements will form a covalent compound?
mcqs.why: Carbon and oxygen are both non-metals, so they share electrons and form the covalent compound CO2. Sodium, copper and magnesium are metals, so their compounds with oxygen are ionic.

mcqs.q: vi. In the formation of an ionic bond, the atoms taking part:
mcqs.why: In ionic bonding one atom (the metal) loses electrons and forms a cation while the other atom (the non-metal) gains those electrons and forms an anion. The attraction between these oppositely charged ions is the ionic bond, as in NaCl.

mcqs.q: vii. Fluorine has an electronic configuration 2, 7 and Oxygen 2, 6. The formula of fluorine oxide will be:
mcqs.why: Fluorine gains one electron to form F- and oxygen gains two electrons to form O2-. Two F- ions are needed to balance one O2- ion, so the formula of fluorine oxide is F2O.

mcqs.q: viii. Which of these statements about covalent bonds is incorrect?
options: HCl contains one pair of shared electron
H2O contains three pairs of shared electrons
CCl4 contains four pairs of shared electrons
NH3 contains three pairs of shared electrons
mcqs.why: Water has two O-H bonds, so it contains two pairs of shared electrons, not three; its other two pairs on oxygen are lone pairs. HCl has one shared pair, CCl4 has four and NH3 has three, so those statements are correct.

mcqs.q: ix. Which of the following ions do not have the electronic configuration of an argon atom?
mcqs.why: Argon has 18 electrons (2,8,8). Ca2+, S2- and K+ each have 18 electrons, but O2- has only 10 electrons (2,8), the configuration of neon, not argon.

mcqs.q: x. Which one of the groups below contains only ionic compounds?
options: Calcium Oxide, Hydrogen Chloride, Magnesium Oxide
Carbon Dioxide, Copper Sulphate, Hydrogen Chloride
Calcium Oxide, Magnesium Oxide, Sodium Chloride
mcqs.why: Calcium oxide, magnesium oxide and sodium chloride are all formed between a metal and a non-metal, so all three are ionic. Hydrogen chloride, carbon dioxide and methane are covalent, so every other group contains a covalent compound.

lessons.title: Short Answers
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • Electron-sea model: positive metal ions in fixed positions surrounded by delocalised electrons; their attraction is metallic bonding.
  • Atoms bond because incomplete outer shells are unstable; bonding gives the stable noble-gas configuration.
  • Four bond types: ionic (transfer), covalent (sharing), dative (shared pair donated by one atom) and metallic (ions in an electron sea).
  • Strength order: ionic bond > covalent bond > hydrogen bond > dipole-dipole interaction.
  • Ionic compounds conduct when molten or in solution because the ions are free to move; in the solid they are fixed in the lattice.
  • Ionic bonding is metal + non-metal; covalent bonding is non-metal + non-metal; metallic bonding is between metal atoms.
  • CO2 is a non-polar molecule with polar bonds because its linear shape makes the bond polarities cancel; a dative bond is always polar because the pair is donated by one atom only.

Solved Exercises

Exercise — Short Questions

Q: i. What is electron-sea model of metallic bonding?

Ans: In the electron-sea model, the metal atoms in a metallic lattice lose their outer electrons and become positively charged metal ions arranged in fixed positions. The lost electrons no longer belong to any one atom; they are delocalised and move freely between the metal ions like a sea (cloud) of negative charge around them. The chemical bonding that results from the attraction between the positive metal ions and the surrounding sea of electrons is called metallic bonding.

Q: ii. Why most atoms are chemically bonded to other atoms in nature?

Ans: Most atoms have incomplete outermost shells, so an isolated atom is unstable and higher in energy. Atoms tend to lower their energy and attain stability, like every system in the universe. By combining with other atoms - losing, gaining or sharing electrons - they complete their outermost shell and attain the stable noble-gas configuration. That is why most atoms are found chemically bonded to other atoms in nature, and only the noble gases exist as single atoms.

Q: iii. Identify and define the four major types of chemical bonding.

Ans: The four major types are: (1) Ionic bond - formed by the complete transfer of electron(s) from one atom (a metal) to another (a non-metal); the electrostatic attraction between the oppositely charged ions so formed is the ionic bond, e.g. NaCl. (2) Covalent bond - formed by the mutual sharing of electrons between two non-metal atoms, e.g. H2 and CH4. (3) Dative (co-ordinate covalent) bond - a covalent bond in which the shared pair of electrons is donated by only one of the two atoms; the donating atom is the donor and the accepting atom is the acceptor, e.g. the bond formed when NH3 donates its lone pair to H+ to form NH4+. (4) Metallic bond - formed by the attraction between positive metal ions and the surrounding sea of delocalised electrons in a metal, e.g. in copper and iron.

Q: iv. Arrange the following from strongest to weakest attraction: a. Covalent bond b. Dipole-dipole interaction c. Hydrogen bond d. Ionic bond

Ans: Strongest to weakest: d. Ionic bond > a. Covalent bond > c. Hydrogen bond > b. Dipole-dipole interaction. Ionic and covalent bonds are true chemical bonds formed between atoms/ions and are much stronger than intermolecular forces. A hydrogen bond is weaker than a covalent bond (about twenty times weaker, as given in this unit) but about ten times stronger than a dipole-dipole interaction, which is the weakest of the four.

Q: v. Why ionic compounds are good electrolyte in molten and solution form not in solid state?

Ans: An electrolyte conducts electricity through the movement of ions. In the solid state the ions of an ionic compound are held in fixed positions in the crystal lattice by strong electrostatic forces and cannot move, so solid ionic compounds do not conduct electricity. When the compound is melted or dissolved in water, the lattice breaks down and the ions become free to move towards the oppositely charged electrodes. This movement of free ions carries the current, so ionic compounds are good electrolytes in the molten and solution forms.

Q: vi. What types of elements/atoms tend to form the following types of bonding? a. ionic b. covalent c. metallic

Ans: a. Ionic bonding: a metal atom and a non-metal atom - the metal loses electrons and the non-metal gains them, e.g. Na and Cl form NaCl. b. Covalent bonding: two non-metal atoms, which share electrons with each other, e.g. H and Cl form HCl. c. Metallic bonding: atoms of the same or different metals in a metallic lattice, whose outer electrons form the electron sea around the positive metal ions, e.g. atoms in copper, iron and aluminium.

Q: vii. Give an example of a non-polar molecule with polar bonds. Give reasons.

Ans: Carbon dioxide, CO2, is a non-polar molecule with polar bonds. Each C=O bond is polar because oxygen is more electronegative than carbon, so each shared pair is pulled towards oxygen, making each oxygen partially negative and carbon partially positive. However, CO2 is a linear molecule (O=C=O, bond angle 180 degrees), so the two equal and opposite bond polarities cancel each other exactly. The molecule as a whole therefore has no positive or negative end and is non-polar.

Q: viii. Predict the bond type (ionic, polar covalent, non-polar covalent) in each of the following: a. CaCl2 b. H2O c. CO2 d. C2H4

Ans: a. CaCl2: ionic - calcium is a metal and chlorine is a non-metal; calcium transfers one electron to each of two chlorine atoms, forming Ca2+ and two Cl- ions. b. H2O: polar covalent - hydrogen and oxygen are non-metals that share electrons, but oxygen is much more electronegative, so the shared pairs are pulled towards oxygen. c. CO2: polar covalent bonds - carbon and oxygen share electrons unequally because oxygen is more electronegative (the molecule as a whole is non-polar because its linear shape makes the two bond polarities cancel). d. C2H4: non-polar covalent - it is formed only of carbon and hydrogen, whose electronegativities are almost equal, so the electrons are shared almost equally.

Q: ix. Why ionic compounds are good conductor compared to covalent compounds?

Ans: Ionic compounds contain charged particles (ions). In the molten state or in aqueous solution these ions are free to move and carry electric current to the electrodes, so ionic compounds conduct electricity well in these forms. Covalent compounds consist of neutral molecules; they have no ions and no free electrons to carry charge, in any state. Therefore covalent compounds are non-electrolytes and poor conductors, while ionic compounds are good conductors (electrolytes) when molten or in solution.

Q: x. Give the reason that why dative bond is always polar?

Ans: In a dative (co-ordinate) bond the shared pair of electrons is provided by one atom only, the donor, while the other atom, the acceptor, contributes nothing. The two atoms are therefore different in their pull on the shared pair, and the electron pair is not shared equally: it stays closer to the donor side in origin and the acceptor gains a share of electrons it did not provide, producing partial charges on the two atoms. Because the sharing is unequal and poles are created, a dative bond is always polar.

mcqs.q: In the electron-sea model of metallic bonding, the metal consists of:
options: Neutral metal atoms sharing pairs of electrons
Positive metal ions in fixed positions surrounded by a sea of delocalised electrons
Positive and negative ions in a crystal lattice
Metal atoms held together by hydrogen bonds
mcqs.why: Metal atoms lose their outer electrons and become positively charged ions in fixed positions. The lost electrons are delocalised and move freely between the ions like a sea, and the attraction between the ions and this electron sea is metallic bonding.

mcqs.q: Why are most atoms chemically bonded to other atoms in nature?
options: Most atoms are too large to exist on their own
Atoms bond only when they are heated strongly
Only metal atoms can exist as single atoms
Most atoms have incomplete outermost shells and are unstable, so they combine to attain a stable noble-gas configuration
mcqs.why: An isolated atom with an incomplete outer shell is unstable and higher in energy. By losing, gaining or sharing electrons, atoms complete their outermost shell and attain stability, which is why only the noble gases exist as single atoms.

mcqs.q: A dative (co-ordinate covalent) bond is a covalent bond in which:
options: The shared pair of electrons is donated by only one of the two atoms
Electrons are completely transferred from a metal to a non-metal
Both atoms contribute two electrons each to the shared pair
Positive metal ions are held in a sea of electrons
mcqs.why: In a dative bond the donating atom (donor) provides both electrons of the shared pair and the other atom (acceptor) provides none, for example when NH3 donates its lone pair to H+ to form NH4+. The four major bond types are ionic, covalent, dative and metallic.

mcqs.q: Arrange the following from strongest to weakest attraction: covalent bond, dipole-dipole interaction, hydrogen bond, ionic bond.
options: Covalent bond > ionic bond > hydrogen bond > dipole-dipole interaction
Hydrogen bond > ionic bond > covalent bond > dipole-dipole interaction
Ionic bond > covalent bond > hydrogen bond > dipole-dipole interaction
Ionic bond > hydrogen bond > covalent bond > dipole-dipole interaction
mcqs.why: Ionic and covalent bonds are true chemical bonds and are much stronger than intermolecular forces. A hydrogen bond is about twenty times weaker than a covalent bond but about ten times stronger than a dipole-dipole interaction, which is the weakest of the four.

mcqs.q: Why do ionic compounds conduct electricity when molten or in solution but not in the solid state?
options: Ionic compounds contain free electrons only when they melt
Water changes the ions into neutral atoms
In the solid the ions are fixed in the lattice, but when molten or dissolved the ions are free to move
In the solid state the ions lose their charges
mcqs.why: An electrolyte conducts through the movement of ions. In the solid, strong electrostatic forces hold the ions in fixed lattice positions so they cannot move; melting or dissolving breaks the lattice down and the free ions can carry current to the electrodes.

mcqs.q: Which types of atoms tend to form ionic bonding?
options: A metal atom and a non-metal atom
Atoms of metals only, in a metallic lattice
Two atoms of the same non-metal
mcqs.why: In ionic bonding the metal atom loses electrons and the non-metal atom gains them, for example sodium and chlorine form NaCl. Two non-metals share electrons in covalent bonding, and metal atoms alone form metallic bonding.

mcqs.q: Which is an example of a non-polar molecule with polar bonds?
mcqs.why: Each C=O bond in CO2 is polar because oxygen is more electronegative than carbon, but CO2 is a linear molecule (O=C=O, 180 degrees), so the two equal and opposite bond polarities cancel and the molecule as a whole is non-polar.

mcqs.q: What is the bond type in calcium chloride, CaCl2?
mcqs.why: Calcium is a metal and chlorine is a non-metal. Calcium transfers one electron to each of two chlorine atoms, forming Ca2+ and two Cl- ions, so CaCl2 is an ionic compound.

mcqs.q: Why are ionic compounds good conductors compared to covalent compounds?
options: Ionic compounds contain ions that are free to move when molten or in solution, while covalent compounds consist of neutral molecules with no ions
Covalent compounds contain ions that are fixed in a lattice
Ionic compounds are made only of non-metal atoms
Covalent compounds conduct only in the solid state
mcqs.why: Ionic compounds contain charged particles; when molten or dissolved these ions move freely and carry current, making them good electrolytes. Covalent compounds are neutral molecules with no ions and no free electrons, so they are poor conductors in any state.

mcqs.q: Why is a dative bond always polar?
options: A dative bond is formed between a metal and a non-metal
A dative bond contains three shared pairs of electrons
The shared pair is provided by one atom only, so the sharing is unequal and partial charges are produced
Both atoms in a dative bond have equal electronegativity
mcqs.why: In a dative bond the donor provides the whole shared pair while the acceptor contributes nothing, so the pair is not shared equally and poles (partial charges) appear on the two atoms. Unequal sharing is exactly what makes a bond polar.

lessons.title: Detailed Answers
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • Octet rule: atoms tend to attain eight electrons in the outermost shell (duplet for the first shell) to become stable like the noble gases.
  • Ionic bonding transfers electrons (NaCl: Na+ 2,8 and Cl- 2,8,8); covalent bonding shares electrons between non-metals (CH4).
  • Electronegativity difference more than 1.7 gives an ionic bond; less than 1.7 gives a covalent bond; zero difference gives a non-polar covalent bond.
  • Lewis structures: CCl4 has four single bonds tetrahedrally; BF3 has three single bonds and boron has only six electrons (incomplete octet).
  • Metals are malleable and ductile because layers of ions slide while the electron sea holds them; ionic crystals shatter because like charges repel when layers shift.
  • A polar bond has unequal sharing with delta+ and delta- ends (HCl); a non-polar bond has equal sharing between identical atoms (H2, Cl2, O2).

Solved Exercises

Exercise — Long Questions

Q: (i) Describe the octet rule in terms of noble-gas configurations and stability.

Ans: The octet rule (rule of eight) states that atoms tend to attain eight electrons in their outermost shell in order to attain stability. The noble gases of group VIII - helium, neon, argon, krypton, etc. - are very stable and rarely take part in chemical reactions because their outermost shells are completely filled: except for helium, which has a duplet of 2 electrons, every noble gas has an octet of 8 electrons in its outermost shell (Ne 2,8; Ar 2,8,8). All other atoms have incomplete outer shells and are unstable. When such atoms react, they lose, gain or share electrons so that their outermost shell also gets eight electrons (or two, for the first shell - the duplet rule) and they attain the electronic configuration of the nearest noble gas. For example, sodium (2,8,1) loses one electron to attain the neon configuration, chlorine (2,8,7) gains one electron to attain the argon configuration, and oxygen (2,6) shares or gains two electrons to complete its octet. Stability therefore comes from the completely filled outermost shell.

Q: (ii)(a) What is the main distinction between ionic and covalent bonding? Explain your answer with suitable examples.

Ans: The main distinction is in how the atoms complete their outer shells. In ionic bonding, electrons are completely transferred from one atom to the other: a metal atom loses electrons and forms a positive ion (cation) and a non-metal atom gains those electrons and forms a negative ion (anion); the electrostatic attraction between these oppositely charged ions is the ionic bond. Example: in NaCl, sodium (2,8,1) transfers its outer electron to chlorine (2,8,7), forming Na+ (2,8) and Cl- (2,8,8), which attract each other and form a crystalline lattice. In covalent bonding, no electron is transferred; two non-metal atoms mutually share pairs of electrons, and the shared pair, attracted by both nuclei, holds the atoms together. Example: in CH4, carbon shares one electron with each of four hydrogen atoms, forming four shared pairs, so carbon completes its octet and each hydrogen its duplet, and a molecule - not a lattice of ions - is formed.

Q: (ii)(b) How is electronegativity used in determining the ionic or covalent character of the bonding between two elements?

Ans: Electronegativity is the tendency of an atom to attract the shared pair of electrons towards itself. The character of a bond is decided by the difference in electronegativity of the two bonded atoms, as stated in this unit. If the electronegativity difference is more than 1.7, the more electronegative atom pulls the electrons so strongly that they are effectively transferred to it; ions are formed and the bond is ionic, e.g. NaCl. If the difference is less than 1.7, the electrons are shared rather than transferred and the bond is covalent, e.g. HCl. Within covalent bonds, a difference of zero (same atoms, e.g. H2, Cl2) gives a non-polar covalent bond with equal sharing, while a moderate difference between two different non-metals gives a polar covalent bond with unequal sharing.

Q: (iii) Draw the Lewis structure for each of the following compounds: a. CO b. HCl c. SO2 d. CCl4 e. BF3 f. NH3 (Describe each structure in words.)

Ans: a. CO (carbon monoxide): Carbon (4 valence electrons) and oxygen (6 valence electrons) are joined by a triple bond (three shared pairs, shown as three lines between C and O). One lone pair remains on carbon and one lone pair remains on oxygen, so both atoms complete their octet (10 valence electrons in total). b. HCl: Hydrogen and chlorine are joined by a single bond (one shared pair, one line). Chlorine carries three lone pairs; hydrogen has no lone pair and completes its duplet. c. SO2: Sulphur is the central atom joined to two oxygen atoms in a bent arrangement - in one form sulphur is joined to one oxygen by a double bond (two lines) and to the other oxygen by a single bond (one line), and the two forms exchange places (resonance). Sulphur carries one lone pair; the double-bonded oxygen carries two lone pairs and the single-bonded oxygen carries three lone pairs. d. CCl4: Carbon is the central atom joined to four chlorine atoms by four single bonds, arranged tetrahedrally. Each chlorine carries three lone pairs; carbon has no lone pair and completes its octet. e. BF3: Boron is the central atom joined to three fluorine atoms by three single bonds, arranged in a trigonal planar shape (120 degrees). Each fluorine carries three lone pairs; boron has no lone pair and has only six electrons around it (an incomplete octet). f. NH3: Nitrogen is the central atom joined to three hydrogen atoms by three single bonds. Nitrogen carries one lone pair and completes its octet; each hydrogen completes its duplet. The molecule is trigonal pyramidal.

Q: (iv) Explain why most metals are malleable and ductile but ionic crystals are not.

Ans: Metals are malleable (can be beaten into sheets) and ductile (can be drawn into wires) because of metallic bonding. In a metal, the positive metal ions are arranged in layers in a lattice, held together by the sea of delocalised electrons, which attracts every ion from all sides and is non-directional. When a force is applied, one layer of ions can slide over another layer into a new position, but the electron sea still surrounds and holds the ions, so the metal changes shape without breaking. In an ionic crystal, the ions are arranged in a regular lattice in which each positive ion is surrounded by negative ions and vice versa. If the crystal is struck and the layers shift even slightly, ions of the same charge come opposite each other and repel strongly, so the crystal splits and shatters along that plane. Ionic crystals are therefore brittle - they are neither malleable nor ductile.

Q: (v) a. What is the meaning of the term polar, as applied to chemical bonding? b. Distinguish between polar-covalent and non-polar-covalent bonds.

Ans: a. A bond is called polar when the shared pair of electrons is attracted unequally by the two bonded atoms, so that one end of the bond becomes partially positively charged (delta+) and the other end partially negatively charged (delta-); the bond thus has two poles, like a dipole. This happens when the two atoms have different electronegativities, e.g. in H-Cl the shared pair is pulled more towards chlorine, so H becomes delta+ and Cl becomes delta-. b. Polar covalent bond: formed between two different atoms with different electronegativities; the shared pair is displaced towards the more electronegative atom and opposite partial charges appear, e.g. HCl, H2O and NH3. Non-polar covalent bond: formed between two similar atoms with equal (or almost equal) electronegativities; the shared pair lies midway between the atoms, is attracted equally by both, and no charges or poles are created, e.g. H2, Cl2 and O2.

mcqs.q: The octet rule states that atoms tend to:
options: Attain eight electrons in their innermost shell
Attain eight electrons in their outermost shell in order to attain stability
Lose all the electrons of their outermost shell
Gain eight electrons from other atoms
mcqs.why: The octet rule (rule of eight) states that atoms tend to attain eight electrons in their outermost shell, like the noble gases, in order to become stable. They do this by losing, gaining or sharing electrons; the first shell follows the duplet rule of two electrons.

mcqs.q: Why are the noble gases very stable and rarely take part in chemical reactions?
options: They have the largest atoms in each period
They have equal numbers of protons and neutrons
Their atoms are bonded to each other in molecules
Their outermost shells are completely filled (an octet, or a duplet for helium)
mcqs.why: Except for helium, which has a duplet of 2 electrons, every noble gas has an octet of 8 electrons in its completely filled outermost shell, for example Ne 2,8 and Ar 2,8,8. This complete shell makes them stable and unreactive.

mcqs.q: What is the main distinction between ionic and covalent bonding?
options: In ionic bonding electrons are transferred, while in covalent bonding electrons are shared
In ionic bonding electrons are shared, while in covalent bonding they are transferred
Ionic bonding occurs between two non-metals, covalent bonding between a metal and a non-metal
Covalent bonding forms a lattice of ions, ionic bonding forms molecules
mcqs.why: In ionic bonding a metal atom loses electrons to form a cation and a non-metal gains them to form an anion, and the ions attract each other. In covalent bonding no transfer takes place; two non-metal atoms mutually share pairs of electrons, as in CH4.

mcqs.q: In the formation of sodium chloride, NaCl, sodium (2,8,1) and chlorine (2,8,7) form ions with configurations:
mcqs.why: Sodium transfers its one outer electron to chlorine. Sodium becomes Na+ with the neon configuration 2,8, and chlorine becomes Cl- with the argon configuration 2,8,8, and the oppositely charged ions form a crystalline lattice.

mcqs.q: If the electronegativity difference between two bonded atoms is more than 1.7, the bond is:
mcqs.why: A difference of more than 1.7 means the more electronegative atom pulls the electrons so strongly that they are effectively transferred to it, forming ions and an ionic bond, as in NaCl. A smaller difference gives a covalent bond, as in HCl.

mcqs.q: A covalent bond between two identical atoms, such as H2 or Cl2, is non-polar because:
options: The electronegativity difference is zero and the electrons are shared equally
The electronegativity difference is more than 1.7
One atom donates both electrons of the pair
The atoms carry partial positive and negative charges
mcqs.why: Identical atoms have equal electronegativity, so the difference is zero and the shared pair is attracted equally by both nuclei and lies midway between them. No poles or partial charges are created, so the bond is non-polar covalent.

mcqs.q: In the Lewis structure of BF3, boron has:
options: A complete octet and one lone pair
A triple bond to one fluorine atom
Only six electrons around it, an incomplete octet, with three single bonds to fluorine atoms
mcqs.why: Boron is the central atom in BF3, joined to three fluorine atoms by three single bonds in a trigonal planar shape (120 degrees). Boron has no lone pair and only six electrons around it, so it is an exception with an incomplete octet.

mcqs.q: In the Lewis structure of CCl4, carbon is:
options: Joined to four chlorine atoms by two double bonds
Joined to four chlorine atoms by four single bonds, arranged tetrahedrally, with no lone pair on carbon
Joined to three chlorine atoms with one lone pair on carbon
Joined to four chlorine atoms by ionic bonds in a lattice
mcqs.why: Carbon is the central atom in CCl4 and shares one electron with each of four chlorine atoms, forming four single covalent bonds in a tetrahedral arrangement. Each chlorine carries three lone pairs and carbon completes its octet with no lone pair.

mcqs.q: Why are most metals malleable and ductile?
options: Layers of positive metal ions can slide over each other while the electron sea still holds them together
Metal ions are held by weak forces that break easily
Metals are made of neutral molecules that roll over each other
Metallic bonds exist only at the surface of the metal
mcqs.why: In a metal the positive ions sit in layers held by the non-directional sea of delocalised electrons. When a force is applied one layer slides over another, but the electron sea still surrounds and holds the ions, so the metal changes shape without breaking; ionic crystals instead shatter because like charges come opposite each other and repel.

mcqs.q: A bond is called polar when:
options: The shared pair lies exactly midway between the two atoms
Electrons are completely transferred from one atom to the other
The shared pair of electrons is attracted unequally, so one end becomes delta+ and the other delta-
The two atoms have exactly equal electronegativities
mcqs.why: Polar means the bond has two poles: because the atoms have different electronegativities, the shared pair is pulled towards the more electronegative atom, making it partially negative (delta-) and the other atom partially positive (delta+), as in H-Cl.

lessons.title: Test Yourself and Practice Problems
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • Atoms form ions by losing electrons (metals, cations) or gaining electrons (non-metals, anions) to attain a noble-gas configuration.
  • Ions formed: Ca2+, F-, Li+ and O2-; ionic bonds form between a metal and a non-metal, e.g. MgO (1:1) and MgCl2 (1:2).
  • H2O has two single bonds and two lone pairs on oxygen; NH3 has three single bonds and one lone pair on nitrogen.
  • Ionic substances: NaCl and MgCl2; covalent substances: CO2, H2O, C6H6 and HCl; helium exists as uncombined atoms and HgO consists of ions.
  • A single bond shares 2 electrons and a double bond shares 4 electrons; covalent bonds form between non-metals.
  • NH3, H2O, HCl and SO2 have polar covalent bonds; N2, O2, CH4, H2, PH3 and Cl2 have non-polar covalent bonds.
  • H2O, CH3OH and NH3 form hydrogen bonds; metals are ductile (wires), malleable (sheets), lustrous, sonorous and good conductors of heat and electricity.

Solved Exercises

Test Yourself (p.97)

Q: 1a. In what ways do atoms form ions?

Ans: Atoms form ions in two ways. (1) By losing electrons: a metal atom loses one or more electrons from its outermost shell and becomes a positively charged ion, called a cation, e.g. Na loses one electron to form Na+. (2) By gaining electrons: a non-metal atom gains one or more electrons in its outermost shell and becomes a negatively charged ion, called an anion, e.g. Cl gains one electron to form Cl-.

Q: 1b. Why do atoms form ions?

Ans: Atoms form ions to complete their outermost shell and attain the stable electronic configuration of a noble gas - an octet of eight electrons, or a duplet of two electrons in the case of the first shell. An isolated atom with an incomplete outer shell is unstable and higher in energy, so it loses or gains electrons to become stable like the noble gases.

Q: 2. Ionic bonds are formed between which two types of elements?

Ans: Ionic bonds are formed between a metal and a non-metal. The metal atom loses electrons and forms a cation, the non-metal atom gains those electrons and forms an anion, and the electrostatic force of attraction between the oppositely charged ions is the ionic bond, e.g. sodium (metal) and chlorine (non-metal) form NaCl.

Q: 3. State the formula of the ions formed by the following atoms: a. Calcium (2,8,8,2) b. Fluorine (2,7) c. Lithium (2,1) d. Oxygen (2,6)

Ans: a. Calcium (2,8,8,2) loses its 2 outermost electrons to attain the argon configuration, so it forms Ca2+. b. Fluorine (2,7) gains 1 electron to complete its octet, so it forms F-. c. Lithium (2,1) loses its 1 outermost electron to attain the helium duplet, so it forms Li+. d. Oxygen (2,6) gains 2 electrons to complete its octet, so it forms O2-.

Q: 4. Draw a diagram to show the ionic bonds in magnesium oxide (MgO) and magnesium chloride (MgCl2). (Describe the diagrams in words.)

Ans: Magnesium oxide (MgO): Magnesium (2,8,2) has 2 electrons in its outermost shell and oxygen (2,6) needs 2 electrons. The magnesium atom transfers both its outer electrons to one oxygen atom. Magnesium becomes Mg2+ (2,8) with the neon configuration and oxygen becomes O2- (2,8) with the neon configuration. The oppositely charged Mg2+ and O2- ions attract each other strongly and form the ionic lattice of MgO, so one magnesium ion combines with one oxide ion (ratio 1:1). Magnesium chloride (MgCl2): The magnesium atom transfers one of its 2 outer electrons to one chlorine atom (2,8,7) and the second electron to a second chlorine atom. Magnesium becomes Mg2+ (2,8) and each chlorine becomes Cl- (2,8,8) with the argon configuration. One Mg2+ ion is held to two Cl- ions by ionic bonds, giving MgCl2 (ratio 1:2).

Practice Problem 4.1

Q: Draw an electron dot and cross diagram for H2O. Label the single bond and the lone pairs.

Ans: In the dot and cross diagram of water, the central oxygen atom (6 valence electrons) is placed between two hydrogen atoms (1 electron each). Oxygen shares one electron with each hydrogen atom, forming two shared pairs of electrons, i.e. two single covalent bonds (O-H and O-H); these are the single bond pairs.
