After sharing, oxygen has 8 electrons in its outer shell (octet) and each hydrogen has 2 electrons (duplet). The remaining four electrons of oxygen, which do not take part in bonding, stay on oxygen as two lone pairs. So the diagram shows: oxygen in the centre, one shared pair between oxygen and each hydrogen labelled 'single bond', and two pairs of dots on oxygen labelled 'lone pairs'.

Activity 4.1

Q: Classify the following substances as covalent or ionic: CO2, NaCl, H2O, C6H6, MgCl2 and HCl.

Ans: Ionic substances (formed between a metal and a non-metal by transfer of electrons): NaCl (sodium chloride) and MgCl2 (magnesium chloride). Covalent substances (formed between non-metals by sharing of electrons): CO2 (carbon dioxide), H2O (water), C6H6 (benzene) and HCl (hydrogen chloride).

Practice Problem 4.2

Q: Which one of the following is (1) uncombined atoms (2) molecules and (3) consist of ions? (a) H2 (b) He (c) HCl (d) HgO

Ans: (1) Uncombined atoms: (b) He - helium is a noble gas and exists as single, uncombined atoms. (2) Molecules: (a) H2 consists of molecules of two hydrogen atoms joined by a covalent bond, and (c) HCl consists of covalent molecules of hydrogen and chlorine. (3) Consist of ions: (d) HgO - mercury is a metal and oxygen is a non-metal, so mercury oxide is an ionic compound consisting of Hg2+ and O2- ions.

Practice Problem 4.3

Q: Draw the Lewis structure of ammonia, NH3.

Ans: Nitrogen (2,5) is the central atom with 5 valence electrons, and each hydrogen has 1 electron. Nitrogen shares one electron with each of the three hydrogen atoms, forming three single covalent bonds (N-H, N-H and N-H), shown as three lines from nitrogen to the three hydrogens. In this way nitrogen completes its octet (3 shared pairs + 1 lone pair = 8 electrons) and each hydrogen completes its duplet. The one pair of electrons of nitrogen that is not shared remains on nitrogen as a lone pair, shown as two dots on nitrogen. The molecule is trigonal pyramidal in shape.

Test Yourself (p.105)

Q: 1a. Which group of the elements form covalent bonds?

Ans: Covalent bonds are formed between non-metal elements. Two non-metal atoms, which both need electrons to complete their outer shells and cannot lose electrons easily, share pairs of electrons with each other and form a covalent bond, e.g. H2, Cl2, HCl and CH4.

Q: 1b. How is a covalent bond formed between two atoms?

Ans: A covalent bond is formed by the mutual sharing of electrons between two atoms. Each atom contributes one or more electrons to the shared pair(s), which remain between the two atoms and are attracted by both nuclei. By sharing, both atoms complete their outermost shell (octet or duplet) and attain a noble-gas configuration, e.g. two hydrogen atoms share one electron each to form the single covalent bond in H2.

Q: 2. How many electrons are shared in a. a single bond b. a double bond?

Ans: a. Single bond: 2 electrons are shared, i.e. one pair of electrons, one electron contributed by each atom. b. Double bond: 4 electrons are shared, i.e. two pairs of electrons, two electrons contributed by each atom.

Q: 3a. Draw a 'dot and cross' diagram to show the bonding in chlorine, Cl2. (Describe it in words.)

Ans: Each chlorine atom (2,8,7) has 7 electrons in its outer shell. The two chlorine atoms overlap their outer shells and share one pair of electrons - one electron (shown as a dot) from one atom and one electron (shown as a cross) from the other - forming a single covalent bond, Cl-Cl. After sharing, each chlorine atom has 8 electrons in its outer shell (octet, argon configuration): the one shared pair between the atoms and three lone pairs (6 electrons) remaining on each chlorine atom.

Q: 3b. Draw a 'dot and cross' diagram to show the bonding in hydrogen chloride, HCl. (Describe it in words.)

Ans: Hydrogen (1 electron) shares its one electron (shown as a cross) with one electron (shown as a dot) of chlorine (2,8,7), forming one shared pair, i.e. a single covalent bond H-Cl. After sharing, hydrogen has 2 electrons (duplet, helium configuration) and chlorine has 8 electrons in its outer shell (octet): the one shared pair between H and Cl and three lone pairs remaining on chlorine.

Q: 3c. Draw a 'dot and cross' diagram to show the bonding in ammonia, NH3. (Describe it in words.)

Ans: Nitrogen (2,5) is the central atom. It shares three of its five outer electrons, one with each of three hydrogen atoms, forming three shared pairs, i.e. three single covalent bonds N-H. After sharing, nitrogen has 8 electrons in its outer shell (3 shared pairs + 1 lone pair) and each hydrogen has 2 electrons (duplet). The remaining two electrons of nitrogen stay on it as one lone pair, shown as a pair of dots on nitrogen.

Test Yourself (p.108) — Lewis Structure and Type of Bond

Q: 1. Ammonia, NH3 — give its Lewis structure (in words) and type of bond (polar / non-polar covalent).

Ans: Lewis structure: nitrogen is the central atom, joined to three hydrogen atoms by three single bonds (three lines), with one lone pair of electrons on nitrogen. Type of bond: polar covalent, because nitrogen is more electronegative than hydrogen, so the shared pairs are attracted more towards nitrogen.

Q: 2. Water, H2O — give its Lewis structure (in words) and type of bond (polar / non-polar covalent).

Ans: Lewis structure: oxygen is the central atom, joined to two hydrogen atoms by two single bonds, with two lone pairs of electrons on oxygen. The molecule is angular (bent). Type of bond: polar covalent, because oxygen is much more electronegative than hydrogen, so the shared pairs are pulled towards oxygen.

Q: 3. Hydrogen chloride, HCl — give its Lewis structure (in words) and type of bond (polar / non-polar covalent).

Ans: Lewis structure: hydrogen is joined to chlorine by a single bond (one line), and chlorine carries three lone pairs of electrons. Type of bond: polar covalent, because chlorine is more electronegative than hydrogen, so the shared pair is attracted more towards chlorine, giving H a partial positive charge and Cl a partial negative charge.

Q: 4. Nitrogen, N2 — give its Lewis structure (in words) and type of bond (polar / non-polar covalent).

Ans: Lewis structure: the two nitrogen atoms are joined by a triple bond (three lines, N triple-bond N), and each nitrogen carries one lone pair of electrons. Type of bond: non-polar covalent, because both atoms are identical and have equal electronegativity, so the shared pairs are attracted equally by both atoms.

Q: 5. Oxygen, O2 — give its Lewis structure (in words) and type of bond (polar / non-polar covalent).

Ans: Lewis structure: the two oxygen atoms are joined by a double bond (two lines, O double-bond O), and each oxygen carries two lone pairs of electrons. Type of bond: non-polar covalent, because both atoms are identical and share the electrons equally.

Q: 6. Methane, CH4 — give its Lewis structure (in words) and type of bond (polar / non-polar covalent).

Ans: Lewis structure: carbon is the central atom, joined to four hydrogen atoms by four single bonds; there is no lone pair on carbon. The molecule is tetrahedral. Type of bond: non-polar covalent, because carbon and hydrogen have almost equal electronegativities and the symmetrical tetrahedral molecule has no overall poles.

Q: 7. Hydrogen, H2 — give its Lewis structure (in words) and type of bond (polar / non-polar covalent).

Ans: Lewis structure: the two hydrogen atoms are joined by a single bond (one line, H-H); neither atom has a lone pair. Type of bond: non-polar covalent, because both atoms are identical and share the pair of electrons equally.

Q: 8. Phosphine, PH3 — give its Lewis structure (in words) and type of bond (polar / non-polar covalent).

Ans: Lewis structure: phosphorus is the central atom, joined to three hydrogen atoms by three single bonds, with one lone pair of electrons on phosphorus. Type of bond: non-polar covalent, because phosphorus and hydrogen have almost equal electronegativities, so the shared pairs are attracted almost equally.

Q: 9. Sulphur dioxide, SO2 — give its Lewis structure (in words) and type of bond (polar / non-polar covalent).

Ans: Lewis structure: sulphur is the central atom joined to two oxygen atoms - one by a double bond and one by a single bond in one form, with the positions exchanged in the other form (resonance); sulphur carries one lone pair, the double-bonded oxygen carries two lone pairs and the single-bonded oxygen carries three lone pairs. The molecule is bent. Type of bond: polar covalent, because oxygen is more electronegative than sulphur, so the shared pairs are pulled towards oxygen.

Q: 10. Chlorine, Cl2 — give its Lewis structure (in words) and type of bond (polar / non-polar covalent).

Ans: Lewis structure: the two chlorine atoms are joined by a single bond (one line, Cl-Cl), and each chlorine carries three lone pairs of electrons. Type of bond: non-polar covalent, because both atoms are identical and share the pair of electrons equally.

Activity 4.3

Q: Identify ten common substances in and around your home and indicate whether you would expect these substances to contain ionic, covalent or metallic bonds.

Ans: Metallic bonds: (1) iron in nails and tools, (2) copper in electric wires, (3) aluminium in cooking pots and foil. Ionic bonds: (4) common salt, NaCl, used in food, (5) washing soda / baking soda, (6) lime (calcium oxide / calcium hydroxide) used in whitewash. Covalent bonds: (7) water, H2O, (8) sugar, (9) cooking oil / ghee, (10) plastic and wood, which are made of covalent molecules. Metals contain metallic bonds, metal-non-metal compounds such as salts contain ionic bonds, and substances made only of non-metals contain covalent bonds.

Practice Problem 4.4

Q: Which of the following substances are expected to form hydrogen bonds? (a) H2O (b) CH3OH (c) NH3

Ans: All three substances form hydrogen bonds. (a) H2O: hydrogen is covalently bonded to highly electronegative oxygen, and oxygen has lone pairs, so the partially positively charged hydrogen of one water molecule is attracted to the oxygen of a neighbouring molecule. (b) CH3OH (methanol): it contains an -OH group, i.e. hydrogen bonded to oxygen, and oxygen has lone pairs, so hydrogen bonds form between its molecules. (c) NH3: hydrogen is bonded to highly electronegative nitrogen, and nitrogen has a lone pair, so hydrogen bonds form between ammonia molecules.

Activity 4.4

Q: Complete the table: General property of metals: 'can be drawn into wires' — give the correct name for this property and one use that depends on it.

Ans: Correct name: ductility (the metal is ductile). Use: making electric wires, e.g. copper and aluminium wires, which depends on the metal being drawn into thin wires without breaking.

Q: Complete the table: General property of metals: 'can be bent into shape' — give the correct name for this property and one use that depends on it.

Ans: Correct name: malleability (the metal is malleable). Use: beating metals into sheets and foils and bending them into the shapes of utensils, sheets for roofs and bodies of vehicles.

Q: Complete the table: General property of metals: 'reflect light' — give the correct name for this property and one use that depends on it.

Ans: Correct name: lustre (metals are lustrous). Use: jewellery and ornaments of gold and silver, and shiny utensils and mirrors, which look attractive because their surfaces reflect light.

Q: Complete the table: General property of metals: 'make a ringing sound when struck' — give the correct name for this property and one use that depends on it.

Ans: Correct name: sonorous (metals are sonorous). Use: school bells and musical instruments are made of metals because they produce a specific ringing sound when struck.

Q: Complete the table: General property of metals: 'allow electricity to pass through' — give the correct name for this property and one use that depends on it.

Ans: Correct name: electrical conductivity (metals are good conductors of electricity). Use: copper and aluminium are used for electric wires and cables to carry electric current.

Q: Complete the table: General property of metals: 'heavy for their volume' — give the correct name for this property and one use that depends on it.

Ans: Correct name: high density. Use: heavy metals such as lead and iron are used for weights, machinery parts and sinkers, where a large mass in a small volume is needed.

Q: Complete the table: General property of metals: 'transfer heat well' — give the correct name for this property and one use that depends on it.

Ans: Correct name: thermal conductivity (metals are good conductors of heat). Use: cooking utensils and pots are made of aluminium and steel because they transfer heat quickly and evenly to the food.

mcqs.q: In what way does a metal atom form an ion?
options: By gaining electrons to form an anion
By losing one or more electrons from its outermost shell to form a cation
By sharing electrons with a non-metal atom
By losing protons from its nucleus
mcqs.why: A metal atom loses one or more electrons from its outermost shell and becomes a positively charged ion, called a cation, for example Na loses one electron to form Na+. Non-metal atoms gain electrons and form anions.

mcqs.q: Why do atoms form ions?
options: To change into a different element
To complete their outermost shell and attain the stable configuration of a noble gas (octet, or duplet in the first shell)
mcqs.why: An atom with an incomplete outer shell is unstable and higher in energy. By losing or gaining electrons it completes its outermost shell with an octet of eight electrons (or a duplet of two in the first shell) and becomes stable like the noble gases.

mcqs.q: Ionic bonds are formed between which two types of elements?
options: A noble gas and a metal
mcqs.why: In ionic bonding the metal atom loses electrons and forms a cation while the non-metal gains them and forms an anion, and the electrostatic attraction between the ions is the ionic bond, as when sodium and chlorine form NaCl.

mcqs.q: Calcium has the configuration (2,8,8,2). What is the formula of the ion it forms?
mcqs.why: Calcium loses its 2 outermost electrons to attain the argon configuration. Losing two negatively charged electrons leaves a charge of 2+, so calcium forms the Ca2+ ion.

mcqs.q: Oxygen has the configuration (2,6). What is the formula of the ion it forms?
mcqs.why: Oxygen has six electrons in its outer shell and gains 2 electrons to complete its octet. Gaining two negatively charged electrons gives the oxide ion a charge of 2-, written O2-.

mcqs.q: In the dot and cross diagram of H2O, the central oxygen atom has:
options: Two single covalent bonds and two lone pairs
Three single covalent bonds and one lone pair
One double bond and two lone pairs
Four single covalent bonds and no lone pairs
mcqs.why: Oxygen shares one electron with each of two hydrogen atoms, forming two single covalent bonds, so oxygen reaches an octet and each hydrogen a duplet. The remaining four electrons of oxygen do not take part in bonding and stay as two lone pairs.

mcqs.q: Which of the following substances is ionic?
mcqs.why: Sodium chloride is formed between the metal sodium and the non-metal chlorine by transfer of electrons, so it is ionic, as is MgCl2. CO2, H2O, C6H6 and HCl are formed between non-metals by sharing electrons, so they are covalent.

mcqs.q: Which of the following consists of uncombined atoms?
mcqs.why: Helium is a noble gas and exists as single, uncombined atoms. H2 and HCl consist of covalent molecules, while HgO is an ionic compound consisting of Hg2+ and O2- ions.

mcqs.q: In the Lewis structure of ammonia, NH3, nitrogen is joined to the three hydrogen atoms by:
options: Three single covalent bonds, with one lone pair left on nitrogen
One triple bond and two single bonds
Three single bonds, with no lone pair on nitrogen
Ionic bonds to three H+ ions
mcqs.why: Nitrogen (2,5) shares one electron with each of three hydrogen atoms, forming three single covalent bonds shown as three lines. Nitrogen completes its octet (3 shared pairs + 1 lone pair) and the unshared pair remains on nitrogen as a lone pair; the molecule is trigonal pyramidal.

mcqs.q: Covalent bonds are formed between which group of elements?
mcqs.why: Two non-metal atoms both need electrons to complete their outer shells and cannot lose electrons easily, so they share pairs of electrons and form a covalent bond, as in H2, Cl2, HCl and CH4.

mcqs.q: How many electrons are shared in a double bond?
mcqs.why: A single bond shares 2 electrons, one pair, with one electron from each atom. A double bond shares 4 electrons, two pairs, with two electrons contributed by each atom.

mcqs.q: What type of bond is present in ammonia, NH3?
mcqs.why: In NH3 nitrogen is joined to three hydrogens by three single bonds with one lone pair on nitrogen. Nitrogen is more electronegative than hydrogen, so the shared pairs are attracted more towards nitrogen and the bonds are polar covalent.

mcqs.q: In nitrogen, N2, the two atoms are joined by a triple bond and the bond type is:
mcqs.why: The two nitrogen atoms in N2 are identical and have equal electronegativity, so the three shared pairs are attracted equally by both atoms. The Lewis structure shows a triple bond with one lone pair on each nitrogen, and the bond is non-polar covalent.

mcqs.q: Which of the following substances is expected to form hydrogen bonds?
mcqs.why: In water, hydrogen is covalently bonded to highly electronegative oxygen, which has lone pairs, so the partially positive hydrogen of one molecule is attracted to the oxygen of a neighbouring molecule. H2O, CH3OH and NH3 all form hydrogen bonds in this way.

mcqs.q: The property of metals that allows them to be drawn into wires is called:
mcqs.why: Ductility is the property of being drawn into thin wires without breaking, used in making copper and aluminium electric wires. Malleability is being bent or beaten into shape, lustre is reflecting light, and sonorous metals ring when struck.

lessons.title: Project Work
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • Linus Pauling wrote The Nature of the Chemical Bond (1939), applying quantum mechanics to chemical bonding.
  • Pauling introduced the electronegativity scale; fluorine has the highest value, 4.0.
  • The difference of electronegativity values predicts the bond type: more than 1.7 gives an ionic bond, less gives a covalent bond.
  • Pauling explained resonance (a molecule combining more than one Lewis structure) and hybridisation of orbitals for molecular shapes.
  • Pauling received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1954 and the Nobel Peace Prize in 1962.

Solved Exercises

Project Work

Q: Prepare a report on the work of Linus Pauling. Discuss his work on the nature of the chemical bond.

Ans: Linus Pauling (1901-1994) was an American chemist whose book 'The Nature of the Chemical Bond' (1939) is one of the most important chemistry books of the twentieth century. Applying quantum mechanics to chemistry, he explained how atoms share electrons in covalent bonds, described resonance - a molecule being a combination of more than one Lewis structure, as in SO2 and benzene - and introduced the idea of hybridisation of atomic orbitals to explain the shapes of molecules such as tetrahedral CH4. His most lasting contribution to this unit is the electronegativity scale: he assigned each element a number measuring its power to attract the shared pair of electrons in a bond (fluorine, the highest, is 4.0). The difference between the electronegativity values of two bonded atoms predicts whether their bond will be ionic, polar covalent or non-polar covalent - the rule used in this unit, that a difference of more than 1.7 gives an ionic bond and a smaller difference gives a covalent bond, comes directly from Pauling's work. He also worked out the structures of proteins and was awarded the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1954 (and the Nobel Peace Prize in 1962).

lessons.title: Multiple Choice Questions
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • Diffusion is the spontaneous mixing of particles of different substances.
  • Solid particles are closely packed in a regular pattern with strong forces and very little space between them.
  • A liquid boils when its vapour pressure equals the external pressure, 101.325 kilo Pascal at normal pressure.
  • Vapour pressure of a liquid increases with increase of temperature and depends only on temperature in a closed container.
  • Lowering external pressure lowers the boiling point, so water can boil at 50 C at reduced pressure.
  • Glucose is a crystalline solid, while rubber, glass and plastic are amorphous solids.
  • At the freezing point liquid and solid coexist in dynamic equilibrium.

Solved Exercises

Exercise — Choose the Correct Option

Q: i. The spontaneous mixing of particles is called:

Options: (a) evaporation (b) sublimation (c) diffusion (d) boiling

Correct answer: diffusion

Q: ii. Which statement for the particles of solid is not correct?

Options: (a) they move at great speed (b) they are arranged in regular pattern (c) there is a very little space between the particles (d) the force of attraction between the particles are strong

Correct answer: they move at great speed

Q: iii. A liquid boils when its vapour pressure becomes equal to:

Options: (a) 760 cm of Hg (b) 1 Pascal (c) 101.325 kilo Pascal (d) 0.1 atm

Correct answer: 101.325 kilo Pascal

Q: iv. The vapour pressure of a liquid increases with the:

Options: (a) increase of pressure (b) increase of temperature (c) increase of intermolecular forces (d) increase of polarity of molecules

Correct answer: increase of temperature

Q: v. Water normally boils at 100°C but it is possible to boil at 50°C which variable would you have to change to do this?

Options: (a) increase external pressure (b) decrease external pressure (c) increase surface area (d) decrease surface area

Correct answer: decrease external pressure

Q: vi. The vapour pressure of a liquid in a closed container depends upon:

Options: (a) amount of liquid (b) surface area of the liquid (c) temperature (d) both (b) and (c)

Correct answer: temperature

Q: vii. Which one of the following is not an example of amorphous solid?

Options: (a) rubber (b) glass (c) glucose (d) plastic

Correct answer: glucose

Q: viii. At freezing point which one of the following coexists in dynamic equilibrium?

Options: (a) gas and solid (b) liquid and gas (c) liquid and solid (d) all of these

Correct answer: liquid and solid

Q: ix. Ink spreads in water because of:

Options: (a) vapour pressure (b) expansion (c) diffusion (d) compressibility of water

Correct answer: diffusion

Q: x. What will be the pressure of a gas, if the volume of the gas at 2 atmospheres is increased from 1.5 dm³ to 3 dm³?

Options: (a) 1 atmosphere (b) 1.5 atmosphere (c) 2 atmosphere (d) 2.5 atmosphere

Correct answer: 1 atmosphere

mcqs.q: i. The spontaneous mixing of particles is called:
mcqs.why: Diffusion is the spontaneous mixing of particles by their random motion until they are evenly distributed. Evaporation, sublimation and boiling are changes of state, not mixing.

mcqs.q: ii. Which statement for the particles of solid is not correct?
options: they are arranged in regular pattern
there is a very little space between the particles
the force of attraction between the particles are strong
mcqs.why: Solid particles are closely packed in a regular pattern, held by strong forces with very little space between them, so they only vibrate and do not move at great speed.

mcqs.q: iii. A liquid boils when its vapour pressure becomes equal to:
mcqs.why: A liquid boils when its vapour pressure becomes equal to the external atmospheric pressure. Normal atmospheric pressure is 101.325 kilo Pascal, which is 760 mm of Hg and 1 atm.

mcqs.q: iv. The vapour pressure of a liquid increases with the:
mcqs.why: Raising the temperature gives liquid molecules more kinetic energy, so more of them escape as vapour and the vapour pressure increases. Stronger intermolecular forces would lower it.

mcqs.q: v. Water normally boils at 100°C but it is possible to boil at 50°C which variable would you have to change to do this?
mcqs.why: Boiling occurs when vapour pressure equals external pressure. If external pressure is decreased, the vapour pressure needed is reached at a lower temperature, so water can boil at 50 C.

mcqs.q: vi. The vapour pressure of a liquid in a closed container depends upon:
mcqs.why: In a closed container vapour pressure at equilibrium depends only on temperature. Changing the amount of liquid, its surface area or the container volume does not change the equilibrium vapour pressure.

mcqs.q: vii. Which one of the following is not an example of amorphous solid?
mcqs.why: Glucose is a crystalline solid with particles in a regular pattern and a sharp melting point. Rubber, glass and plastic are amorphous solids with no regular arrangement.

mcqs.q: viii. At freezing point which one of the following coexists in dynamic equilibrium?
mcqs.why: At the freezing point the liquid and its solid coexist in dynamic equilibrium, with freezing and melting taking place at equal rates so both phases remain present.

mcqs.q: ix. Ink spreads in water because of:
mcqs.why: Ink particles mix spontaneously with water particles by random motion and spread evenly through the water. This spontaneous mixing of particles is diffusion.

mcqs.q: x. What will be the pressure of a gas, if the volume of the gas at 2 atmospheres is increased from 1.5 dm³ to 3 dm³?
mcqs.why: By Boyle law P1V1 = P2V2 at constant temperature. So P2 = P1V1 / V2 = 2 x 1.5 / 3 = 1 atmosphere. Doubling the volume halves the pressure.

lessons.title: Numerical and Short Answers
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • Boyle law: P1V1 = P2V2 at constant temperature, used for all pressure-volume numericals in this lesson.
  • Charles law: V1 / T1 = V2 / T2 at constant pressure, with temperature always in Kelvin, K = C + 273.
  • At high altitude external pressure is lower, water boils below 100 C and food cooks slowly.
  • Glass is amorphous and softens over a range; ice is crystalline and melts at a sharp temperature.
  • Gases have low density because molecules are far apart with large empty spaces between them.
  • A gas is compressible because its molecules can be pushed closer; a solid is not, as its particles are already closely packed.
  • A floating gas balloon comes down because the light gas escapes by effusion through tiny pores in the rubber.

Solved Exercises

Practice Problem 5.1

Q: Calculate the initial volume of a sample of gas at 1.20 atm. If its volume is changed to 70.4 cm³ as its pressure is changed to 3 atm at constant temperature.

Ans: Given: Initial pressure, P1 = 1.20 atm
Final pressure, P2 = 3 atm
Final volume, V2 = 70.4 cm³
Initial volume, V1 = ?
Temperature is constant, so Boyle's law applies.
Formula (Boyle's law): P1V1 = P2V2
Rearranged for V1: V1 = P2V2 / P1
Substitution: V1 = (3 atm × 70.4 cm³) / 1.20 atm
V1 = 211.2 / 1.20 cm³
Answer: V1 = 176 cm³

Point to Ponder (p.124)

Q: Why a gas filled balloon floating up in the room, comes down after a day or two?

Ans: The balloon is filled with a light gas whose molecules are very small. These molecules gradually escape out of the balloon, one by one, through the extremely tiny pores in the rubber skin. This escape of gas molecules through a hole of molecular size is called effusion, as described in this unit. As the light gas inside decreases, the balloon loses its lifting power, shrinks and slowly comes down after a day or two.

Exercise — Numerical Questions

Q: i. Calculate the final pressure of a sample of gas that is changed at constant temperature to 14.3 dm³ from 7.55 dm³ at 828 torr.

Ans: Given: Initial pressure, P1 = 828 torr
Initial volume, V1 = 7.55 dm³
Final volume, V2 = 14.3 dm³
Final pressure, P2 = ?
Temperature is constant, so Boyle's law applies.
Formula (Boyle's law): P1V1 = P2V2
Rearranged for P2: P2 = P1V1 / V2
Substitution: P2 = (828 torr × 7.55 dm³) / 14.3 dm³
P2 = 6251.4 / 14.3 torr
Answer: P2 = 437.16 torr

Q: ii. Calculate the final volume at 302 K of a 5.41 dm³ sample of gas originally at 353 K if the pressure does not change.

Ans: Given: Initial volume, V1 = 5.41 dm³
Initial temperature, T1 = 353 K
Final temperature, T2 = 302 K
Final volume, V2 = ?
Pressure is constant, so Charles's law applies.
Formula (Charles's law): V1 / T1 = V2 / T2
Rearranged for V2: V2 = V1 × T2 / T1
Substitution: V2 = (5.41 dm³ × 302 K) / 353 K
V2 = 1633.82 / 353 dm³
Answer: V2 = 4.63 dm³ (the book prints 4.62 dm³)

Q: iii. Calculate the initial volume at 0°C of a sample of gas that is changed to 731 cm³ by cooling to −14°C at constant pressure.

Ans: Given: Final volume, V2 = 731 cm³
Initial temperature, t1 = 0°C
Final temperature, t2 = −14°C
Initial volume, V1 = ?
Step 1 — Convert temperatures to Kelvin (K = °C + 273):
T1 = 0 + 273 = 273 K
T2 = −14 + 273 = 259 K
Pressure is constant, so Charles's law applies.
Formula (Charles's law): V1 / T1 = V2 / T2
Rearranged for V1: V1 = V2 × T1 / T2
Substitution: V1 = (731 cm³ × 273 K) / 259 K
V1 = 199563 / 259 cm³
Answer: V1 = 770.51 cm³ (the book prints 770.513 cm³)

Q: iv. A sample of a gas at room temperature occupies 0.80 dm³ at 1.5 atm. What will be its volume when the pressure of the gas is raised to 2.1 atm?

Ans: Given: Initial pressure, P1 = 1.5 atm
Initial volume, V1 = 0.80 dm³
Final pressure, P2 = 2.1 atm
Final volume, V2 = ?
Temperature (room temperature) is constant, so Boyle's law applies.
Formula (Boyle's law): P1V1 = P2V2
Rearranged for V2: V2 = P1V1 / P2
Substitution: V2 = (1.5 atm × 0.80 dm³) / 2.1 atm
V2 = 1.20 / 2.1 dm³
Answer: V2 = 0.571 dm³

Q: v. Calculate the final volume of 319°C of a sample of gas originally 5.13 dm³ at 171°C, if the pressure does not change.

Ans: Given: Initial volume, V1 = 5.13 dm³
Initial temperature, t1 = 171°C
Final temperature, t2 = 319°C
Final volume, V2 = ?
Step 1 — Convert temperatures to Kelvin (K = °C + 273):
T1 = 171 + 273 = 444 K
T2 = 319 + 273 = 592 K
Pressure does not change, so Charles's law applies.
Formula (Charles's law): V1 / T1 = V2 / T2
Rearranged for V2: V2 = V1 × T2 / T1
Substitution: V2 = (5.13 dm³ × 592 K) / 444 K
V2 = 3036.96 / 444 dm³
Answer: V2 = 6.84 dm³
Note: The book prints (Ans: 9.57 dm³). That value is obtained by using the Celsius temperatures directly (5.13 × 319 / 171 = 9.57). Charles's law, as stated in this unit, uses absolute (Kelvin) temperature, so with Kelvin conversion the correct answer is 6.84 dm³.

Exercise — Short Questions

Q: i. Can you give reason why it takes longer time to cook at high altitude?

Ans: At high altitude the atmospheric (external) pressure is lower than at sea level. A liquid boils when its vapour pressure becomes equal to the external pressure, so at high altitude water boils at a temperature less than 100°C. Food cooked in this lower-temperature water receives less heat, so it cooks slowly and takes a longer time. This is why pressure cookers, which raise the pressure and hence the boiling point, are used at high altitude.

Q: ii. Glass softens over a wide range of temperature. Ice melts at a specific temperature. Explain the reason for this difference.

Ans: Glass is an amorphous solid. Its particles are not arranged in a regular, ordered pattern, so it has no sharp melting point and softens gradually over a wide range of temperature. Ice is a crystalline solid. Its particles are arranged in a regular three-dimensional pattern, so it melts at one specific, sharp temperature (its melting point, 0°C), and the temperature stays constant until the whole solid has melted.

Q: iii. Explain why it happens that on a hot summer day when there is sweat on the body of a person, one feels cool under fast moving fan.

Ans: Evaporation causes cooling. The molecules of sweat with higher kinetic energy escape from the skin surface into the air as vapours, and they take their energy from the body, so the body feels cool. A fast moving fan blows away the vapours near the skin and brings fresh, drier air in their place, which increases the rate of evaporation of sweat. Faster evaporation removes more heat from the body, so a person feels cooler under the fan.

Q: iv. Why are the densities of gases lower than that of liquids?

Ans: Density is mass per unit volume. In gases the molecules are far away from each other, there are large empty spaces between them and the intermolecular forces are very weak, so a given mass of a gas occupies a very large volume and its density is very low. In liquids the molecules are close to each other with much smaller empty spaces, so the same mass occupies a much smaller volume and the density is higher. For example, gaseous oxygen has a density of 0.00142 g/cm³ at 0°C and 1 atmosphere, while liquid oxygen has a density of 1.149 g/cm³.

Q: v. What is the relationship between the atmospheric pressure and boiling point of a liquid?

Ans: A liquid boils when its vapour pressure becomes equal to the atmospheric (external) pressure. The boiling point therefore depends directly on the atmospheric pressure: with the increase in external pressure, the boiling point of a liquid also increases, and with the decrease in external pressure, the boiling point decreases. That is why at high altitude, where the atmospheric pressure is less than 760 mm of Hg, water boils at a temperature lower than 100°C, while a pressure cooker raises the boiling point by increasing the pressure.

Q: vi. Why a gas is compressible but a solid is not compressible? Give reason(s).

Ans: Gas molecules have large empty spaces between them and very weak intermolecular forces. When pressure is applied, the molecules are pushed closer together, the distance between them decreases and the volume decreases considerably, so a gas is highly compressible. In a solid, the particles are already closely packed in a fixed pattern and are held together by strong intermolecular forces, leaving almost no empty space between them. They cannot be pushed any closer, so a solid is not compressible.

mcqs.q: A gas at 1.20 atm has its volume changed to 70.4 cm3 when its pressure is changed to 3 atm at constant temperature. What was its initial volume?
mcqs.why: Boyle law: P1V1 = P2V2, so V1 = P2V2 / P1. Substitution: V1 = (3 atm x 70.4 cm3) / 1.20 atm = 211.2 / 1.20 = 176 cm3. This is Practice Problem 5.1.

mcqs.q: A gas at 828 torr and 7.55 dm3 is changed at constant temperature to 14.3 dm3. What is its final pressure?
mcqs.why: Boyle law: P1V1 = P2V2, so P2 = P1V1 / V2. Substitution: P2 = (828 torr x 7.55 dm3) / 14.3 dm3 = 6251.4 / 14.3 = 437.16 torr.

mcqs.q: A 5.41 dm3 gas sample originally at 353 K is cooled to 302 K at constant pressure. What is its final volume?
mcqs.why: Charles law: V1 / T1 = V2 / T2, so V2 = V1 x T2 / T1. Substitution: V2 = (5.41 dm3 x 302 K) / 353 K = 1633.82 / 353 = 4.63 dm3. The book prints 4.62 dm3, which is a rounding slip.

mcqs.q: A gas is cooled to -14 C at constant pressure and its final volume is 731 cm3. Its initial temperature was 0 C. What was its initial volume?
mcqs.why: Convert to Kelvin: T1 = 0 + 273 = 273 K, T2 = -14 + 273 = 259 K. Charles law: V1 = V2 x T1 / T2. Substitution: V1 = (731 cm3 x 273 K) / 259 K = 199563 / 259 = 770.51 cm3.

mcqs.q: A gas occupies 0.80 dm3 at 1.5 atm at room temperature. What volume will it occupy when the pressure is raised to 2.1 atm?
mcqs.why: Boyle law: P1V1 = P2V2, so V2 = P1V1 / P2. Substitution: V2 = (1.5 atm x 0.80 dm3) / 2.1 atm = 1.20 / 2.1 = 0.571 dm3. Higher pressure gives a smaller volume.

mcqs.q: A 5.13 dm3 gas sample at 171 C is heated to 319 C at constant pressure. What is its final volume?
mcqs.why: Convert to Kelvin: T1 = 171 + 273 = 444 K, T2 = 319 + 273 = 592 K. Charles law: V2 = V1 x T2 / T1 = (5.13 x 592) / 444 = 3036.96 / 444 = 6.84 dm3. The book prints 9.57 dm3 because it wrongly used Celsius temperatures directly; Charles law requires Kelvin.

mcqs.q: Why does food take longer to cook at high altitude?
options: Water boils at a higher temperature there, so food burns slowly
Atmospheric pressure is higher there, so water cannot boil
Food loses its heat to the cold air before cooking
Water boils at a temperature less than 100 C there, so food receives less heat
mcqs.why: At high altitude atmospheric pressure is lower, so water boils when its vapour pressure equals that lower pressure, at less than 100 C. Food in this cooler water receives less heat and cooks slowly.

mcqs.q: Why does glass soften over a wide range of temperature while ice melts at a specific temperature?
options: Glass is crystalline and ice is amorphous
Glass is amorphous with no regular particle pattern, while ice is crystalline with a regular pattern
Both are amorphous but glass contains more water
Ice contains impurities that give it a sharp melting point
mcqs.why: Glass is an amorphous solid; its particles are not regularly arranged, so it has no sharp melting point and softens gradually. Ice is crystalline, with a regular three dimensional pattern, so it melts sharply at 0 C.

mcqs.q: Why are the densities of gases lower than those of liquids?
options: Gas molecules are far apart with large empty spaces, so a given mass occupies a very large volume
Gas molecules are heavier than liquid molecules
Liquids have large empty spaces between their molecules
Gases have stronger intermolecular forces than liquids
mcqs.why: Density is mass per unit volume. In gases molecules are far apart with weak forces, so the same mass occupies a much larger volume and density is low, for example gaseous oxygen is 0.00142 g/cm3 against 1.149 g/cm3 for liquid oxygen.

mcqs.q: Why does a gas filled balloon floating in a room come down after a day or two?
options: The gas inside condenses into a liquid and becomes heavy
Air diffuses into the balloon and makes it heavier at once
The light gas escapes by effusion through tiny pores in the rubber, so the balloon loses lifting power
The rubber absorbs all the gas in one day
mcqs.why: The balloon contains a light gas with very small molecules. They escape one by one through extremely tiny pores in the rubber by effusion. As the light gas decreases, the balloon shrinks, loses lifting power and comes down.

lessons.title: Detailed Answers
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • Boyle law: volume of a given mass of gas is inversely proportional to pressure at constant temperature, P1V1 = P2V2.
  • Evaporation is a slow surface process at all temperatures that causes cooling; boiling is rapid, throughout the liquid, at a fixed temperature.
  • Diffusion is free mixing in all directions; effusion is escape one by one through a hole of molecular size.
  • Condensation is the reverse of evaporation; at equilibrium their rates are equal and the vapour exerts vapour pressure.
  • Allotropy is existence of an element in more than one form, for example diamond, graphite and buckyball for carbon.
  • Diamond: each carbon bonded to four others, very hard, bad conductor. Graphite: bonded to three, layers slide, good conductor.
  • Charles law: volume is directly proportional to absolute temperature at constant pressure, V1 / T1 = V2 / T2.

Solved Exercises

Exercise — Long Questions

Q: i. Define Boyle's law and verify it experimentally.

Ans: Boyle's law (1662) states that the volume (V) of a given mass of a gas decreases with the increase of pressure (P) and vice versa, provided the temperature remains constant. Mathematically, V ∝ 1/P, so PV = Kb (constant for Boyle's law), and for a change from V1, P1 to V2, P2: P1V1 = P2V2. In other words, the product of pressure and volume of a given mass of gas remains constant at constant temperature.
Experimental verification: The apparatus is shown in Fig. 5.4 of the unit. A certain mass of gas is enclosed in a cylinder fitted with a pressure gauge and a thermometer to keep and check the temperature. The volume of the gas is changed by increasing and decreasing the pressure applied on it, and the volume at various pressures is noted. In each case, the product of pressure and volume (PV) remains constant at constant temperature, which verifies Boyle's law.

Q: ii. (a) Differentiate between Evaporation and Boiling point.

Ans: Evaporation is the spontaneous change of a liquid into the gaseous state at the surface of the liquid, without external heating. It takes place at all temperatures, it is a slow process, it occurs only from the surface, and it causes cooling because the higher-energy molecules escape and the temperature of the remaining liquid falls. Boiling is the rapid change of the whole liquid into vapours when it is heated. It takes place at one fixed temperature, the boiling point, at which the vapour pressure of the liquid becomes equal to the atmospheric or external pressure. During boiling, bubbles form throughout the liquid and rise to the surface, and the temperature of the liquid remains constant during boiling.

Q: ii. (b) Differentiate between Effusion and Diffusion of gases.

Ans: Diffusion is the spontaneous mixing of the molecules of different gases to form a homogeneous mixture by random motion and collision of the molecules. In diffusion, molecules move from a region of higher concentration to a region of lower concentration, freely and in all directions, until they are evenly distributed; for example, the smell of perfume spreads through a whole room. Effusion is the escape of molecules of a gas from its container one by one, without collision, through a hole of molecular dimension, that is, a hole about the size of one molecule, so that only one molecule can pass through it at a time; for example, we can smell onions even when the bag containing them is tightly sealed, due to effusion.

Q: ii. (c) Differentiate between Condensation and Evaporation.

Ans: Evaporation is the conversion of a liquid into its vapours from the surface of the liquid: the molecules whose kinetic energies are higher than the average overcome the intermolecular attractive forces, come out of the liquid and convert into the gaseous state. It takes place at all temperatures and causes cooling. Condensation is the opposite process, the conversion of vapours back into liquid: when a liquid evaporates in a closed container, some of the vapour molecules strike the surface of the liquid, lose their energy and become liquid again. When the rate of evaporation becomes equal to the rate of condensation, a state of equilibrium is reached, and the pressure exerted by the vapours at this equilibrium is called vapour pressure.

Q: iii. Define the term allotropy with examples. Explain the three allotropic forms of carbon in detail.

Ans: Allotropy is the existence of an element in more than one physical state or form; the different forms are called allotropic forms or allotropes, and this phenomenon is called allotropy. Allotropes have different physical properties but the same chemical properties. Examples: oxygen exists as oxygen (O2) and ozone (O3); sulphur shows allotropy in monoclinic and orthorhombic forms due to different arrangement of S8 molecules in the crystals; carbon exists as diamond, graphite and bucky balls, besides non-crystalline forms such as coke, charcoal and lampblack.
(i) Diamond: In diamond, carbon exists in cubic form. Each carbon atom is tetrahedrally bonded by four covalent bonds with other carbon atoms. The covalent bond is very strong, so diamond is very hard and has a high melting point. Diamond is a bad conductor of electricity because all the four valence electrons are used in the formation of covalent bonds, which are tightly held with each other.
(ii) Graphite: In graphite, each carbon atom is covalently bonded to only three other carbon atoms, rather than to four atoms as in diamond. Carbon exists in hexagonal form in sheets or layers. These sheets are linked with other carbon atoms by weak attractive forces, so the sheets slide over each other. Graphite is soft and is used as a lubricant in heavy machinery. It is a good conductor of electricity because it has a free electron available.
(iii) Buckyball: Buckyball is a crystalline allotropic form of carbon, recently discovered in 1985. A Buckyball consists of 20–100 carbon atoms arranged in a hollow, cage-like structure. The carbon atoms link with each other and adopt the shape of a football, joining together to make pentagonal, hexagonal etc. structures. Buckyballs are used as semiconductors, superconductors and lubricants.

Q: iv. What are solids? Differentiate between amorphous and crystalline solids.

Ans: The solid state is the state of matter in which the particles (molecules, ions) are closely packed in a fixed pattern. There is a strong force of attraction between the particles, which holds them firmly together, so they cannot leave their position and possess only vibrational motion. Hence solids have a definite shape and a definite volume, are rigid and have high density.
Difference between amorphous and crystalline solids: (1) Arrangement of particles — in amorphous solids the particles are not regularly arranged and lack ordered arrangement in three dimensions; in crystalline solids the particles (ions, atoms or molecules) are arranged in a regular three-dimensional pattern. (2) Melting point — amorphous solids do not have a sharp melting point and melt over a range of temperature, for example glass, wax and butter; crystalline solids have a sharp melting point, for example sodium chloride (NaCl) and naphthalene. (3) Shape and faces — amorphous solids are shapeless and have no definite faces; crystalline solids have definite surfaces or faces, and each face has a definite angle with the other face. Examples of amorphous solids: glass, wax, butter, plastics, rubber and cotton candy. Examples of crystalline solids: sodium chloride, naphthalene, diamond, graphite and glucose.

Q: v. Define Charles's law and verify it graphically and diagrammatically.

Ans: Charles's law (1787) states that the volume of a given mass of a gas is directly proportional to the absolute temperature at constant pressure. Mathematically, V ∝ T (at constant pressure), V = KcT, or V/T = Kc, so for a change from V1, T1 to V2, T2: V1/T1 = V2/T2. Absolute temperature means the temperature on the Kelvin scale, which is 273 units greater than the same temperature on the Celsius scale (K = °C + 273).
Graphical verification: If the values of volume 'V' are plotted against absolute temperature 'T', a straight line is obtained (Fig. 5.8). This straight line shows that the volume is directly proportional to the absolute temperature, which verifies Charles's law.
Diagrammatic verification: Charles's law can be represented diagrammatically as in Fig. 5.9. At constant pressure, as the temperature is increased step by step (T1, T2, T3, T4), the volume of the gas increases in the same proportion (V1, V2, V3, V4). This shows that increase in temperature causes a proportional increase in volume at constant pressure.

mcqs.q: According to Boyle law, for a given mass of gas at constant temperature, what remains constant?
options: The ratio of pressure to volume, P / V
The product of pressure and volume, PV
The sum of pressure and volume, P + V
The volume alone, whatever the pressure
mcqs.why: Boyle law states V is inversely proportional to P at constant temperature, so PV = Kb, a constant, and P1V1 = P2V2. In the experimental verification PV stays constant at each pressure.

mcqs.q: Which feature belongs to evaporation and not to boiling?
options: It takes place at one fixed temperature throughout the liquid
Bubbles form throughout the liquid during it
Its temperature remains constant while the whole liquid changes
It takes place only from the surface at all temperatures and causes cooling
mcqs.why: Evaporation is the spontaneous change of a liquid to gas from its surface only, at all temperatures, and it is slow and causes cooling. Boiling is rapid, occurs throughout the liquid at a fixed boiling point with bubbles forming inside.

mcqs.q: How does effusion differ from diffusion?
options: In effusion molecules escape one by one through a hole of molecular size, while in diffusion they mix freely in all directions
In effusion molecules mix freely, while in diffusion they escape through a tiny hole
Effusion occurs only in liquids, diffusion only in solids
Effusion needs heating, diffusion needs cooling
mcqs.why: Diffusion is spontaneous mixing of gas molecules moving from higher to lower concentration in all directions. Effusion is escape of molecules one by one, without collision, through a hole about the size of one molecule.

mcqs.q: When evaporation and condensation in a closed container reach equilibrium, what is the pressure exerted by the vapours called?
mcqs.why: Some vapour molecules strike the liquid surface, lose energy and condense. When the rate of evaporation equals the rate of condensation, equilibrium is reached and the pressure exerted by the vapours at this equilibrium is called vapour pressure.

mcqs.q: Which is a correct example of allotropy?
options: Water exists as ice and steam
Sodium chloride exists as solid and solution
Oxygen exists as O2 and ozone O3
Carbon dioxide exists as gas and dry ice
mcqs.why: Allotropy is the existence of an element in more than one physical form with different physical but same chemical properties. Oxygen as O2 and O3, sulphur in monoclinic and orthorhombic forms, and carbon as diamond and graphite are examples.

mcqs.q: Why is diamond very hard and a bad conductor of electricity?
options: Each carbon atom is bonded by four strong covalent bonds and all four valence electrons are used in bonding
Each carbon atom is bonded to only three others and has a free electron
Its layers slide over each other easily
It has a hollow cage like structure
mcqs.why: In diamond each carbon atom is tetrahedrally bonded to four other carbon atoms by strong covalent bonds, making it very hard with a high melting point. All valence electrons are used in bonds, so none is free to conduct electricity.

mcqs.q: Why is graphite soft and a good conductor of electricity?
options: Each carbon is bonded to four others in a cubic network
It is an amorphous solid with no bonds
Its cage structure traps electrons completely
Each carbon is bonded to three others in layers that slide, and it has a free electron
mcqs.why: In graphite each carbon atom is covalently bonded to only three others, forming hexagonal sheets held by weak forces, so sheets slide and graphite is soft and used as a lubricant. Its free electron makes it a good conductor.

mcqs.q: What is a buckyball?
options: A cubic form of carbon where each atom bonds to four others
A crystalline form of carbon of 20 to 100 atoms in a hollow cage like football shape, discovered in 1985
Sheets of carbon atoms used as a lubricant
A non crystalline form such as coke and charcoal
mcqs.why: A buckyball is a crystalline allotropic form of carbon discovered in 1985. It consists of 20 to 100 carbon atoms in a hollow cage like structure shaped like a football, and is used as a semiconductor, superconductor and lubricant.

mcqs.q: How do amorphous and crystalline solids differ in melting?
options: Amorphous solids have no sharp melting point and melt over a range, crystalline solids have a sharp melting point
Amorphous solids have a sharp melting point, crystalline solids melt over a range
Both melt at exactly the same sharp temperature
mcqs.why: In amorphous solids such as glass, wax and butter the particles are not regularly arranged, so they soften over a range of temperature. Crystalline solids such as sodium chloride and naphthalene have a regular three dimensional pattern and a sharp melting point.

mcqs.q: According to Charles law, what happens to the volume of a given mass of gas at constant pressure when its absolute temperature is increased?
options: Volume decreases in inverse proportion to temperature
Volume stays constant at all temperatures
Volume increases in the same proportion as the absolute temperature
Volume increases only if pressure also increases
mcqs.why: Charles law states volume is directly proportional to absolute temperature at constant pressure, V / T = Kc and V1 / T1 = V2 / T2. A graph of V against T in Kelvin is a straight line, verifying the law.
