Key Points

  • Crystalline solids at home include table salt, sugar, glucose, naphthalene balls and alum.
  • Amorphous solids at home include glass, candle wax, butter, plastic items, rubber and cotton candy.
  • Crystalline solids have particles in a regular pattern and a sharp melting point.
  • Amorphous solids have no regular arrangement and soften over a range of temperature instead of a sharp melting point.

Solved Exercises

Exercise — Project Work

Q: Prepare separate lists of crystalline and amorphous solids found in your home. Compare your lists with those of your classmates and present in the class.

Ans: Sample lists (items may vary from home to home). Crystalline solids found at home: table salt (sodium chloride), sugar, glucose, naphthalene balls, alum, and diamond in jewellery if present. These have particles arranged in a regular pattern and a sharp melting point. Amorphous solids found at home: glass (windows, glasses and mirrors), candle wax, butter, plastic items (buckets, bottles, chairs), rubber (erasers, tyres, balloons) and cotton candy. These have no regular arrangement of particles and no sharp melting point; they soften over a range of temperature.

lessons.title: Multiple Choice Questions
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • The most dilute solution among given molarities is the one with the smallest molarity, 0.005 M.
  • Milk is a colloidal solution, and a water droplet in air is a liquid in gas solution.
  • A solution with a low concentration of solute is called a dilute solution.
  • Dilution keeps moles constant: diluting 250 cm3 of 1.60 M NaNO3 to 400 cm3 gives 1.00 M.
  • When KCl dissolves in water it produces K+ and Cl- ions.
  • Molarity is the number of moles of solute dissolved in 1 dm3 of solution.
  • 4 g NaOH in 250 ml gives a 0.4 M solution.

Solved Exercises

Exercise — Choose the Correct Option

Q: i. Which of the following solution is more dilute?

Options: (a) 1.0M (b) 0.5M (c) 0.05M (d) 0.005M

Correct answer: 0.005M

Q: ii. Milk is an example of:

Options: (a) Compound (b) Saturated solution (c) Colloidal solution (d) Suspension

Correct answer: Colloidal solution

Q: iii. Water droplet in air is an example of solution:

Options: (a) Gas in gas (b) Gas in liquid (c) Liquid in gas (d) Liquid in liquid

Correct answer: Liquid in gas

Q: iv. When there is a low concentration of solute in a solution, it is known as:

Options: (a) dilute solution (b) saturated solution (c) concentrated solution (d) super saturated solution

Correct answer: dilute solution

Q: v. What is the molarity of a NaNO3 solution made by diluting 250.0 cm3 of a 1.60 M solution to a final volume of 400 cm3?

Options: (a) 1.20 M (b) 1.00 M (c) 0.200 M (d) 0.160 M

Correct answer: 1.00 M

Q: vi. What is the concentration, in % mass by volume (m/v) of a solution containing 15.0 g KCl in 600.0 cm3 solution?

Options: (a) 5.00% (b) 2.00% (c) 0.200% (d) 2.50%

Correct answer: 2.50%

Q: vii. When KCl dissolves in water, the following will be produced:

Options: (a) K and Cl (b) K+ and Cl- (c) K and Cl2 (d) K+ and Cl2

Correct answer: K+ and Cl-

Q: viii. 2 moles of Na2SO4 are dissolved in one dm3 of solution. Molarity of solution is:

Options: (a) 1 M (b) 2 M (c) 3 M (d) 0.5 M

Correct answer: 2 M

Q: ix. Molarity is the number of moles of solute dissolved in:

Options: (a) 1 kg of solvent (b) 1 kg of solution (c) 1 dm3 of solvent (d) 1 dm3 of solution

Correct answer: 1 dm3 of solution

Q: x. The molarity of a NaOH solution by dissolving 4 g of it in 250 ml water is:

Options: (a) 0.4 M (b) 0.8 M (c) 0.2 M (d) 0.1 M

Correct answer: 0.4 M

mcqs.q: i. Which of the following solution is more dilute?
mcqs.why: Dilute means a low concentration of solute. Among 1.0 M, 0.5 M, 0.05 M and 0.005 M, the smallest molarity is 0.005 M, so that solution contains the least solute per dm3 and is the most dilute.

mcqs.q: ii. Milk is an example of:
mcqs.why: Milk is a colloidal solution, an emulsion of tiny fat and protein particles dispersed in water. The particles are intermediate in size, scatter light and do not settle on standing.

mcqs.q: iii. Water droplet in air is an example of solution:
mcqs.why: In a water droplet in air the solute is liquid water in the form of tiny droplets and the solvent is air, a gas. So this is a liquid in gas type of solution, like fog and humidity in air.

mcqs.q: iv. When there is a low concentration of solute in a solution, it is known as:
mcqs.why: A solution containing a small, low amount of solute dissolved in the solvent is called a dilute solution. A concentrated solution contains a large amount, while a saturated solution can dissolve no more solute at that temperature.

mcqs.q: v. What is the molarity of a NaNO3 solution made by diluting 250.0 cm3 of a 1.60 M solution to a final volume of 400 cm3?
mcqs.why: On dilution moles stay the same, so M1V1 = M2V2. M2 = M1V1 / V2 = 1.60 x 250.0 / 400 = 400 / 400 = 1.00 M. Increasing the volume lowers the molarity.

mcqs.q: vi. What is the concentration, in % mass by volume (m/v) of a solution containing 15.0 g KCl in 600.0 cm3 solution?
mcqs.why: % mass by volume = mass of solute in g / volume of solution in cm3 x 100. So 15.0 / 600.0 x 100 = 0.025 x 100 = 2.50 percent m/v.

mcqs.q: vii. When KCl dissolves in water, the following will be produced:
mcqs.why: KCl is an ionic compound. In water it dissociates into its ions, potassium ions K+ and chloride ions Cl-, which move freely in the solution. It does not produce neutral atoms or Cl2 gas.

mcqs.q: viii. 2 moles of Na2SO4 are dissolved in one dm3 of solution. Molarity of solution is:
mcqs.why: Molarity = moles of solute / volume of solution in dm3. Here M = 2 mol / 1 dm3 = 2 mol dm-3, that is 2 M.

mcqs.q: ix. Molarity is the number of moles of solute dissolved in:
mcqs.why: Molarity is defined using the volume of the solution, not the solvent. It is the number of moles of solute dissolved in 1 dm3, that is one litre, of solution and is represented by M.

mcqs.q: x. The molarity of a NaOH solution by dissolving 4 g of it in 250 ml water is:
mcqs.why: Moles of NaOH = mass / molar mass = 4 g / 40 g mol-1 = 0.1 mol. Volume = 250 ml = 0.250 dm3. Molarity = 0.1 / 0.250 = 0.4 M.

lessons.title: Numerical and Short Answers
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • Molarity M = moles of solute / volume of solution in dm3; moles = mass / molar mass.
  • Molar masses used: KI 166, NaOH 40, NH4Br 98, H2SO4 98 and CaCl2 111 g mol-1.
  • Volumes in cm3 must be divided by 1000 to convert them to dm3 before calculating molarity.
  • A pure liquid leaves no residue on evaporation; a solution leaves the dissolved solute as residue.
  • Like dissolves like: polar CH3OH dissolves best in a polar solvent such as water.
  • Mixing salt or alcohol with water can reduce total volume because particles occupy gaps between water molecules.
  • Colloids show the Tyndall effect because their 1 to 1000 nm particles scatter light; paint is stirred because pigment settles on standing.

Solved Exercises

Test Yourself (p. 153)

Q: Suggest a method for differentiation between pure liquid and solution.

Ans: Take a small amount of the liquid in an evaporating dish and evaporate it (or boil and collect/condense the vapour). A pure liquid evaporates completely and leaves no residue, and it boils at one fixed temperature throughout. A solution leaves the dissolved solid (solute) behind as a residue on evaporation, and its boiling point rises as it becomes more concentrated. So, leaving a residue on evaporation proves the liquid is a solution, while no residue proves it is a pure liquid.

Practice Problem 6.1

Q: Calculate the molarity of 11.6 cm3 of solution containing 0.750 g of CaCl2.

Ans: Given: Mass of CaCl2 = 0.750 g
Volume of solution = 11.6 cm3
Step 1 — Molar mass of CaCl2:
Formula: Molar mass = Ca + 2 x Cl = 40 + 2(35.5) = 111 g mol-1
Step 2 — Number of moles of solute:
Formula: Moles = Mass of solute / Molar mass
Substitution: Moles = 0.750 g / 111 g mol-1 = 0.00676 mol
Step 3 — Convert volume into dm3:
Formula: Volume in dm3 = Volume in cm3 / 1000
Substitution: Volume = 11.6 / 1000 = 0.0116 dm3
Step 4 — Molarity:
Formula: Molarity (M) = Moles of solute / Volume of solution in dm3
Substitution: M = 0.00676 mol / 0.0116 dm3 = 0.582 mol dm-3
Answer: 0.582 M

Practice Problem 6.2

Q: Which type of solvent, polar or non polar, is most likely to dissolve methyl alcohol, CH3OH?

Ans: A polar solvent. Methyl alcohol (CH3OH) is a polar covalent compound: its -OH group can form hydrogen bonds, just like water. By the rule 'like dissolves like', a polar solute dissolves best in a polar solvent (for example water or liquid ammonia) and is not expected to dissolve well in a non-polar solvent such as benzene.

Point to Ponder (p. 170)

Q: If you pour a handful of salt into a full glass of water, the water level will actually go down rather than overflowing the glass. Similarly, if you mix half a liter of alcohol and half a liter of water, the total volume of the liquid will be less than one liter. Explain why?

Ans: The particles of the two substances do not simply add their volumes. When salt dissolves, its Na+ and Cl- ions occupy the empty spaces (gaps) between the water molecules and pull the water molecules closer around them (hydration), so the total volume increases very little and can even fall. In the same way, the smaller water and alcohol molecules pack into the spaces between each other's molecules and attract each other by hydrogen bonding, so the molecules come closer together. Hence the volume of the mixture is less than the sum of the separate volumes.

Exercise — Solve the Following Numerical Questions

Q: i. What is the molarity of a solution composed of 5.85 g of potassium iodide (KI) dissolved in enough water to make 0.125 dm3 of solution?

Ans: Given: Mass of KI = 5.85 g
Volume of solution = 0.125 dm3
Step 1 — Molar mass of KI:
Formula: Molar mass of KI = K + I = 39 + 127 = 166 g mol-1
Step 2 — Number of moles of solute:
Formula: Moles = Mass of solute / Molar mass
Substitution: Moles = 5.85 g / 166 g mol-1 = 0.0352 mol
Step 3 — Molarity:
Formula: Molarity (M) = Moles of solute / Volume of solution in dm3
Substitution: M = 0.0352 mol / 0.125 dm3 = 0.282 mol dm-3
Answer: 0.282 M

Q: ii. How many moles of H2SO4 are present in 0.500 dm3 of 0.150 M H2SO4 solution?

Ans: Given: Molarity of H2SO4 solution = 0.150 M
Volume of solution = 0.500 dm3
Formula: Molarity (M) = Moles of solute / Volume of solution in dm3
Rearranged formula: Moles of solute = Molarity x Volume of solution in dm3
Substitution: Moles = 0.150 mol dm-3 x 0.500 dm3 = 0.075 mol
Answer: 0.075 moles of H2SO4

Q: iii. Suppose you wanted to dissolve 40.0 g NaOH in enough H2O to make 6.00 dm3 of solution. (a) What is the molar mass of NaOH? (b) What is the molarity of this solution?

Ans: Given: Mass of NaOH = 40.0 g
Volume of solution = 6.00 dm3
(a) Molar mass of NaOH:
Formula: Molar mass = Na + O + H = 23 + 16 + 1 = 40 g mol-1
Answer (a): Molar mass of NaOH = 40 g mol-1
(b) Molarity:
Step 1 — Number of moles:
Formula: Moles = Mass of solute / Molar mass
Substitution: Moles = 40.0 g / 40 g mol-1 = 1.00 mol
Step 2 — Molarity:
Formula: Molarity (M) = Moles of solute / Volume of solution in dm3
Substitution: M = 1.00 mol / 6.00 dm3 = 0.167 mol dm-3
Answer (b): 0.167 M (0.166 M)

Q: iv. What is the molarity of a solution of 14.0 g NH4Br in enough H2O to make 150 cm3 of solution?

Ans: Given: Mass of NH4Br = 14.0 g
Volume of solution = 150 cm3
Step 1 — Molar mass of NH4Br:
Formula: Molar mass = N + 4(H) + Br = 14 + 4(1) + 80 = 98 g mol-1
Step 2 — Number of moles of solute:
Formula: Moles = Mass of solute / Molar mass
Substitution: Moles = 14.0 g / 98 g mol-1 = 0.143 mol
Step 3 — Convert volume into dm3:
Formula: Volume in dm3 = Volume in cm3 / 1000
Substitution: Volume = 150 / 1000 = 0.150 dm3
Step 4 — Molarity:
Formula: Molarity (M) = Moles of solute / Volume of solution in dm3
Substitution: M = 0.143 mol / 0.150 dm3 = 0.953 mol dm-3
Answer: 0.953 M

Q: v. Suppose you want to produce 1.00 dm3 of 3.50 M solution of H2SO4. (a) Which one is the solute? (b) Which one is the solvent? (c) How many grams of solute are needed to make this solution?

Ans: Given: Volume of solution = 1.00 dm3
Molarity required = 3.50 M
(a) The solute is H2SO4, because it is the substance present in the smaller amount that is dissolved.
(b) The solvent is H2O (water), because it is present in the larger amount and dissolves the solute.
(c) Mass of solute needed:
Step 1 — Number of moles:
Formula: Moles of solute = Molarity x Volume of solution in dm3
Substitution: Moles = 3.50 mol dm-3 x 1.00 dm3 = 3.50 mol
Step 2 — Molar mass of H2SO4:
Formula: Molar mass = 2(H) + S + 4(O) = 2(1) + 32 + 4(16) = 98 g mol-1
Step 3 — Mass of solute:
Formula: Mass = Moles x Molar mass
Substitution: Mass = 3.50 mol x 98 g mol-1 = 343 g
Answer: (a) H2SO4 (b) H2O (c) 343 g of H2SO4

Exercise — Short Questions

Q: i. Is seawater a solution? How would you prove with a simple experiment whether it is pure water or a solution?

Ans: Yes, seawater is a solution: it is a homogeneous mixture of salts (mainly sodium chloride) and other minerals dissolved in water, which is the solvent. Experiment: take some seawater in an evaporating dish and heat it until all the water evaporates. A white solid residue of salts is left behind in the dish. Pure water would leave no residue at all. The residue proves that seawater contains dissolved solids, so it is a solution and not pure water.

Q: ii. A bottle in a drug store contains a label "3 percent hydrogen peroxide." What does it mean?

Ans: It means the solution contains 3 parts of hydrogen peroxide (H2O2, the solute) in every 100 parts of the solution — i.e. about 3 g (or 3 cm3) of hydrogen peroxide dissolved in enough water to make 100 parts of solution. The remaining 97 parts are mainly water, the solvent. It is the percentage composition (concentration) of the solution.

Q: iii. Classify the following as a solution, colloid or suspension and explain why? (i) Milk (ii) Hot cup of tea (iii) Orange juice with pulp (iv) Mayonnaise (v) Listerine mouthwash (vi) Milk of Magnesia (vii) Cheese (viii) Mist (ix) Bottled water

Ans: (i) Milk — Colloid: it is a liquid emulsion of tiny fat and protein particles (1–1000 nm) dispersed in water; the particles scatter light and do not settle on standing. (ii) Hot cup of tea — Solution: the tea substances are dissolved completely in hot water forming a homogeneous mixture whose particles cannot be seen and do not settle. (iii) Orange juice with pulp — Suspension: the pulp particles are large (over 1000 nm), can be seen with the naked eye and settle down on standing. (iv) Mayonnaise — Colloid: it is a liquid emulsion of oil droplets dispersed in water. (v) Listerine mouthwash — Solution: all its components are dissolved uniformly in water/alcohol, forming a clear homogeneous mixture. (vi) Milk of Magnesia — Suspension: solid magnesium hydroxide particles are suspended in water, they settle on standing, which is why such medicines are shaken before use. (vii) Cheese — Colloid: it is a solid emulsion/gel of liquid fat dispersed in a solid, with intermediate-sized particles. (viii) Mist — Colloid: it is a liquid aerosol of tiny water droplets dispersed in air; the droplets scatter light. (ix) Bottled water — Solution: it contains minerals and gases dissolved uniformly in water, forming a homogeneous mixture.

Q: iv. Why we stir paints thoroughly before using it?

Ans: Paint is a colloid/suspension in which the heavy pigment particles slowly settle down at the bottom of the tin on standing, leaving the liquid on top. Stirring mixes the settled particles uniformly through the liquid again, so the paint gets its proper colour, composition and covering power on every part of the surface.

Q: v. Why suspensions and solutions do not show Tyndall Effect, while colloids do?

Ans: The Tyndall effect is the scattering of light by the particles of a mixture. In a true solution the particles (0.01–1 nm, atoms, ions or molecules) are too small to scatter light, so the beam passes invisibly. In a suspension the particles are very large (over 1000 nm), they settle down and the mixture is opaque, so no proper Tyndall cone is seen. Colloid particles (1–1000 nm) are of just the right size to scatter light without settling, so a visible bright cone appears when light passes through a colloid.

mcqs.q: What is the molarity of a solution of 5.85 g of potassium iodide, KI, dissolved in enough water to make 0.125 dm3 of solution?
mcqs.why: Step 1 molar mass of KI = 39 + 127 = 166 g mol-1. Step 2 moles = mass / molar mass = 5.85 / 166 = 0.0352 mol. Step 3 molarity = moles / volume = 0.0352 / 0.125 = 0.282 M.

mcqs.q: How many moles of H2SO4 are present in 0.500 dm3 of 0.150 M H2SO4 solution?
mcqs.why: Formula: moles = molarity x volume in dm3. Substitution: moles = 0.150 mol dm-3 x 0.500 dm3 = 0.075 mol of H2SO4.

mcqs.q: What is the molar mass of NaOH?
mcqs.why: Molar mass of NaOH = Na + O + H. Substitution: 23 + 16 + 1 = 40 g mol-1. This value is then used to find moles from a given mass of NaOH.

mcqs.q: 40.0 g NaOH is dissolved in enough water to make 6.00 dm3 of solution. What is the molarity of this solution?
mcqs.why: Step 1 moles = mass / molar mass = 40.0 g / 40 g mol-1 = 1.00 mol. Step 2 molarity = moles / volume = 1.00 mol / 6.00 dm3 = 0.167 M.

mcqs.q: What is the molarity of a solution of 14.0 g NH4Br in enough water to make 150 cm3 of solution?
mcqs.why: Step 1 molar mass = 14 + 4(1) + 80 = 98 g mol-1. Step 2 moles = 14.0 / 98 = 0.143 mol. Step 3 volume = 150 / 1000 = 0.150 dm3. Step 4 molarity = 0.143 / 0.150 = 0.953 M.

mcqs.q: How many grams of H2SO4 are needed to make 1.00 dm3 of 3.50 M H2SO4 solution?
mcqs.why: Step 1 moles = molarity x volume = 3.50 x 1.00 = 3.50 mol. Step 2 molar mass of H2SO4 = 2(1) + 32 + 4(16) = 98 g mol-1. Step 3 mass = moles x molar mass = 3.50 x 98 = 343 g.

mcqs.q: Calculate the molarity of 11.6 cm3 of solution containing 0.750 g of CaCl2.
mcqs.why: Step 1 molar mass of CaCl2 = 40 + 2(35.5) = 111 g mol-1. Step 2 moles = 0.750 / 111 = 0.00676 mol. Step 3 volume = 11.6 / 1000 = 0.0116 dm3. Step 4 molarity = 0.00676 / 0.0116 = 0.582 M. This is Practice Problem 6.1.

mcqs.q: To make an H2SO4 solution, which substance is the solute and which is the solvent?
options: Water is the solute and H2SO4 is the solvent
H2SO4 is the solute and water is the solvent
Both H2SO4 and water are solutes
H2SO4 is the solvent because it is an acid
mcqs.why: The solute is the substance present in the smaller amount that is dissolved, here H2SO4. The solvent is present in the larger amount and dissolves the solute, here water, H2O.

mcqs.q: How can you differentiate between a pure liquid and a solution?
options: Evaporate it: a solution leaves a residue of dissolved solid, a pure liquid leaves no residue
Boil it: a solution boils at a lower temperature than a pure liquid
Filter it: a solution is stopped by filter paper
Cool it: only a pure liquid can freeze
mcqs.why: Take the liquid in an evaporating dish and evaporate it. A pure liquid evaporates completely, leaves no residue and boils at one fixed temperature. A solution leaves the dissolved solute behind as a residue and its boiling point rises as it concentrates.

mcqs.q: Which type of solvent is most likely to dissolve methyl alcohol, CH3OH?
options: A non polar solvent such as benzene
A liquid metal such as mercury
A polar solvent such as water
mcqs.why: Methyl alcohol is a polar covalent compound whose -OH group can form hydrogen bonds, like water. By the rule like dissolves like, a polar solute dissolves best in a polar solvent and poorly in a non polar solvent such as benzene. This is Practice Problem 6.2.

mcqs.q: Why does the water level go down when a handful of salt is poured into a full glass of water, and why is alcohol plus water less than the sum of volumes?
options: The salt and alcohol evaporate instantly on mixing
The particles occupy the empty spaces between water molecules and are pulled closer together
Water is destroyed when salt dissolves in it
The glass expands and holds more volume
mcqs.why: Volumes do not simply add. Na+ and Cl- ions occupy gaps between water molecules and pull them closer by hydration, and water and alcohol molecules pack into each others spaces and attract by hydrogen bonding, so the total volume is less than the sum.

mcqs.q: Why do we stir paints thoroughly before using them?
options: Stirring dissolves the pigment permanently so it never settles
Stirring increases the volume of paint in the tin
Paint becomes a true solution after stirring
Heavy pigment particles settle at the bottom on standing, and stirring mixes them uniformly again
mcqs.why: Paint is a colloid or suspension in which heavy pigment particles slowly settle at the bottom on standing, leaving liquid on top. Stirring redistributes them uniformly so the paint has proper colour, composition and covering power.

mcqs.q: A drug store bottle is labelled 3 percent hydrogen peroxide. What does this mean?
options: It contains 3 g of water in 100 g of hydrogen peroxide
It is 3 M hydrogen peroxide solution
It contains 97 parts hydrogen peroxide and 3 parts water
It contains 3 parts of hydrogen peroxide in every 100 parts of solution, the rest mainly water
mcqs.why: The label gives percentage composition: about 3 g or 3 cm3 of hydrogen peroxide, the solute, in enough water to make 100 parts of solution. The remaining 97 parts are mainly water, the solvent.

mcqs.q: How should milk of magnesia and mist be classified?
options: Milk of magnesia is a suspension and mist is a colloid
Milk of magnesia is a colloid and mist is a suspension
Both are suspensions that never settle
mcqs.why: Milk of magnesia has solid magnesium hydroxide particles suspended in water that settle on standing, so it is a suspension and is shaken before use. Mist is a colloid, tiny water droplets dispersed in air that scatter light.

mcqs.q: Why do colloids show the Tyndall effect while solutions do not?
options: Solution particles are larger than colloid particles and block light
Colloids are always coloured and solutions are colourless
Colloid particles, 1 to 1000 nm, are the right size to scatter light, while solution particles are too small to scatter it
Suspensions scatter light best because they are clear
mcqs.why: The Tyndall effect is scattering of light by particles. True solution particles, 0.01 to 1 nm, are too small to scatter light. Colloid particles, 1 to 1000 nm, scatter light without settling, giving a visible bright cone. Suspension particles are over 1000 nm and settle.

lessons.title: Detailed Answers
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • A solution is a homogeneous mixture of a solute in smaller amount and a solvent in larger amount.
  • There are nine types of solution by states of matter, for example air is gas in gas and brass is solid in solid.
  • Solubility is the grams of solute dissolved in 100 g of solvent to form a saturated solution at a given temperature.
  • Solubility depends on nature of solute and solvent, temperature and, for gases, pressure; like dissolves like.
  • A dilute solution has a small amount of solute; a concentrated solution has a large amount, relative to comparison.
  • Unsaturated can dissolve more solute, saturated can dissolve no more, supersaturated contains more than the saturation amount.
  • Percentage composition gives parts of solute in 100 parts of solution; molarity is moles per dm3 of solution.

Solved Exercises

Exercise — Long Questions

Q: i. Define solution. Explain types of solution on the basis of states of matter.

Ans: A solution is a homogeneous mixture of two or more than two substances, made of a solute (present in smaller amount) and a solvent (present in larger amount). Its composition can be changed within certain limits. On the basis of the states of matter of solute and solvent, there are nine types of solution. Gaseous solutions: (1) Gas in gas — air (oxygen in nitrogen). (2) Gas in liquid — carbon dioxide in water (carbonated drinks). (3) Gas in solid — hydrogen gas adsorbed on palladium. Liquid solutions: (4) Liquid in gas — fog, humidity in air (water vapours in air). (5) Liquid in liquid — alcohol in water. (6) Liquid in solid — mercury amalgams, e.g. amalgam used by dentists (Hg in Ag). Solid solutions: (7) Solid in gas — smoke (carbon particles in air). (8) Solid in liquid — sea water, sugar in water (salts in water). (9) Solid in solid — alloys such as brass (zinc in copper) and bronze (tin in copper).

Q: ii. (a) Discuss the solubility of a substance. (b) Explain the factors that are responsible for the solubility of a substance.

Ans: (a) Solubility is the amount of solute in grams dissolved in 100 grams of the solvent to prepare a saturated solution at a given temperature. In other words, the concentration of a saturated solution is called the solubility of that solute in the given solvent. Different substances have different solubilities in the same solvent at a specific temperature; for example, sodium nitrate (NaNO3) is more soluble than silver chloride (AgCl) in water. Solubility = (Weight of the solute / Weight of the solvent) x 100. (b) Factors: (i) Nature of the solvent — solubility is greater when solute and solvent are similar ('like dissolves like'); NaCl, being ionic, dissolves well in polar water but not in non-polar benzene. (ii) Nature of the solute — changing the solute changes the solubility; NaCl has high solubility in water while sugar has comparatively low solubility in water. (iii) Pressure — solids and liquids are incompressible, so their solubility is not affected by pressure, but the solubility of gases increases with increase in pressure, e.g. CO2 is filled in soda water bottles under pressure. (iv) Temperature — gas solubility usually decreases on heating, while the solubility of most solids increases with temperature (e.g. KNO3), some decrease (e.g. Ce2(SO4)3), and some like NaCl remain almost constant.

Q: iii. (a) What is the difference between a concentrated and a dilute solution? Give examples of each. (b) Differentiate between unsaturated, saturated and supersaturated solutions.

Ans: (a) A dilute solution contains a small amount of solute dissolved in the solvent, while a concentrated solution contains a large amount of solute dissolved in the solvent. Concentration is relative: a solution in which 5 g of sugar is dissolved in 100 cm3 of water is dilute as compared to a solution in which 8 g of sugar is dissolved in 100 cm3 of water, which is concentrated in comparison. Dilute and concentrated describe the relative amount of solute, not the limit of dissolving. (b) Unsaturated solution: a solution which has less solute than is required to saturate it at a particular temperature; it can dissolve further amount of solute at that temperature. Saturated solution: a solution which cannot dissolve further amount of solute at a particular temperature; extra solute remains undissolved and settles down. Supersaturated solution: a solution which contains more amount of solute than the amount required to saturate it at a particular temperature; it is prepared, for example, by heating a saturated solution so it dissolves extra solute. The three can be distinguished by adding a crystal of the solute: it dissolves in unsaturated, remains undissolved in saturated, and excess solute deposits on the crystal in a supersaturated solution.

Q: iv. Describe one way to prove that a mixture of sugar and water is a solution and that a mixture of sand and water is not a solution.

Ans: Stir sugar in water in one beaker and sand in water in another beaker, then leave both undisturbed and also try filtration. The sugar disappears completely, the mixture is clear and uniform throughout, no particles can be seen, nothing settles on standing, and the whole mixture passes through filter paper leaving no residue — this is a true solution. The sand, on the other hand, does not dissolve: its particles can be seen with the naked eye, they settle at the bottom after some time (sedimentation), and on filtration the sand stays on the filter paper while clear water passes through. Hence sand and water form a heterogeneous suspension, not a solution.

Q: v. Explain the following concentration units. (a) Percentage composition (b) Molarity

Ans: (a) Percentage composition: It is the number of parts of solute present in 100 parts of solution, or the fraction of a solute in a solution multiplied by 100. It is expressed in four ways: (1) Percentage mass by mass (m/m) = [mass of solute (g) / mass of solution (g)] x 100; e.g. 10% sugar solution by mass has 10 g sugar in 90 g solvent making 100 g solution. (2) Percentage mass by volume (m/v) = [mass of solute (g) / volume of solution (cm3)] x 100; e.g. 10% NaCl (m/v) has 10 g NaCl in solvent to make 100 cm3 of solution. (3) Percentage volume by mass (v/m) = [volume of solute (cm3) / mass of solution (g)] x 100. (4) Percentage volume by volume (v/v) = [volume of solute (cm3) / volume of solution (cm3)] x 100; e.g. 10% alcohol (v/v) has 10 cm3 alcohol in solution of total volume 100 cm3. (b) Molarity: Molarity is the number of moles of solute dissolved per dm3 (litre) of solution. It is represented by 'M'. Molarity (M) = Number of moles of solute / Volume of solution in dm3. Since Mole = Amount of solute in grams / Molecular mass of solute, Molarity can also be written as M = Amount of solute in gram / (Molecular mass of solute x Volume of solution in dm3). A 1 M solution contains one mole of solute per dm3 of solution, e.g. 1 M NaOH contains 40 g NaOH in 1 dm3 of solution.

mcqs.q: What is a solution?
options: A heterogeneous mixture in which particles settle on standing
A homogeneous mixture of a solute in smaller amount dissolved in a solvent in larger amount
A pure substance made of only one kind of particle
A mixture that can always be separated by filtration
mcqs.why: A solution is a homogeneous mixture of two or more substances. The solute is present in the smaller amount and the solvent in the larger amount, and the composition can be changed within certain limits.

mcqs.q: Brass, an alloy of zinc in copper, and air, oxygen in nitrogen, are examples of which types of solution?
options: Both are liquid in liquid solutions
Brass is gas in solid and air is solid in gas
Brass is liquid in solid and air is liquid in gas
Brass is solid in solid and air is gas in gas
mcqs.why: On the basis of states of matter there are nine types of solution. Air is a gaseous solution, gas in gas. Brass is a solid solution, solid in solid, like bronze which is tin in copper.

mcqs.q: What is solubility of a substance?
options: The amount of solute in grams dissolved in 100 g of solvent to prepare a saturated solution at a given temperature
The total mass of solution formed in any experiment
The number of moles of solute in 1 dm3 of any solution
The amount of solvent needed to dissolve 1 g of solute at any temperature
mcqs.why: Solubility is the concentration of a saturated solution: grams of solute dissolved in 100 g of solvent at a given temperature. Solubility = weight of solute / weight of solvent x 100. Different substances differ, for example NaNO3 is more soluble than AgCl in water.

mcqs.q: Which statement about factors affecting solubility is correct?
options: Pressure greatly increases the solubility of all solids in water
Heating always increases the solubility of gases in water
Ionic NaCl dissolves well in polar water but not in non polar benzene, because like dissolves like
Nature of the solute has no effect on solubility
mcqs.why: Solubility is greater when solute and solvent are similar in nature. NaCl, being ionic, dissolves in polar water but not in non polar benzene. Pressure does not affect solids and liquids, but gas solubility increases with pressure, and usually decreases on heating.

mcqs.q: What is the difference between a dilute and a concentrated solution?
options: A dilute solution is saturated and a concentrated solution is unsaturated
A dilute solution cannot dissolve any more solute
A dilute solution contains a small amount of solute, a concentrated solution contains a large amount of solute in the solvent
A concentrated solution always contains exactly 100 g of solute
mcqs.why: Dilute and concentrated are relative terms for amount of solute. For example 5 g sugar in 100 cm3 water is dilute compared with 8 g sugar in 100 cm3 water, which is concentrated in comparison. They do not describe the limit of dissolving.

mcqs.q: What is an unsaturated solution?
options: A solution that has less solute than is required to saturate it and can dissolve more solute at that temperature
A solution that cannot dissolve any more solute at that temperature
A solution that contains more solute than the saturation amount
A solution in which extra solute has already settled down
mcqs.why: An unsaturated solution contains less solute than is needed for saturation at a particular temperature, so it can dissolve further solute. A saturated solution can dissolve no more, and extra solute remains undissolved and settles.

mcqs.q: How can unsaturated, saturated and supersaturated solutions be distinguished by adding a crystal of solute?
options: The crystal dissolves in all three in the same way
The crystal deposits solute only in an unsaturated solution
The crystal melts in a saturated solution
The crystal dissolves in unsaturated, stays undissolved in saturated, and excess solute deposits on it in supersaturated
mcqs.why: Adding a solute crystal is the test given in the book: it dissolves in an unsaturated solution, remains undissolved in a saturated solution, and in a supersaturated solution excess solute deposits on the crystal.

mcqs.q: How does a sugar and water mixture prove it is a solution, unlike sand and water?
options: Sugar settles at the bottom and is caught by filter paper
Sugar disappears, the mixture is clear and uniform, nothing settles and it passes through filter paper with no residue
Sand dissolves completely and leaves no residue
Both mixtures behave in exactly the same way
mcqs.why: Sugar dissolves completely, forming a clear uniform solution with no visible particles, no settling and no residue on filtration. Sand does not dissolve, its particles are visible, settle by sedimentation and stay on the filter paper, forming a suspension.

mcqs.q: What does a 10 percent NaCl solution by mass by volume, m/v, contain?
options: 10 g NaCl dissolved in solvent to make 100 cm3 of solution
10 g NaCl in 100 g of solution
10 cm3 NaCl in 100 cm3 of solution
10 moles NaCl in 1 dm3 of solution
mcqs.why: Percentage mass by volume = mass of solute in g / volume of solution in cm3 x 100. So a 10 percent NaCl m/v solution has 10 g NaCl made up to 100 cm3 of solution. Mass by mass would use 100 g of solution instead.

mcqs.q: How is molarity expressed and what does a 1 M NaOH solution contain?
options: Molarity = grams of solute / 100 g of solvent; 1 M NaOH contains 1 g in 100 cm3
Molarity = moles of solute / 1 kg of solvent; 1 M NaOH contains 40 g in 1 kg water
Molarity = moles of solute / volume of solution in dm3; 1 M NaOH contains 40 g NaOH in 1 dm3 of solution
Molarity = volume of solute / volume of solvent x 100; 1 M has 1 cm3 in 100 cm3
mcqs.why: Molarity is the number of moles of solute dissolved per dm3 of solution, M = moles / volume in dm3. A 1 M NaOH solution contains one mole, 40 g, of NaOH in 1 dm3 of solution.

Q: Which of the following substances are pure substances and which are mixtures? a. Sea water b. Cooking oil c. Coal d. Steel e. Chilli sauce f. Bronze g. Sand h. Gold i. Orange squash j. Salt k. Milk l. Oxygen gas m. Air n. Orange juice o. Coke p. Soil
