lessons.title: Multiple Choice Questions
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • Oxidation number of an element in the free state, such as N2, is 0.
  • Oxidation is loss of electrons and reduction is gain of electrons.
  • A reducing agent loses electrons and is itself oxidized.
  • A cation is a positively charged ion.
  • Oxidation always occurs at the anode in an electrochemical cell.
  • Electrons flow from anode to cathode through the external circuit.
  • In KMnO4 the oxidation number of manganese is +7.

Solved Exercises

Exercise — Choose the Correct Option

Q: i. The oxidation number of nitrogen N2 is:

Options: (a) +1 (b) +3 (c) 0 (d) -3

Correct answer: 0

Q: ii. What is the oxidation number of C in CH3OH?

Options: (a) -2 (b) -1 (c) 0 (d) +1

Correct answer: -2

Q: iii. A cation is:

Options: (a) neutral (b) negatively charged (c) without charge (d) positively charged

Correct answer: positively charged

Q: iv. Electrons are lost by the:

Options: (a) reducing agent as it undergoes oxidation. (b) reducing agent as it undergoes reduction. (c) oxidizing agent as it undergoes oxidation. (d) oxidizing agent as it undergoes reduction.

Correct answer: reducing agent as it undergoes oxidation.

Q: v. What is the oxidation number assigned to manganese in KMnO4?

Options: (a) +7 (b) +3 (c) +2 (d) +4

Correct answer: +7

Q: vi. In a particular redox reaction, the oxidation number of phosphorus changed from -3 to 0. From this information, it may be concluded that phosphorus:

Options: (a) Lost 3 electrons and was reduced. (b) Lost 3 electrons and was oxidized. (c) Gained 3 electrons and was reduced. (d) Gained 3 electrons and was oxidized.

Correct answer: Lost 3 electrons and was oxidized.

Q: vii. Which statement is true for an electrochemical cell?

Options: (a) Oxidation occurs at the anode only. (b) Reduction occurs at the anode only. (c) Oxidation occurs at both the anode and cathode. (d) Reduction occurs at both the anode and cathode.

Correct answer: Oxidation occurs at the anode only.

Q: viii. In which of the following does sulphur have an oxidation number of +7?

Options: (a) HSO3- (b) SO3 (c) H2SO4 (d) H2S2O8

Correct answer: H2S2O8

Q: ix. What happens to the reducing agent in an oxidation-reduction reaction?

Options: (a) It is oxidized as it gains electrons. (b) It is oxidized as it loses electrons. (c) It is reduced as it gains electrons. (d) It is reduced as it loses electrons.

Correct answer: It is oxidized as it loses electrons.

Q: x. In an electrochemical cell, electrons travel in which direction?

Options: (a) From the anode to the cathode through the external circuit. (b) From the anode to the cathode through the salt bridge. (c) From the cathode to the anode through the external circuit. (d) From the cathode to the anode through the salt bridge.

Correct answer: From the anode to the cathode through the external circuit.

mcqs.q: i. The oxidation number of nitrogen N2 is:
mcqs.why: Nitrogen in N2 is in the free elemental state. The oxidation number of any element in its free state is always 0, so nitrogen in N2 has oxidation number 0.

mcqs.q: ii. What is the oxidation number of C in CH3OH?
mcqs.why: Let C = x. Each H is +1 and O is -2, so x + 4(+1) + (-2) = 0, giving x + 2 = 0 and x = -2. Hence carbon in CH3OH has oxidation number -2.

mcqs.q: iii. A cation is:
mcqs.why: A cation is formed when an atom loses one or more electrons. Losing negatively charged electrons leaves the ion with a net positive charge, so a cation is positively charged.

mcqs.q: iv. Electrons are lost by the:
options: reducing agent as it undergoes reduction.
oxidizing agent as it undergoes oxidation.
reducing agent as it undergoes oxidation.
oxidizing agent as it undergoes reduction.
mcqs.why: A reducing agent donates electrons to another substance and loses them itself. Loss of electrons is oxidation, so the reducing agent loses electrons as it undergoes oxidation.

mcqs.q: v. What is the oxidation number assigned to manganese in KMnO4?
mcqs.why: Let Mn = x. K is +1 and each O is -2, so (+1) + x + 4(-2) = 0, giving x - 7 = 0 and x = +7. Hence manganese in KMnO4 has oxidation number +7.

mcqs.q: vi. In a particular redox reaction, the oxidation number of phosphorus changed from -3 to 0. From this information, it may be concluded that phosphorus:
mcqs.why: The oxidation number increased from -3 to 0, a rise of 3. An increase in oxidation number means electrons were lost, and loss of electrons is oxidation, so phosphorus lost 3 electrons and was oxidized.

mcqs.q: vii. Which statement is true for an electrochemical cell?
options: Reduction occurs at the anode only.
Oxidation occurs at both the anode and cathode.
Reduction occurs at both the anode and cathode.
Oxidation occurs at the anode only.
mcqs.why: In every electrochemical cell oxidation takes place at the anode and reduction takes place at the cathode. Oxidation therefore occurs at the anode only, never at the cathode.

mcqs.q: viii. In which of the following does sulphur have an oxidation number of +7?
mcqs.why: In H2S2O8, let S = x: 2(+1) + 2x + 8(-2) = 0 gives 2x = 14 and x = +7 for the average sulphur. In H2SO4 sulphur is only +6, so H2S2O8 is the correct choice.

mcqs.q: ix. What happens to the reducing agent in an oxidation-reduction reaction?
options: It is oxidized as it loses electrons.
It is oxidized as it gains electrons.
It is reduced as it gains electrons.
It is reduced as it loses electrons.
mcqs.why: The reducing agent gives electrons to the substance being reduced. Because it loses electrons itself, and loss of electrons is oxidation, the reducing agent is oxidized as it loses electrons.

mcqs.q: x. In an electrochemical cell, electrons travel in which direction?
options: From the anode to the cathode through the salt bridge.
From the cathode to the anode through the external circuit.
From the anode to the cathode through the external circuit.
From the cathode to the anode through the salt bridge.
mcqs.why: Electrons released by oxidation at the anode travel through the external wire to the cathode, where they are used in reduction. The salt bridge carries ions, not electrons.

lessons.title: Short Answers
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • In Ca + Br2 -> CaBr2, bromine is reduced from 0 to -1.
  • In 2HCl + Zn -> ZnCl2 + H2, hydrogen is reduced from +1 to 0.
  • Silver is 0 as free metal and +1 in Ag2O.
  • NaOH ionizes completely, so it is a strong electrolyte; NH4OH ionizes only partially, so it is weak.
  • Corrosion is prevented by coatings, alloying, galvanizing and cathodic protection.
  • Nelson cell overall reaction: 2NaCl + 2H2O -> 2NaOH + H2 + Cl2.
  • Rusting needs oxygen and moisture and forms Fe2O3.xH2O.
  • In the Daniel cell zinc is the anode and copper is the cathode, with about 1.10 V.

Solved Exercises

Practice Problem 7.1

Q: Determine the oxidation number of carbon in CO.

Ans: Given: Compound = CO (a neutral molecule).
Formula: Sum of the oxidation numbers of all atoms in a neutral molecule = 0.
Oxidation number of oxygen in its compounds = -2.
Let the oxidation number of carbon = x.
Substitution: x + (-2) = 0
x = 0 + 2
x = +2
Answer: The oxidation number of carbon in CO is +2.

Q: What is the oxidation number of sulphur in the sulphite ion, SO3^2-?

Ans: Given: Ion = SO3^2- (sulphite ion), charge on the ion = -2.
Formula: Sum of the oxidation numbers of all atoms in an ion = charge on the ion.
Oxidation number of each oxygen atom = -2. Number of oxygen atoms = 3.
Let the oxidation number of sulphur = x.
Substitution: x + 3(-2) = -2
x - 6 = -2
x = -2 + 6
x = +4
Answer: The oxidation number of sulphur in the sulphite ion SO3^2- is +4.

Exercise — Short Questions

Q: (i) Indicate which element is reduced in the following reactions: a. Ca(s) + Br2(g) → CaBr2(s) b. 2HCl + Zn → ZnCl2 + H2

Ans: Reduction is the gain of electrons, shown by a decrease in oxidation number. a. In Ca + Br2 → CaBr2, bromine changes from 0 in Br2 to -1 in CaBr2, so bromine (Br2) is reduced; calcium is oxidized (0 to +2) and is the reducing agent. b. In 2HCl + Zn → ZnCl2 + H2, hydrogen changes from +1 in HCl to 0 in H2, so hydrogen is reduced; zinc is oxidized (0 to +2) and is the reducing agent.

Q: (ii) What is the oxidation number of silver on each side of the following equation? 4Ag(s) + O2(g) —Heat→ 2Ag2O(s)

Ans: Given: Equation: 4Ag(s) + O2(g) —Heat→ 2Ag2O(s).
Rule: The oxidation number of an element in the free state is zero.
Left side: Silver is present as free metal Ag(s), so its oxidation number = 0.
Right side: Silver is present in Ag2O. Oxidation number of oxygen = -2.
Formula: Sum of oxidation numbers in a neutral compound = 0.
Let the oxidation number of silver = x. Substitution: 2x + (-2) = 0
2x = +2
x = +1
Answer: Silver has oxidation number 0 on the left side and +1 on the right side. Silver is oxidized, so it acts as the reducing agent.

Q: (iii) Why NaOH is a strong but NH4OH is weak electrolyte?

Ans: An electrolyte is strong or weak according to its degree of dissociation or ionization. NaOH is a strong electrolyte because it dissociates or ionizes completely in aqueous solution, producing a large number of Na+ and OH- ions, so it conducts electric current to a larger extent. NH4OH is a weak electrolyte because it dissociates or ionizes only partially (slightly) in aqueous solution: NH4OH(aq) ⇌ NH4+(aq) + OH-(aq). It produces very few ions, so it conducts current only to a very small extent.

Q: (iv) How to prevent corrosion? Enlist few of the methods.

Ans: Corrosion can be prevented by the following methods: (a) Removal of stains — the surface of iron is properly cleaned and stains, which act as sites for corrosion, are removed. (b) Paints and other coatings — paint and organic coatings keep air and moisture away from the metal. (c) Alloying — e.g. stainless steel, a solid mixture of iron, chromium and nickel, strongly resists corrosion. (d) Metallic coating or plating — a thin coating of zinc (galvanizing), nickel, chromium or tin is applied on iron. (e) Corrosion inhibitors — chemicals such as glycine or polyethylene interrupt the corrosion reaction. (f) Cathodic protection — a more active metal such as magnesium or zinc is connected to the iron; it is oxidized instead of the iron.

Q: (v) Write chemical reactions that occur in Nelson's cell.

Ans: In Nelson's cell, concentrated aqueous NaCl (brine) is electrolysed. Ionization: 2NaCl(aq) → 2Na+(aq) + 2Cl-(aq), and water ionizes as H2O(l) ⇌ H+(aq) + OH-(aq). Reaction at cathode (reduction): 2H+(aq) + 2e- → 2H(aq); H + H → H2(g). The Na+ ions are not reduced; they combine with OH- ions: 2Na+(aq) + 2OH-(aq) → 2NaOH(aq). Reaction at anode (oxidation): 2Cl-(aq) → 2Cl(g) + 2e-; Cl + Cl → Cl2(g). Overall reaction: 2NaCl(aq) + 2H2O(l) → 2NaOH(aq) + H2(g) + Cl2(g).

Q: (vi) Write one example from daily life which involves the oxidation-reduction reaction.

Ans: Rusting of iron is a daily-life redox reaction. Iron articles such as gates, tools and car bodies slowly combine with oxygen of the air in the presence of moisture (water) and form brown hydrated ferric oxide, Fe2O3.xH2O, called rust. Iron is oxidized (it loses electrons: Fe → Fe2+ + 2e-) while oxygen is reduced, so oxidation and reduction take place simultaneously. Burning of fuel and the metabolism of food in the human body are other daily-life examples of redox reactions.

Q: (vii) Assign oxidation numbers to each atom in the following compounds. a. HI b. PBr3 c. CaCO3 d. H3PO4 e. As2O3 f. H2SO4

Ans: Formula used in each part: Sum of the oxidation numbers of all atoms in a neutral compound = 0. Known values: H = +1, O = -2, Ca (Group II) = +2, halogens in binary compounds = -1.
a. HI: H is +1, so I = -1. Check: (+1) + (-1) = 0.
b. PBr3: Each Br = -1. Let P = x. Substitution: x + 3(-1) = 0 → x - 3 = 0 → x = +3. So P = +3, Br = -1.
c. CaCO3: Ca = +2, each O = -2. Let C = x. Substitution: (+2) + x + 3(-2) = 0 → x - 4 = 0 → x = +4. So Ca = +2, C = +4, O = -2.
d. H3PO4: Each H = +1, each O = -2. Let P = x. Substitution: 3(+1) + x + 4(-2) = 0 → x - 5 = 0 → x = +5. So H = +1, P = +5, O = -2.
e. As2O3: Each O = -2. Let As = x. Substitution: 2x + 3(-2) = 0 → 2x = +6 → x = +3. So As = +3, O = -2.
f. H2SO4: Each H = +1, each O = -2. Let S = x. Substitution: 2(+1) + x + 4(-2) = 0 → x - 6 = 0 → x = +6. So H = +1, S = +6, O = -2.

Q: (viii) Why O2 is necessary for rusting?

Ans: Rusting is the oxidation of iron. Iron rusts only when it combines with oxygen in the presence of water, forming brown hydrated ferric oxide (rust), Fe2O3.xH2O. At the cathodic sites on the iron surface, oxygen and water take up the electrons lost by iron: 2H2O + O2 + 4e- → 4OH-. The Fe2+ ions formed at the anode are further oxidized by atmospheric oxygen to Fe3+, which forms rust. Therefore there is no rusting in air free from oxygen; both oxygen (air) and moisture are necessary for rusting.

Q: (ix) Sketch the Daniel cell, labeling the cathode, anode and the direction of flow of the electrons. (Describe the sketch in words.)

Ans: Description of the sketch: Draw two separate beakers (half-cells) side by side. In the left beaker place a zinc rod dipped in 1M zinc sulphate solution (ZnSO4); label this rod 'Zinc — Anode (negative)'. In the right beaker place a copper rod dipped in 1M copper sulphate solution (CuSO4); label this rod 'Copper — Cathode (positive)'. Connect the two rods at the top with a wire passing through a voltmeter (reading about 1.10 V). Join the two solutions with an inverted U-shaped salt bridge filled with agar gel containing K2SO4 or Na2SO4 solution; label it 'Salt Bridge'. Show the direction of electron flow by arrows on the wire from the zinc anode to the copper cathode through the external circuit. Working: at the anode Zn(s) → Zn2+(aq) + 2e- (oxidation); at the cathode Cu2+(aq) + 2e- → Cu(s) (reduction); overall: Zn(s) + Cu2+(aq) → Zn2+(aq) + Cu(s).

Q: (x) Write down some possible uses of an electrolytic cell.

Ans: Possible uses of an electrolytic cell are: (1) Extraction of active metals, e.g. sodium metal is obtained by electrolysis of fused NaCl in the Down cell. (2) Manufacture of important chemicals, e.g. sodium hydroxide (caustic soda) is prepared from brine in the Nelson cell, with hydrogen and chlorine as by-products. (3) Electrolytic refining of metals, e.g. impure copper is purified to 99.99% pure copper. (4) Electroplating of one metal over another, e.g. tin, zinc and chromium plating on steel for protection and decoration. (5) Decomposition of compounds that do not react spontaneously, using electrical energy.

mcqs.q: What is the oxidation number of carbon in CO?
mcqs.why: CO is a neutral molecule, so the sum of oxidation numbers = 0. Oxygen is -2. Let carbon = x. Step 1: x + (-2) = 0. Step 2: x = 0 + 2. Step 3: x = +2. So carbon in CO is +2.

mcqs.q: What is the oxidation number of sulphur in the sulphite ion, SO3^2-?
mcqs.why: For an ion, the sum of oxidation numbers = charge on the ion = -2. Each oxygen is -2 and there are 3 oxygens. Let sulphur = x. Step 1: x + 3(-2) = -2. Step 2: x - 6 = -2. Step 3: x = -2 + 6 = +4. So sulphur is +4.

mcqs.q: In the reaction Ca(s) + Br2(g) -> CaBr2(s), which element is reduced?
mcqs.why: Reduction is gain of electrons, shown by a decrease in oxidation number. Bromine falls from 0 in Br2 to -1 in CaBr2, so bromine is reduced, while calcium rises from 0 to +2 and is oxidized.

mcqs.q: In the reaction 2HCl + Zn -> ZnCl2 + H2, which element is reduced?
mcqs.why: Hydrogen falls from +1 in HCl to 0 in H2, a decrease in oxidation number, which means it gains electrons and is reduced. Zinc rises from 0 to +2, so zinc is oxidized and acts as the reducing agent.

mcqs.q: In the equation 4Ag(s) + O2(g) -> 2Ag2O(s), what is the oxidation number of silver on each side?
options: +1 on the left side and 0 on the right side
0 on the left side and +1 on the right side
+2 on the left side and +1 on the right side
mcqs.why: Free silver metal has oxidation number 0. In Ag2O, oxygen is -2 and 2x + (-2) = 0 gives x = +1. Step 1: 2x = +2. Step 2: x = +1. So silver goes from 0 to +1 and is oxidized.

mcqs.q: Why is NaOH a strong electrolyte but NH4OH a weak electrolyte?
options: NaOH ionizes completely in water, while NH4OH ionizes only partially
NaOH ionizes only partially, while NH4OH ionizes completely
NaOH does not ionize in water at all
NH4OH produces no ions in water at all
mcqs.why: Strength of an electrolyte depends on its degree of ionization. NaOH dissociates completely into many Na+ and OH- ions and conducts strongly, while NH4OH dissociates only slightly into very few ions and conducts weakly.

mcqs.q: In cathodic protection against corrosion, what is connected to the iron?
options: A less active metal such as copper, which is oxidized instead of the iron
A coat of paint, which is oxidized instead of the iron
Stainless steel, which is oxidized instead of the iron
A more active metal such as magnesium or zinc, which is oxidized instead of the iron
mcqs.why: In cathodic protection a more active metal like magnesium or zinc is attached to iron. It loses electrons and is oxidized in place of the iron, so the iron is protected from corrosion.

mcqs.q: What is the overall reaction in Nelson's cell?
mcqs.why: In Nelson's cell brine is electrolysed: H+ is reduced to H2 at the cathode, Cl- is oxidized to Cl2 at the anode, and Na+ combines with OH- to form NaOH, giving the stated overall reaction.

mcqs.q: What is the oxidation number of phosphorus in PBr3?
mcqs.why: PBr3 is neutral, so the sum of oxidation numbers = 0. Each Br is -1. Let phosphorus = x. Step 1: x + 3(-1) = 0. Step 2: x - 3 = 0. Step 3: x = +3. So phosphorus in PBr3 is +3, and each Br is -1.

mcqs.q: Why is O2 necessary for rusting of iron?
options: Oxygen dissolves the iron surface as an acid
Oxygen removes moisture from the iron surface
Rusting is oxidation of iron, and iron combines with oxygen in the presence of water to form rust
Rusting takes place only when oxygen is absent
mcqs.why: Rust is hydrated ferric oxide, Fe2O3.xH2O, formed when iron is oxidized by oxygen in the presence of water. At cathodic sites 2H2O + O2 + 4e- -> 4OH-, so without oxygen there is no rusting.

lessons.title: Detailed Answers
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • Electroplating deposits a thin metal layer for protection, repair and decoration.
  • In electroplating the object is the cathode and the pure coating metal is the anode.
  • Oxidation is addition of oxygen, loss of hydrogen, loss of electrons, or increase in oxidation number.
  • Reduction is removal of oxygen, addition of hydrogen, gain of electrons, or decrease in oxidation number.
  • A voltaic cell converts chemical energy into electrical energy; an electrolytic cell does the reverse.
  • In a voltaic cell the anode is negative; in an electrolytic cell the anode is positive.
  • Sodium is extracted by electrolysis of molten NaCl in the Down cell.
  • Electrolytic refining gives copper up to 99.99 percent pure; Au and Ag collect as anode sludge.

Solved Exercises

Exercise — Long Questions

Q: I. a. What is electroplating?

Ans: Electroplating is an electrolytic process in which a thin layer of one metal is deposited on another metal surface. The metal ion is reduced by passing electricity, and a solid metal is deposited on the surface. The purposes of electroplating are: (i) Protection — to protect the inner metal from atmospheric effects and corrosion, e.g. Ni and Cr are deposited over iron to prevent it from corrosion. (ii) Repair — to weld the broken parts of machinery by depositing metal on them. (iii) Decoration — to deposit noble metals like gold and silver on inferior metals to enhance their beauty. Examples are electroplating of tin, zinc and chromium on steel.

Q: I. b. Distinguish between the nature of the anode and cathode in such a process.

Ans: In electroplating, the object to be electroplated is made the cathode, while a sheet or rod of the pure metal to be deposited is made the anode. The cathode is the object itself: it is first cleaned with sand, washed with caustic soda (NaOH) and thoroughly washed with water, and it is connected to the negative terminal of the battery. Metal ions from the solution are discharged and deposited on it as a thin layer. The anode is made of the pure coating metal and is connected to the positive terminal of the battery. When current is passed, the anode dissolves and is converted into ions, which replace the ions deposited at the cathode, so the concentration of the electrolyte (a salt solution of the respective metal) remains almost unchanged. For example, in tin plating: at anode Sn(s) → Sn2+(aq) + 2e-; at cathode Sn2+(aq) + 2e- → Sn(s).

Q: II. Differentiate between the processes of oxidation and reduction. Write an equation to illustrate each.

Ans: Oxidation is: (a) the addition of oxygen to a substance, (b) the removal of hydrogen or other electropositive element from a substance, (c) the removal (loss) of electron(s) from a substance, and (d) an increase in oxidation number. Example: C + O2 → CO2 (carbon is oxidized by addition of oxygen); also Fe2+ → Fe3+ + e- (loss of electron). Reduction is: (a) the removal of oxygen from a substance, (b) the addition of hydrogen to a substance, (c) the addition (gain) of electron(s) by a substance, and (d) a decrease in oxidation number. Example: 2HgO —Heat→ 2Hg + O2 (HgO is reduced by removal of oxygen); also Sn4+ + 2e- → Sn2+ (gain of electrons). Oxidation and reduction always take place simultaneously in a redox reaction, and the electrons lost in oxidation equal the electrons gained in reduction.

Q: III. a. What is corrosion? Explain rusting of iron as an example of corrosion.

Ans: Corrosion is the slow and continuous eating away (deterioration) of a metal by the environment or surroundings, i.e. the deterioration of a substance or its properties because of a reaction with its environment. It is a naturally occurring spontaneous oxidation-reduction process which takes place by the action of air in the presence of moisture, and it drives the material to its lowest possible energy state. Rusting of iron is its most common example. Iron combines with oxygen in the presence of water to form brown hydrated ferric oxide, Fe2O3.xH2O (rust). Dents and stains act as anodic sites: at the anode 2Fe(s) → 2Fe2+(aq) + 4e-. The electrons move through the metal to oxygen-rich sites which act as cathode: 2H2O + O2 + 4e- → 4OH-. Fe2+ is further oxidized by atmospheric oxygen to Fe3+ (Fe2+(aq) → Fe3+(aq) + e-), and Fe3+(aq) + 3OH-(aq) → Fe(OH)3(s), the rust. The rust mass is soft and porous, so it cannot prevent further atmospheric action and corrosion continues.

Q: III. b. Differentiate between electrolytic cell and voltaic cell.

Ans: Voltaic (galvanic) cell: (1) It converts chemical energy into electrical energy. (2) The redox reaction is spontaneous and is responsible for the production of electrical energy. (3) The two half-cells are set up in different containers, connected through a salt bridge or porous partition; a salt bridge is required. (4) The anode is the negative electrode and the cathode is the positive electrode. (5) The electrons are supplied by the species getting oxidized; they move from anode to cathode through the external circuit. Electrolytic cell: (1) It converts electrical energy into chemical energy. (2) The redox reaction is non-spontaneous and electrical energy has to be supplied to initiate the reaction. (3) Both electrodes are placed in the same container in the solution or molten electrolyte; no salt bridge is required. (4) The anode is the positive electrode and the cathode is the negative electrode. (5) The external battery supplies the electrons; they enter through the cathode and come out through the anode. In both cells, oxidation takes place at the anode and reduction at the cathode.

Q: III. c. Discuss the method of recovering/extracting of metal from its ore.

Ans: Reactive metals and pure metals are recovered from their ores/compounds by electrolysis in an electrolytic cell, because their chemical reactions do not occur spontaneously. (1) Extraction of sodium: sodium metal is obtained commercially by electrolysis of molten sodium chloride in the Down cell. Molten NaCl ionizes: 2NaCl(l) → 2Na+(l) + 2Cl-(l). At the cathode (reduction): 2Na+(l) + 2e- → 2Na(l). At the anode (oxidation): 2Cl-(l) → Cl2(g) + 2e-. Overall: 2NaCl(fused) → 2Na(l) + Cl2(g). The graphite anode and the circular copper/iron cathode are separated by an iron screen so that sodium and chlorine are kept apart and collected separately. (2) Refining of copper (electrolytic purification): large blocks of blister (impure) copper are suspended as anode in copper sulphate (CuSO4) and sulphuric acid solution between thin sheets of pure copper which act as cathode, at 50°C and about 0.3 volts. At the anode (oxidation): Cu(s) → Cu2+(aq) + 2e-. At the cathode (reduction): Cu2+(aq) + 2e- → Cu(s). More active impurities like Zn and Fe also dissolve, while less active precious metals like Au and Ag remain undissolved and settle at the bottom as 'anode sludge', from which they are recovered. By electrolytic refining, up to 99.99% pure copper is obtained.

Q: V. Discuss the preparation of Sodium Hydroxide (NaOH) from Brine along with diagram and reactions at cathode and anode. (Describe the diagram in words.)

Ans: Sodium hydroxide is prepared by the electrolysis of a concentrated aqueous solution of sodium chloride, NaCl (brine), in a special apparatus called the Nelson cell. Description of the diagram: Draw a steel tank containing saturated brine. Inside it hangs a U-shaped perforated steel tube which acts as the cathode; the tube is coated (lined) with porous asbestos, which separates the anode from the cathode. A graphite rod suspended in the U-shaped tube acts as the anode (positive). Show an inlet for brine at the top, a chlorine outlet near the anode at the top, a hydrogen outlet near the cathode, a steam inlet at the side, and a catch basin placed under the U-shaped tube where sodium hydroxide collects. Reactions: Ionization: 2NaCl(aq) → 2Na+(aq) + 2Cl-(aq); H2O(l) ⇌ H+(aq) + OH-(aq). When the electrodes are connected to the battery, Na+ and H+ move towards the cathode. H+ has a greater tendency to pick up electrons than Na+, so at the cathode (reduction): 2H+(aq) + 2e- → 2H(aq), and H + H → H2(g); hydrogen gas is collected at the hydrogen outlet. The Na+ ions are not reduced; they combine with OH- ions present in the solution: 2Na+(aq) + 2OH-(aq) → 2NaOH(aq), which is collected in the catch basin. At the anode (oxidation), Cl- ions give electrons to the electrode: 2Cl-(aq) → 2Cl(g) + 2e-, and Cl + Cl → Cl2(g); chlorine is collected at the chlorine outlet. Overall reaction: 2NaCl(aq) + 2H2O(l) → 2NaOH(aq) + H2(g) + Cl2(g). Thus hydrogen, chlorine and sodium hydroxide are produced at the same time.

mcqs.q: What is the main purpose of electroplating iron with nickel or chromium?
options: To protect the iron from atmospheric effects and corrosion
To convert the iron into an alloy throughout
To make the iron a better insulator
mcqs.why: Electroplating deposits a thin layer of a metal such as nickel or chromium over iron. This layer shields the inner iron from air and moisture and so protects it from corrosion; plating is also used for repair and decoration.

mcqs.q: In electroplating, which electrode is the object to be plated?
options: The anode, connected to the positive terminal
The anode, connected to the negative terminal
The cathode, connected to the positive terminal
The cathode, connected to the negative terminal
mcqs.why: The object to be electroplated is made the cathode and joined to the negative terminal. Metal ions are discharged and deposited on it, while the anode is a sheet of the pure coating metal joined to the positive terminal.

mcqs.q: Which change is an example of oxidation?
options: Addition of hydrogen to a substance
mcqs.why: Oxidation is loss of electrons or an increase in oxidation number. In Fe2+ -> Fe3+ + e- an electron is lost and the oxidation number rises, so it is oxidation; the other choices show gain of electrons or loss of oxygen, which is reduction.

mcqs.q: Which change is an example of reduction?
options: C + O2 -> CO2, where carbon gains oxygen
Loss of electrons from a substance
mcqs.why: Reduction is gain of electrons or a decrease in oxidation number. Sn4+ gains 2 electrons to form Sn2+ and its oxidation number falls from +4 to +2, so this is reduction.

mcqs.q: What is rust, formed during corrosion of iron?
mcqs.why: Corrosion slowly eats away a metal by reaction with its environment. Iron reacts with oxygen in the presence of water to form brown hydrated ferric oxide, Fe2O3.xH2O, which is called rust.

mcqs.q: How does a voltaic cell differ from an electrolytic cell in energy conversion?
options: A voltaic cell converts chemical energy into electrical energy, while an electrolytic cell converts electrical energy into chemical energy
A voltaic cell converts electrical energy into chemical energy, while an electrolytic cell does the reverse
Both cells convert heat energy into electrical energy
Both cells convert chemical energy into electrical energy
mcqs.why: In a voltaic cell a spontaneous redox reaction produces electrical energy. In an electrolytic cell electrical energy from a battery is supplied to drive a non-spontaneous redox reaction, so the conversions are opposite.

mcqs.q: What are the signs of the anode in a voltaic cell and in an electrolytic cell?
options: Positive in a voltaic cell and negative in an electrolytic cell
Negative in both types of cell
Positive in both types of cell
Negative in a voltaic cell and positive in an electrolytic cell
mcqs.why: In a voltaic cell the anode, where oxidation occurs, is the negative electrode and the cathode is positive. In an electrolytic cell the battery makes the anode positive and the cathode negative, though oxidation is still at the anode.

mcqs.q: In the Down cell, what happens at the cathode during extraction of sodium?
mcqs.why: Molten NaCl ionizes into Na+ and Cl- ions. At the cathode the Na+ ions gain electrons and are reduced to sodium metal, 2Na+ + 2e- -> 2Na, while Cl- ions are oxidized to Cl2 at the anode.

mcqs.q: During electrolytic refining of copper, where do gold and silver impurities go?
options: They remain undissolved and settle at the bottom as anode sludge
They dissolve and deposit on the cathode with the copper
They escape as gases from the anode
They dissolve and stay in the solution forever
mcqs.why: Impure copper is the anode and pure copper sheets are the cathode. Less active precious metals like gold and silver do not dissolve; they fall below the anode as anode sludge, and copper of up to 99.99 percent purity collects at the cathode.

mcqs.q: In the Nelson cell, which gas is collected at the anode?
mcqs.why: At the graphite anode of the Nelson cell, chloride ions lose electrons: 2Cl- -> 2Cl + 2e- and Cl + Cl -> Cl2, so chlorine is collected at the anode. Hydrogen is collected at the cathode and NaOH collects in the catch basin.

lessons.title: Project Work
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • Lead-acid batteries are cheap and recyclable but heavy, with low energy per kg and short life.
  • Nickel-metal hydride batteries store more energy and last long but are costly and lose charge on standing.
  • Lithium-ion batteries have the highest energy per kg, light weight, long range and fast charging, so they are most used in electric cars.
  • Solid-state batteries are expected to be safer and store more energy but are not yet available on a large commercial scale.
  • A battery is a group of galvanic cells joined in series that supplies electrical energy wherever it is needed.

Solved Exercises

Project Work

Q: Investigate the types of batteries being considered for electric cars. Write a report on the advantages and disadvantages of these types of batteries.

Ans: Report (summary): The main types of batteries considered for electric cars are: (1) Lead-acid batteries — advantages: cheap, well-known technology, easily recycled; disadvantages: very heavy, low energy stored per kg, short life, so the driving range is small. (2) Nickel-metal hydride (Ni-MH) batteries — advantages: more energy than lead-acid, long life, safe; disadvantages: costly, heavy, lose charge on standing, used mostly in hybrid cars. (3) Lithium-ion (Li-ion) batteries — advantages: highest energy per kg, light weight, long driving range, long life and fast charging, so they are the most widely used in electric cars; disadvantages: expensive, need electronic protection, capacity falls slowly with time and they can overheat if damaged. (4) Solid-state batteries (under development) — advantages: expected to be safer, lighter and store even more energy; disadvantages: still costly and not yet available on a large commercial scale. Conclusion: at present lithium-ion batteries are the best choice for electric cars because a group or combination of galvanic cells joined in series (a battery) must supply a limited amount of electrical energy wherever it is needed, and Li-ion packs do this with the least weight.

lessons.title: Multiple Choice Questions
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • Bromine is the non-metal that is liquid at room temperature.
  • Halogens react with metals to form halides.
  • Alkali metals are strong reducing agents.
  • Among alkali metals, lithium has the highest ionization potential.
  • Iodine is the halogen present in solid form.
  • Tendency of a metal to lose electrons is called electropositivity.
  • The word alkali means ashes, and CaO is a basic oxide.

Solved Exercises

Exercise — Choose the Correct Option

Q: i. Bromine is a non-metal in:

Options: (a) Solid state (b) Liquid state (c) Gaseous state (d) Plasma state

Correct answer: Liquid state

Q: ii. Halogens react with metals to form:

Options: (a) Halides (b) Oxides (c) Halogen sulphides (d) Hydrogenated compounds

Correct answer: Halides

Q: iii. Alkali metals are:

Options: (a) Oxidising agents (b) Dehydrating agents (c) Reducing agents (d) All the above

Correct answer: Reducing agents

Q: iv. Among the alkali metals the metal with the highest ionization potential is:

Options: (a) Na (b) Li (c) Rb (d) Cs

Correct answer: Li

Q: v. The halogen present in the solid form is:

Options: (a) Chlorine (b) Fluorine (c) Iodine (d) Bromine

Correct answer: Iodine

Q: vi. Tendency of a metal to lose electrons is called:

Options: (a) Electronegativity (b) Electropositivity (c) Electroplating (d) Electrolysis

Correct answer: Electropositivity

Q: vii. The word Alkali means:

Options: (a) Base (b) Basic salt (c) Acid (d) Ashes

Correct answer: Ashes

Q: viii. The oxide of calcium CaO is:

Options: (a) Acidic (b) Basic (c) Amphoteric (d) Neutral

Correct answer: Basic

Q: ix. Which one of the following is not an alkali metal?

Options: (a) Francium (b) Cesium (c) Rubidium (d) Radium

Correct answer: Radium

Q: x. Group IIA elements are named as Alkaline Earth Metals because:

Options: (a) Their oxides are basic (b) Their oxides and hydroxides are water soluble (c) They are found in earth. (d) All of these

Correct answer: All of these

mcqs.q: i. Bromine is a non-metal in:
mcqs.why: Bromine is the only non-metal that exists as a liquid at room temperature. Chlorine and fluorine are gases and iodine is a solid, so bromine is correctly described as a liquid non-metal.

mcqs.q: ii. Halogens react with metals to form:
mcqs.why: Halogens gain one electron from metals and form ionic compounds called halides, such as sodium chloride. Oxides are formed with oxygen, not with halogens, so halides is correct.

mcqs.q: iii. Alkali metals are:
mcqs.why: Alkali metals readily lose their single valence electron and are themselves oxidized. By giving electrons to other substances they reduce them, so alkali metals act as reducing agents.

mcqs.q: iv. Among the alkali metals the metal with the highest ionization potential is:
mcqs.why: Ionization energy decreases down a group as atomic size increases. Lithium is at the top of Group IA, is the smallest alkali metal, and holds its electron most firmly, so it has the highest ionization potential.

mcqs.q: v. The halogen present in the solid form is:
mcqs.why: Iodine exists as a solid at room temperature. Fluorine and chlorine are gases and bromine is a liquid, so iodine is the halogen present in the solid form.

mcqs.q: vi. Tendency of a metal to lose electrons is called:
mcqs.why: Metals tend to lose electrons and form positive ions; this tendency is called electropositivity. Electronegativity is the opposite tendency, the attraction for electrons shown by non-metals.

mcqs.q: vii. The word Alkali means:
mcqs.why: The word alkali comes from a word meaning ashes, because alkalis were first obtained from the ashes of plants. Group IA metals are therefore called alkali metals.

mcqs.q: viii. The oxide of calcium CaO is:
mcqs.why: Calcium is a metal, and metal oxides are basic in nature. CaO reacts with water to form the alkali calcium hydroxide, which confirms that calcium oxide is a basic oxide.

mcqs.q: ix. Which one of the following is not an alkali metal?
mcqs.why: Francium, cesium and rubidium all belong to Group IA, the alkali metals. Radium belongs to Group IIA, the alkaline earth metals, so radium is not an alkali metal.

mcqs.q: x. Group IIA elements are named as Alkaline Earth Metals because:
options: Their oxides and hydroxides are water soluble
Their oxides are basic, their oxides and hydroxides are soluble in water, and they are found in the earth
mcqs.why: Group IIA elements are called alkaline earth metals for the combined reasons: their oxides are basic (alkaline), their oxides and hydroxides dissolve in water, and these elements are found in the earth.

lessons.title: Short Answers
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • Group IIA and the transition elements contain only metallic elements.
  • Alkali metals burn in oxygen to form oxides, e.g. 4Na + O2 -> 2Na2O; reactivity increases down the group.
  • Metals are lustrous, malleable, ductile, sonorous and good conductors of heat and electricity.
  • Sodium is a powerful reducing agent, e.g. 2Na + MgO -> Na2O + Mg.
  • Ionization energy decreases down a group because atomic size increases.
  • Pure gold is too soft for ornaments, so it is alloyed with copper, silver or platinum.
  • Chlorine with cold dilute NaOH gives NaCl and NaOCl: Cl2 + 2NaOH -> NaCl + NaOCl + H2O.
  • Halogen reactivity falls down the group in the order F > Cl > Br > I; chlorine is a greenish gas used to kill germs in swimming pools.

Solved Exercises

Exercise — Short Questions

Q: i. Identify at least two groups which contain only metallic elements.

Ans: Group IIA (the alkaline earth metals) contains only metals, and the d-block / transition elements are also all metals. Group IA except hydrogen, the lanthanides and the actinides likewise contain only metallic elements.

Q: ii. Write down the reaction of group-IA metals with oxygen, with balance equations.

Ans: Group IA (alkali) metals burn in oxygen to form their oxides. Lithium: 4Li(s) + O2(g) → 2Li2O(s), lithium oxide, a white solid. Sodium: 4Na(s) + O2(g) → 2Na2O(s), white sodium oxide. Potassium: 4K(s) + O2(g) → 2K2O(s), white potassium oxide. Reactivity increases down the group: lithium < sodium < potassium.

Q: iii. State the physical properties of metals.

Ans: Metals are generally solids at room temperature (except mercury, which is liquid), they have a metallic lustre, and they are good conductors of heat and electricity. They are malleable (can be beaten into sheets) and ductile (can be drawn into wires), they are sonorous, and most have high melting points, boiling points and densities.

Q: iv. How does sodium act as reducing agent and write down its reactions also?

Ans: Sodium readily loses its one valence electron and is itself oxidised, so it gives electrons to other substances and reduces them; it is therefore a powerful reducing agent. Examples given in the unit: 2Na(s) + MgO(s) → Na2O(s) + Mg(s), where sodium reduces magnesium oxide to magnesium, and 4Na(s) + TiCl4(l) → 4NaCl(s) + Ti(s), where sodium reduces titanium chloride to titanium metal.

Q: v. Ionization energy of alkaline earth metals is higher than alkali metals, why?

Ans: In the same period an alkaline earth metal has a smaller atomic radius and its nucleus carries one additional positive charge compared with the alkali metal, while its valence electrons are in the same shell (ns2 in place of ns1). The valence electrons are therefore held more firmly by the nucleus, so more energy is needed to remove an electron and the ionization energy is higher.

Q: vi. Pure gold is not used for ornaments, why?

Ans: Pure gold is too soft to resist the stresses applied to many jewellery items, so ornaments made of it would easily bend and wear out. It is therefore alloyed with other metals such as copper, silver and platinum, which increase its hardness and durability.

Q: vii. What are the uses of magnesium?

Ans: Magnesium is of low density, so it is used in light but tough alloys such as duralumin and magnalium, used in aircraft, cars and moving parts of machines. It is used in photographic flashlight powder, flames and fireworks, and as a deoxidant in metallurgy and in the extraction of titanium and uranium. Magnesium oxide (MgO) is mixed with clay to make refractory bricks for furnace lining, and magnesium sulphate (MgSO4) is used in the textile, paper, soap and pharmaceutical industries.

Q: viii. Write down the reaction of chlorine with sodium hydroxide with balance equation.

Ans: Chlorine reacts with (cold, dilute) sodium hydroxide solution to form sodium chloride and sodium hypochlorite (bleach) with water: Cl2(g) + 2NaOH(aq) → NaCl(aq) + NaOCl(aq) + H2O(l).

Q: ix. How does ionization energies values vary in group?

Ans: Ionization energy decreases on going down a group. Down the group a new shell is added in each period, so atomic size increases and the distance between the nucleus and the valence electrons increases. The valence electrons are then held less firmly and are removed more easily, so less energy is required.

Q: x. What happens during displacement reaction in halogens?

Ans: In a halogen displacement reaction a more reactive halogen displaces a less reactive halogen from a solution of its halide. The reactivity of the halogens decreases down the group, in the order F > Cl > Br > I, so for example chlorine displaces bromine from sodium bromide: 2NaBr(aq) + Cl2(g) → 2NaCl(aq) + Br2(l). The displacing halogen is reduced to its halide ions and the displaced halide ions are oxidised to the free halogen.

Test Yourself (p.245)

Q: A. Describe and explain what will happen when bromine water is added to potassium iodide solution. Br2(aq) + 2KI(aq) → I2(aq) + ______

Ans: The missing product is 2KBr(aq), so the completed equation is: Br2(aq) + 2KI(aq) → I2(aq) + 2KBr(aq). Bromine is more reactive than iodine, so it displaces iodine from potassium iodide in a displacement reaction. The iodine formed turns the solution brown/dark in colour.

Q: B. Infer the identity of an element. (i) Element found in period 3. (ii) Will displace iodine from sodium iodide. (iii) Greenish gas, which is denser than air. (iv) Used in swimming pool to kill germs.

Ans: The element is chlorine (Cl). Chlorine is in period 3 of the periodic table, it is a greenish gas denser than air, it is more reactive than iodine so it displaces iodine from sodium iodide, and it is used in swimming pools to kill germs.

Activity 8.2 (p.244)

Q: Activity 8.2: Make a list of elements which are found in uncombined state in nature.

Ans: Elements found in the uncombined (free/native) state in nature are the unreactive ones, for example gold (Au), platinum (Pt), silver (Ag) and copper (Cu) among metals, and noble gases such as argon, as well as carbon (as diamond/graphite) and sulphur among non-metals. They occur free because they are very unreactive and do not easily combine with other elements.

mcqs.q: Which group contains only metallic elements?
options: Group IIA, the alkaline earth metals
mcqs.why: Every element of Group IIA is a metal, and the d-block transition elements are also all metals. The halogens, noble gases and Group VIA contain non-metals, so Group IIA is the group of only metals.

mcqs.q: What is formed when sodium burns in oxygen?
mcqs.why: Group IA metals burn in oxygen to form their oxides. Sodium gives white sodium oxide, 4Na + O2 -> 2Na2O, just as lithium gives Li2O and potassium gives K2O, with reactivity increasing down the group.

mcqs.q: Which set describes the physical properties of metals?
options: Lustrous, malleable, ductile, sonorous and good conductors of heat and electricity
Dull, brittle, non-conductors of heat and electricity
Always gases at room temperature with low densities
Neither malleable nor ductile and poor conductors
mcqs.why: Metals have a metallic lustre, can be beaten into sheets (malleable) and drawn into wires (ductile), are sonorous, and conduct heat and electricity well. Most are solids with high melting points and densities; mercury is the liquid exception.

mcqs.q: How does sodium act as a reducing agent towards magnesium oxide?
options: Na(s) + MgO(s) -> NaMg(s) + O2(g); sodium is oxidized by oxygen gas
2Na(s) + MgO(s) -> Na2O(s) + Mg(s); sodium gives electrons and reduces MgO to Mg
Sodium does not react with magnesium oxide
mcqs.why: Sodium readily loses its valence electron and is itself oxidized, so it reduces other substances. It reduces magnesium oxide to magnesium, 2Na + MgO -> Na2O + Mg, and also reduces TiCl4 to titanium metal.

mcqs.q: Why is the ionization energy of alkaline earth metals higher than that of alkali metals in the same period?
options: They have a larger atomic radius, so valence electrons are held more firmly
They have one less nuclear charge in the same period
They have a smaller atomic radius and one extra nuclear charge, so valence electrons are held more firmly
Their valence electrons are in a shell farther from the nucleus
mcqs.why: An alkaline earth metal has one more proton and a smaller radius than the alkali metal of the same period, while its ns2 electrons are in the same shell. They are held more firmly, so more energy is needed to remove an electron.

mcqs.q: Why is pure gold not used for making ornaments?
options: Pure gold is too soft and would easily bend and wear out
Pure gold is too hard and cannot be shaped
Pure gold reacts quickly with air and rusts
Pure gold is a poor conductor of electricity
mcqs.why: Pure gold is too soft to resist the stresses applied to jewellery, so ornaments of pure gold would bend and wear out easily. It is alloyed with copper, silver or platinum to increase its hardness and durability.

mcqs.q: Why is magnesium used in aircraft and car parts?
options: It has very high density, which makes parts stronger
It is the cheapest metal available for industry
It does not react with oxygen at any temperature
It has low density and forms light but tough alloys such as duralumin and magnalium
mcqs.why: Magnesium is a light metal of low density. Its light but tough alloys, duralumin and magnalium, are used in aircraft, cars and moving machine parts; MgO is also used for refractory furnace bricks.

mcqs.q: What are the products when chlorine reacts with cold dilute sodium hydroxide?
options: NaCl(aq) + NaOCl(aq) + H2O(l), from Cl2(g) + 2NaOH(aq) -> NaCl(aq) + NaOCl(aq) + H2O(l)
mcqs.why: Chlorine reacts with cold dilute NaOH to form sodium chloride and sodium hypochlorite (bleach) with water, as shown by the balanced equation Cl2 + 2NaOH -> NaCl + NaOCl + H2O.

mcqs.q: How does ionization energy vary on going down a group?
options: It decreases, because atomic size increases and valence electrons are held less firmly
It increases, because atomic size increases down the group
It stays exactly the same for every element in the group
It first increases and then becomes zero
mcqs.why: Down a group a new shell is added in each period, so the atom grows and the valence electrons move farther from the nucleus. They are held less firmly and removed more easily, so ionization energy decreases.

mcqs.q: What happens when bromine water is added to potassium iodide solution?
options: No reaction takes place because bromine is less reactive than iodine
Bromine displaces iodine: Br2(aq) + 2KI(aq) -> I2(aq) + 2KBr(aq), and the solution turns brown
Potassium reacts violently with the water
mcqs.why: Bromine is more reactive than iodine, so it displaces iodine from potassium iodide in a displacement reaction. The freed iodine turns the solution brown, and potassium bromide is the other product.

lessons.title: Detailed Answers
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • Alkali metals have one valence electron (ns1) and form M+ ions; alkaline earth metals have two (ns2) and form M2+ ions.
  • Alkali metals are softer, lighter and more reactive, with lower melting points than alkaline earth metals.
  • Soft metals like sodium can be cut with a knife and are stored in kerosene; hard metals like iron have high melting point and tensile strength.
  • Magnesium forms MgH2 with H2, MgCl2 and H2 with HCl, MgO with O2, and MgCl2 with Cl2.
  • Very reactive elements such as sodium and calcium occur only in combined states; unreactive gold and platinum occur free.
  • A metal loses electrons to form a cation; a non-metal gains electrons to form an anion.
  • Metals form basic oxides and ionic chlorides; non-metals form acidic oxides and covalent chlorides.

Solved Exercises

Exercise — Long Questions

Q: I. Compare and contrasts the properties of alkali and alkaline earth metals, with reactions.

Ans: Similarities: both are electropositive metals found only in the combined state in nature because they are very reactive; both lose their valence electrons to form positive ions and ionic compounds, act as reducing agents, and form basic oxides. Differences: alkali metals (Group IA) have one valence electron (ns1) and form M+ ions, while alkaline earth metals (Group IIA) have two valence electrons (ns2) and form M2+ ions. Alkali metals have lower ionization energies, so they are more reactive, softer, and lighter, with lower melting and boiling points; alkaline earth metals have higher ionization energies, are harder and denser, and have higher melting and boiling points. Reactions: with oxygen, 4Na + O2 → 2Na2O and 2Mg + O2 → 2MgO (on heating); with water, 2Na + 2H2O → 2NaOH + H2 (vigorous), while magnesium reacts only slowly with cold water; with chlorine, 2Na + Cl2 → 2NaCl and Mg + Cl2 → MgCl2.

Q: II. a. Differentiate between hard and soft metals.

Ans: Soft metals, such as the Group IA and IIA metals like sodium, are very reactive, have low ionization energies and are very electropositive; sodium is so soft it can be cut with a knife, its atoms are held together by weak metallic bonds, it has a low melting point (97.6°C), low density (0.972 g/cm3), low tensile strength, and it is so reactive that it is stored in kerosene oil. Hard metals, such as the less reactive transition metals like iron and copper, have high ionization energies and are less electropositive; iron is hard, tough and strong because of strong metallic bonding, has a high melting point (1538°C), high density (7.87 g/cm3) and high tensile strength, so it is used in the construction of buildings and bridges and to prepare steel, and it is less reactive than sodium.

Q: II. b. Give the reaction of magnesium with, (i) H2 (ii) HCl (iii) O2 (iv) H2O (v) Cl2

Ans: (i) With hydrogen, on heating magnesium combines directly to form magnesium hydride: Mg(s) + H2(g) → MgH2(s). (ii) With hydrochloric acid it liberates hydrogen gas: Mg(s) + 2HCl(aq) → MgCl2(aq) + H2(g). (iii) With oxygen it burns with a dazzling flame to form magnesium oxide (magnesia): 2Mg(s) + O2(g) → 2MgO(s). (iv) With water (steam/hot water) it forms magnesium hydroxide/oxide and liberates hydrogen: Mg(s) + 2H2O(l) → Mg(OH)2(aq) + H2(g). (v) With chlorine it forms magnesium chloride: Mg(s) + Cl2(g) → MgCl2(s).

Q: III. Discuss the reasons why some elements exist as free elements in nature while other occurs in combined states as compounds. Give two examples of each type.

Ans: Whether an element occurs free depends on its reactivity. Elements that are very reactive readily combine with oxygen, water and other elements around them, so they are never found free and occur only in combined states as compounds; examples are sodium, found as sodium chloride in sea water and rock salt, and calcium, found as calcium carbonate (CaCO3) in limestone, marble and chalk (magnesium and the halogens are other examples). Elements that are unreactive (inert/noble) have high ionization energies and do not readily combine with other elements, so they survive in nature in the free, uncombined state; examples are gold and platinum (silver and copper are other examples of metals found free).

Q: IV. Define metal and non-metal and compare the properties (both physical and chemical) of metals and non-metals.

Ans: A metal is an element that loses electrons and forms a cation, e.g. sodium loses an electron to form Na+; metals are electropositive. A non-metal is an element that gains electrons and forms an anion, e.g. chlorine gains an electron to form Cl-; non-metals are electronegative. Physical comparison: metals are good conductors of heat and electricity, are malleable and ductile, and are usually solids at room temperature (except Hg); non-metals are poor conductors of heat and electricity (except graphite), are neither malleable nor ductile, and are often gases, with a few solids and one liquid, bromine. Chemical comparison: metals are electron donors and reducing agents, they become positively charged ions in solution, some can replace hydrogen from acids to form salts, they form basic oxides whose soluble forms give alkalis in water, they form electrovalent (ionic) chlorides, and they do not combine easily with hydrogen. Non-metals are electron acceptors and oxidising agents, they become negatively charged ions in solution, they cannot replace hydrogen from acids, they form mainly acidic oxides which dissolve in water to form acids, they form covalent chlorides, and they combine easily with hydrogen to form many stable covalent hydrides.

Q: V. Halogens are very reactive elements, write down halogen's reactions with hydrogen, oxygen, metals, non-metals and other compounds.

Ans: Halogens are very reactive because they need only one electron to complete their octet; reactivity decreases from fluorine to iodine. With hydrogen they form the respective hydrides: H2(g) + F2(g) → 2HF(l) (fluorine reacts violently), H2(g) + Cl2(g) → 2HCl(g) (in sunlight), H2(g) + Br2(l) → 2HBr(g) (on heating), and H2(g) + I2(s) ⇌ 2HI(g) (iodine reacts reversibly). With oxygen, fluorine forms fluorine monoxide and dioxide: O2(g) + 2F2(g) → 2OF2(g) and O2(g) + F2(g) → O2F2(g), while other halogens form oxides such as dichlorine heptoxide (Cl2O7), tribromine tetraoxide (Br3O4) and iodine pentoxide (I2O5). With metals they form the corresponding ionic halides, e.g. Cu(s) + Br2(l) → CuBr2(s) and 2K(s) + I2(s) → 2KI(s). With non-metals they form respective covalent halides, e.g. with phosphorus they form tri- and penta-halides: 2P(s) + 3Cl2(g) → 2PCl3(aq), 2P(s) + 3Br2(l) → 2PBr3(aq), 2P(s) + 5Cl2(g) → 2PCl5(aq) and 2P(s) + 5Br2(l) → 2PBr5(aq). With other compounds they act as oxidising agents and are themselves reduced: H2S(aq) + Cl2(g) → 2HCl(aq) + S(s) and 2NH3(aq) + 3Cl2(g) → 6HCl(aq) + N2(g); chlorine reacts with lime water, Ca(OH)2, to form bleaching powder: Ca(OH)2(aq) + Cl2(g) → CaOCl2(aq) + H2O(l).

mcqs.q: How do alkali metals and alkaline earth metals differ in valence electrons and ions formed?
options: Alkali metals have two valence electrons and form M2+ ions; alkaline earth metals have one and form M+ ions
Alkali metals have one valence electron (ns1) and form M+ ions; alkaline earth metals have two (ns2) and form M2+ ions
Both groups have one valence electron and form M+ ions
Both groups gain electrons and form negative ions
mcqs.why: Group IA metals have the ns1 configuration and lose one electron to form M+ ions. Group IIA metals have ns2 and lose two electrons to form M2+ ions. This is the basic difference between the two families.

mcqs.q: Which statement correctly compares the reactivity of alkali and alkaline earth metals?
options: Alkaline earth metals are more reactive because they have lower ionization energies
Both families are equally reactive in every reaction
Alkali metals are less reactive because they are softer
Alkali metals are more reactive because they have lower ionization energies
mcqs.why: Alkali metals have lower ionization energies, so they lose electrons more easily and are more reactive, softer and lighter. Alkaline earth metals have higher ionization energies and are harder, denser and less reactive.

mcqs.q: Which property shows that sodium is a soft metal?
options: It is so soft it can be cut with a knife and is stored in kerosene oil
It has a melting point of 1538 C and high tensile strength
It is used in the construction of buildings and bridges
It is hard, tough and strong due to strong metallic bonding
mcqs.why: Sodium is a soft metal with weak metallic bonding, a low melting point of 97.6 C and low density. It can be cut with a knife and, being very reactive, is stored in kerosene oil; iron shows the opposite, hard-metal properties.

mcqs.q: What happens when magnesium reacts with hydrochloric acid?
options: Mg(s) + 2HCl(aq) -> MgH2(s) + Cl2(g); chlorine gas is liberated
Magnesium does not react with hydrochloric acid
Mg(s) + 2HCl(aq) -> MgCl2(aq) + H2(g); hydrogen gas is liberated
mcqs.why: Magnesium is a reactive metal that reacts with dilute hydrochloric acid to form magnesium chloride solution and hydrogen gas, as shown by Mg + 2HCl -> MgCl2 + H2.

mcqs.q: What is formed when magnesium is heated with hydrogen?
mcqs.why: On heating, magnesium combines directly with hydrogen to form magnesium hydride, Mg + H2 -> MgH2. The other equations are its reactions with oxygen, water and chlorine respectively.

mcqs.q: Why does sodium occur only in the combined state in nature?
options: It is very reactive and readily combines with oxygen, water and other elements around it
It has a very high ionization energy and never reacts
It is a noble element with a complete octet
It is found only as a free metal in sea water
mcqs.why: Very reactive elements combine quickly with oxygen, water and other substances, so they are never found free. Sodium occurs combined as sodium chloride in sea water and rock salt, and calcium occurs as CaCO3 in limestone and marble.

mcqs.q: Which pair of elements is found free (uncombined) in nature because they are unreactive?
mcqs.why: Unreactive elements with high ionization energies do not readily combine with other elements, so they survive free in nature. Gold and platinum are such metals; silver and copper are other examples found in the free state.

mcqs.q: How is a metal defined in terms of electrons and ions?
options: A metal gains electrons and forms an anion, e.g. chlorine forms Cl-
A metal loses electrons and forms a cation, e.g. sodium forms Na+
A metal shares electrons and never forms ions
A metal is electronegative and accepts electrons
mcqs.why: A metal is an electropositive element that loses electrons to form a positive ion (cation); sodium loses one electron to form Na+. A non-metal is electronegative and gains electrons to form an anion, such as Cl-.

mcqs.q: How do the oxides of metals and non-metals differ?
options: Metals form basic oxides that give alkalis in water; non-metals form mainly acidic oxides that give acids in water
Metals form acidic oxides; non-metals form basic oxides
Both metals and non-metals form only neutral oxides
Metal oxides never react with water at all
mcqs.why: Metals are electron donors and reducing agents that form basic oxides, whose soluble forms give alkalis in water. Non-metals are electron acceptors that form mainly acidic oxides, which dissolve in water to form acids.

mcqs.q: Why are halogens very reactive, and how does their reactivity change down the group?
options: They need seven electrons to complete the octet, and reactivity increases down the group
They have complete octets, and reactivity stays the same down the group
They need only one electron to complete the octet, and reactivity decreases from fluorine to iodine
They lose one electron easily, like alkali metals
mcqs.why: Halogens have seven valence electrons and need just one more to complete the octet, so they are very reactive oxidising agents. Reactivity decreases from fluorine to iodine, e.g. H2 + Cl2 -> 2HCl takes place in sunlight.
